# Setup | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/intro/setup.md)
.

These labs utilize containerlab. You will need a Linux server that has containerlab installed, and the proper images loaded into your local docker repo. This page walks you through that process.

I found containerlab to be preferential over EVE-NG or CML for many reasons:

*   Support for containers such as XRd, 8000e, and Routinator.
    
*   Topology files and config files can be shared and version-controlled via github.
    
*   Native SSH access is used to access the nodes, instead of console connections. This allows for scripting via SSH, which I use to transfer all startup configs to the nodes.
    
*   Virtual hard drives of the nodes are not saved, so a single lab can take up literally KBs of storage.
    

Host Requirements[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs#host-requirements)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

You can install containerlab on a VM or bare-metal server. I prefer to use Ubuntu as the OS, but any Linux distro should work.

I recommend to have 16+ vCPU, 128GB+ memory, and 50-100GB of storage. The storage is mostly for the node images, so storage requirements are quite low.

If you are using bare-metal, ensure that CPU virtualization is enabled in BIOS on your server.

If using a VM, ensure that Hardware virtualization is enabled.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FjU5TwC4v1hrPtt2pqwUL%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7d90ae77-f8f9-41be-b2b1-966d64274c8f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1cf6d46c13237d5c55da6e52331f4897&sv=3)

Installing Containerlab[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs#installing-containerlab)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Once the OS is installed, containerlab installation is as simple as running this single command:

Copy

    curl -sL https://containerlab.dev/setup | sudo -E bash -s "all"

*   Source: [https://containerlab.dev/quickstart/](https://containerlab.dev/quickstart/)
    

For XRd nodes, we must set the below setting on the containerlabs server. Reboot after running this command:

Copy

    echo -e "fs.inotify.max_user_instances=192000\nfs.inotify.max_user_watches=192000" | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.conf

*   Source: [https://containerlab.dev/manual/kinds/xrd/#host-server-requirements](https://containerlab.dev/manual/kinds/xrd/#host-server-requirements)
    

Clone the git repo for this workbook:

Copy

    git clone https://github.com/andrewohanian/ccie-spv5.1-labs.git

Install required python packages:

Copy

    sudo apt install python3-pip
    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    pip install -r requirements.txt

The managment network is 10.200.255.0/24 for these labs. All you need to do is create a route in your router pointing 10.200.255.0/24 via the IP address of your containerlab server. For example, if your containerlab server has an IP address of 192.168.1.253:

Copy

    ip route 10.200.255.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.1.253

I would suggest using MTPutty for your terminal manager, because I have already pre-loaded connection files for every lab in the git repo. Download MTPutty here: [https://ttyplus.com/multi-tabbed-putty/](https://ttyplus.com/multi-tabbed-putty/)

Images[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs#images)

-------------------------------------------------------------

Finally, you will need the correct images loaded into your docker container repo in order to run the topologies.

### vrnetlab Images[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs#vrnetlab-images)

For images such as CSR1000v and vIOS, I used vrnetlab to create docker containers out of the qcow2 images. It is as easy as cloning this git repo, placing the image in the associated directory, and running **make**. For example, see this page for CSR1000v: [https://github.com/srl-labs/vrnetlab/tree/master/cisco/csr1000v](https://github.com/srl-labs/vrnetlab/tree/master/cisco/csr1000v)

Copy

    git clone https://github.com/hellt/vrnetlab.git

The following images are needed, and were built with vrnetlab:

*   vrnetlab/cisco\_csr1000v:16.09.08
    
*   vrnetlab/cisco\_xrv:6.6.3
    
*   vrnetlab/cisco\_xrv:6.3.1
    
*   vrnetlab/cisco\_vios:15.9.3M3
    
*   vrnetlab/cisco\_iol:17.15.01
    

If you use other versions besides these, you will need to manually edit the topology files before you run them (changing the version). Additionally, it's possible the default logins might be different with different versions, so watch out for that.

### XRd[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs#xrd)

Cisco ios-xr/xrd-control-plane:7.9.2 is used. This is the XRd Control Plane, not XRd vRouter. It can be downloaded from Cisco here: [https://software.cisco.com/download/home/286331236/type/280805694/release/7.9.2](https://software.cisco.com/download/home/286331236/type/280805694/release/7.9.2)

Once you download the tar file, you can transfer it to your containerlab server via SCP. Then you must untar the file and load the image into docker:

Copy

    tar xzvf xrd-control-plane-container-x86.7.9.2.tgz
    sudo docker load -i xrd-control-plane-container-x64.dockerv1.tgz

XRd Control Plane is extremely useful for running very large topologies, because it has a very light footprint. Even though it is so lightweight, it is on par with XRv9K in terms of functionality. I used XRd for running large 40-50 node topologies before sitting for the lab.

### Arista switch[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs#arista-switch)

Arista cEOS 4.32.0F is used as a basic switch, which can be downloaded from Arista here: [https://www.arista.com/en/support/software-download](https://www.arista.com/en/support/software-download)

Transfer the cEOS64-\*.tar.xz file to the server, and then import it into docker:

Copy

    sudo docker import cEOS64-lab-4.32.0F.tar.xz ceos:4.32.0F

### Other containers[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs#other-containers)

Finally, there are linux containers for NSO, Ubuntu (used as an MDT collector), and Routinator. These can be pulled from public sources using:

Copy

    sudo docker image pull andrewohanian1/nso:6.1
    sudo docker image pull andrewohanian1/canonical_ubuntu:jammy
    sudo docker image pull nlnetlabs/routinator

If you need help with any of these images, just reach out to me and I will try to help.

# Purpose | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/purpose.md)
.

I created this lab workbook as a private study tool while working towards the CCIE-SPv5.1. Instead of creating notes during my studies, I created labs. Notes can be passively reread, but labs are a way of actively retesting, which I felt was _much_ more useful. It seemed a shame to just let these sit in my private notes, when others may be going down the same path as me and could benefit from having these exercises, so I am making these publicly available.

I started creating these labs because I had some trouble retaining knowledge as I went through my studies. For example, I might spend a few weeks on multicast, then a few weeks on VPLS, then a few weeks on RSVP-TE. As time went on, my multicast knowledge became less and less fresh. I felt like I was forgetting the details of what I learned 2+ months ago. When you consider that the CCIE takes more than a year to study for, I was very concerned with being able to retain knowledge throughout the journey.

My solution to this was to create my own lab exercises in the style of the INE RSv5 workbook, so that I could continually retest my knowledge throughout my studies. This helped in multiple ways. First, just the process of creating a lab exercise, writing the prompt, writing the solution, and explaining the solution, was a very useful study tool. If I can't explain how it works, then I don't understand it. Second, I could then easily go back to these lab exercises and quickly refresh my memory. My schedule would be something like this: Monday through Saturday I would work on a new topic and write labs on that topic. On Sunday, I would spend the day on a topic I went over previously and redo those labs.

This idea originally came from this: [https://nickccieprogress.blogspot.com/2019/01/method-post-using-anki-for-ccie.html](https://nickccieprogress.blogspot.com/2019/01/method-post-using-anki-for-ccie.html)

I actually began my CCIE-SP studies by going through INE's training for the old RSv5. I felt that I should get a very solid foundation on the IGPs, BGP, etc, before delving deep into more specific SP technologies. So for six months, I pretended like I was going for the old RSv5 exam.

Towards the end of my RSv5 studies, I used the Anki flashcard deck, which is mentioned in the link above. This flashcard deki was simply composed of one card per lab exercise. I did ~10 new cards per day, so I ended up doing maybe 10-20 cards every day. (Each day you see new cards, and also review old cards based on spaced repetition). I found this to be an amazing experience. Let's say there are 300 lab exercises in that workbook. Just doing each one of those a single time will teach you something, but you likely will not retain it. Going through these labs repeatedly, and focusing on the labs you are struggling with (which happens naturally based on Anki's spaced repetition), solidified those exercises for me. After maybe 2-3 months of drilling those labs, I may have done each one 10 times over. Not only did this help me retain knowledge, but it also naturally teached me how to complete these with speed. I didn't want to spend 4+ hours doing these every day, so I naturally started speeding up as I completed the exercises. Once I was done drilling the workbook exercises, I did a few of INE's mock RSv5 full scale labs, and then moved onto SP studies.

At the beginning of my CCIE-SP study phase, I quickly found that there was no good SP workbook. INE had an SPv4 workbook, but it was extremely minimal compared to their RSv5 workbook. Many of the tasks were a little too easy for me as well. (Simply enabling the IGP, enabling LDP, etc, was not super challenging). However, I did spend maybe a month starting with that workbook. The exercises were still worth doing, but not even close to being enough for the SPv5.1 exam.

Russo's SPv4 workbook is a goldmine. However, the way he is walking you through his lab was not as useful for me as the INE style, where there is a prompt and you must answer it on your own. Łukasz's workbook is also like this too. However, his workbook has the benefit that it is updated for SPv5. But I still didn't feel like it was enough. Therefore, I decided to just create my own lab exercises, using the INE style of: prompt, answer, and explanation. I felt that active study (actively solving lab tasks) was a much better use of time than passive study (reading and following along with someone else's lab).

I should mention that many of these exercises are quite difficult. Don't expect that you will know how to solve every lab at first glance. It may be that you simply want to "walk through" the labs at first to get a feel for them. Later you can come back and actually try to solve them on your own, to see what you retain. It also could be the case that the prompts are not clear enough. If so, I appologize, and I wouldn't be too surprised, as these were created only for myself, so I "knew what I meant" on some of these prompts. I welcome any suggestions to make edits to these. You can reach out to me on Linkedin here: [https://www.linkedin.com/in/andrew-ohanian-972928122/](https://www.linkedin.com/in/andrew-ohanian-972928122/)

I would not suggest using these labs as a _primary_ resource for learning the topics. I would use them to test your knowledge once you've learned a topic, or as "homework" while learning a topic. The resources mentioned here is a great starting point for general SPv5.1 studies: [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-KNqwRJFQs4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-KNqwRJFQs4)

Although, it very well could be the case that you can learn these topics primarily through this workbook. For example, the SR section is quite thorough and explains SR practically from the ground up. But I think you will find that the explanations in this workbook may not fully make sense without understanding the topic beforehand. I tried to make my explanations somewhat brief, because I was using this as a review tool, so I tried to make it as time-efficient as possible to review.

I also have a few full-scale lab exercises that I created during this process. I'm not sure how much use this workbook will get, so I have not bothered posting them here. It would be quite a bit of additional work. If there is enough interest, I'll consider posting them. But you will need to use the official practice labs from Cisco anyways before sitting for the lab. I would suggest doing the official practice lab tasks, and then letting that influence you in creating your _own_ full scale practice labs during your final preparation.

I also may consider creating some short video answers to selected workbook exercises in the future. But again, only if there is enough interest.

I sincerely hope that others find these lab exercises useful for their own studies.

# Containerlab Tips | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/containerlab-tips.md)
.

**docker image ls** displays your docker image repo:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F94bYzZP9gVxXewBZ0R2L%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D34f08681-50b3-453c-a0ca-f906e8ac0e74&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2bb0580a504f0f8051cd2c07768e1a4e&sv=3)

**docker container ls** displays running containers. Once your topology is finished launching, you should see all contianers as **healthy**. Occasionally, a node may fail to boot properly. In that case, I just stop the containerlab topology entirely and restart it.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FR7RTzUqoWKMFYthECNNo%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db1605102-26b3-4060-bed5-9afec8fb40e1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=fed7245378d29935eaf91fffc9407d44&sv=3)

You can use **docker logs clab-<topology name>-<node name> -f** to watch logs as a node boots up. For example:

In general, **telnet <mgmt ip> 5000** will allow you to access a node's console port. Use ctrl+\], **quit** to exit.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFrTQbvUCicFtDZFlVn6q%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da0448e98-3cec-45cf-9f00-7fc95de4d247&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2a0ecafe0c4ea50259b6db1a3366ebef&sv=3)

Ensure you have transfered config files to all nodes before running labs on XR nodes. If your config file does not exist on the node, you will commit and replace a blank config and lose access to the node. For example, if you enter 'y' here, you will lose access:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMffLzjWn9qO8mLL1Kgsa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D33c1194b-0dae-481b-81a6-d0768e6999f6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d26d1118d9cb55547e5a316c89f9840c&sv=3)

In MTPutty, you can use ctrl+tab and ctrl+shift+tab to navigate between tabs without a mouse.

I use **docker system prune** periodically to safely free up disk space. This clears out build cache and stopped containers.

**containerlab destroy -a** will destroy any running topology.

**containerlab inspect --all** will show all running topologies.

# Start | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/start.md)
.

These labs use INE's topology from their SPv4 workbook. Labs are influenced primarily from Cisco documentation, _OSPF and IS-IS_ by Jeff Doyle, and Russo's SPv4 workbook.

To begin, run the following command on your containerlab machine:

Copy

    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    containerlab deploy -t ine-spv4/ine-spv4.clab.yml --reconfigure

Once all nodes are started, run the following command to transfer the config files to all nodes. These files will be used to change between startup configs for subsequent labs.

Copy

    python3 transfer_configs_to_nodes.py

The script will prompt you for a directory name. Enter "ine-spv4".

Use the MTPutty session file located in **ine-spv4/ine-spv4\_putty\_sessions.xml** to quickly setup your SSH sessions to the nodes. Go to **Server - Import Tree** and browse for the file.

When you are done with the lab, use the following command to wipe it:

Copy

    containerlab destroy -t ine-spv4/ine-spv4.clab.yml

# Prefix Suppression | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-suppression.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure ISIS so that only the loopbacks are advertised into the IGP. Only use interface-level commands on R2 and XR2.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-suppression#id-61bb6e65-ca64-4ac6-974d-0d0f2d9877ac)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-suppression#id-1b38dde3-d4d1-80f1-a16e-c97ac2affaf7)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Previously, routers advertised their loopback (using the passive-interface Lo0 command) and their directly connected interface network on all interfaces that had ISIS activated:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5owbhsYbul3mdqXu6f03%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4c0a7560-551f-493a-913c-cafe5758084a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=492a95e2d90731d0ed0b80e14b561f14&sv=3)

In ISIS, the link address is not part of the underlying topology. It is simply advertised as an additional prefix in the IP reachability TLV. By configuring **advertise passive-only** we instruct the router to suppress all prefixes except for the passive interfaces, which in our case is only Lo0.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrIOPnz8eVdvEDQrrYmLJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9a76aaff-8277-48ec-b278-a009bf80194d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=448afe072ef2c0d7b55a8dad34d47364&sv=3)

This can be done on a router-by-router basis. It does not need to match within the network.

The question might arise then: How does R2 have the correct nexthop for R1’s loopback? We don’t see R1 advertising its nexthop anywhere in the LSP. The answer is that R1 advertises its interface address in the Hello. This is how R2 knows what to use for the nexthop to 1.1.1.1.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FaTSOIWU9IcU6YlsxaLzQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D09bd9490-e7d1-4888-b0ca-cb95b829a7ab&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3e3f2a652b2e15ebef95db85822e9490&sv=3)

[PreviousTopology](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/topology)
[NextHello padding](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-padding)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-suppression#id-61bb6e65-ca64-4ac6-974d-0d0f2d9877ac)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-suppression#id-1b38dde3-d4d1-80f1-a16e-c97ac2affaf7)

    router isis
     advertise passive-only
    
    #R2

    int gi2.24
     no isis advertise prefix
    
    #XRv1
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      advertise passive-only
    
    #XRv2
    router isis 1
     int gi0/0/0/0.1920
      suppressed

# Hello/Hold Timer | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-hold-timer.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Change the R1-R2 link to be p2p. Configure the Hello/Hold timers to be 2/6 seconds.

Change the hello/hold timer on R3 so that its Gi2.23 interface uses a hold timer of 3 seconds when it is elected DIS on the LAN.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-hold-timer#b2637125-28ff-451b-af64-e2b4ec207a5f)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-hold-timer#fdb4e72d-64d9-44f2-a3b5-5494e7621ebb)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On p2p circuits, **debug isis adj-packets** does not appear to list the hold time. Instead we can check the neighbor table to verify the holdtime oscillates between 5-6 seconds.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FeUUzvsmlh66doSVMK8hG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd4759226-ad53-4654-8764-972fc01806cb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a0d0aa2c2bb95cd9760db31d17da538b&sv=3)

On LAN circuits, we can use the debug command (**debug isis adj-packets**). The hold time is specified as **ht()**.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbU7g6uriCLGXXmqhJIUk%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D075b8e25-f257-4470-8527-141b26f800a0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=33421c1fa3768f8ae6c1c1955199baff&sv=3)

On a LAN circuit, the DIS will lower its hello/hold to three times lower than the default. This allows the DIS re-election to happen more quickly if the DIS is lost. Because we want R3 to use a hold period of 3 seconds, we must set the default to 9 seconds. We do this by setting the hello to 3 and the hold multiplier to 3. Since R3 is the DIS, it indicates to its neighbors that its hold time is 3 seconds, and sends hellos at a 1 second interval.

In ISIS, the hello/hold period does not need to match between routers. This gives you more flexibility than with OSPF. In ISIS the hello is asymmetrical, so the routers just report their hold time in the Hello. A router sets the hold time for an adjacency to the hold time received from the neighbor, not the locally configured hold time.

Also note that the **hello-multiplier** command was not strictly necessary above. This is because the default value is 3.

[PreviousDefault metric](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-metric)
[NextMesh groups](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/mesh-groups)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-hold-timer#b2637125-28ff-451b-af64-e2b4ec207a5f)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-hold-timer#fdb4e72d-64d9-44f2-a3b5-5494e7621ebb)
    

Copy

    #R1, R2 
    int gi2.12
     isis net point-to-point
     isis hello-interval 2
     isis hello-multiplier 3
    
    #R3
    int gi2.23
     isis hello-interval 3
     isis hello-multiplier 3

# Hello padding | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-padding.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure R1 and XR2 so that Hellos are only padded the first six times.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-padding#id-1c3ce97f-865b-417f-914e-85500f6b4222)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-padding#id-1b38dde3-d4d1-80ff-81b2-ebff19a2a6b8)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, the router will always pad Hellos. This can be considered an unnecessary waste of bandwidth, as once you’ve verified MTU via the padded Hellos, you no longer really need to continue to pad Hellos.

When using the above configuration, the router will only pad the first 6 Hellos. After this, all subsequent Hellos are not padded, which saves some bandwidth.

If for some reason you wanted to never pad Hellos, not even at the beginning of the adjacency, you can use **no isis hello padding always** under the interface on IOS-XE, or **hello-padding disable** on IOS-XR. This is similar to OSPF’s **ip ospf mtu-ignore** setting.

Verfiy that R1 is not padding Hellos on Gi2.12:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FDXeC9F0Cu4nGuzr4fSrr%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D11409af8-1e91-4837-be64-794b020ff03d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f180a5e38e62259e94e7320c1e4e02e8&sv=3)

When you use **no isis hello padding always**, you will instead see “Never pad hello PDU”:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FaWZAcb7d6ZZh3paG8E0a%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9dd7b471-cce7-4f2e-8fd7-07e07c276daa&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e83563a4cb59d9801997a800895cc3cc&sv=3)

I cannot find an equivalent way to verify on IOS-XR.

[NextOverload Bit](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-padding#id-1c3ce97f-865b-417f-914e-85500f6b4222)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-padding#id-1b38dde3-d4d1-80ff-81b2-ebff19a2a6b8)
    

Copy

    #R1
    int Gi2.12
     no isis hello padding
    
    ! or
    
    router isis
     no hello padding [multi-point|point-to-point]

# Overload Bit | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Set the overload bit on routers R2, R3, and XR1:

*   On R2, set overload bit on startup, wait for BGP, and supress all external routes
    
*   On R3, set overload bit right now, and advertise all prefixes
    
*   On XR1, set overload bit on startup, wait for BGP, and suppress both inter-area and external routes
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit#id-744066d0-e8e0-45a8-9bdc-4bfb683e965b)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit#bd4e7ca4-7d99-4aa9-9192-5e985a13317c)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The overload bit in ISIS is set in a router’s LSP. It can be displayed using **show isis database**. For example, verify that R3 is currently setting the OL bit in its LSP:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FEP54YrhSaFS3CTK5pksH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df02e0302-fbd9-4acc-8818-286eb3e5ebbd&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0a1849d604c3ef4f15260fe31711efad&sv=3)

ATT/P/OL means Attached bit/Partition repair/Overload bit. Parition repair is not implemented in any modern ISIS implementation. The attached bit is used in a L1 LSP to signal that the router is attached to the L2 backbone.

The original purpose of the OL bit was for an ISIS router to indicate that it has run out of memory, and that its LSDB might be out of sync. Therefore, other routers should not use this router as transit in their paths. Note that when the OL bit is set, the router is _never_ used for transit, even if no other paths exist. The node can still be used to reach leaf prefixes advertised directly from the node itself, such as its own loopback.

The OL bit has been re-purposed to be used as a sort of BGP sync mechanism. You can have the router set the OL bit upon startup and clear it when BGP has come up. This allows you to ensure that the router won’t blackhole traffic that is forwarded in the global table via iBGP.

You can also set the OL bit at any time as a way to take a router out of service. When other routers see the OL bit set, they know not to use that router as transit.

The OSPF equivalent of this feature is the max-metric command. The router can set its interfaces in the Router LSA to maximum metric to discourage use of itself as transit. This is essentially how LDP sync works. The big difference is that with ISIS, when using the OL bit, the metric of links within the LSP is not actually manipulated. Additionally, in OSPF, the router can still be used for transit if no other paths exist, while this is not the case for the ISIS node with OL bit set.

On IOS-XE, you can control what to advertise when the OL bit is set using **suppress \[external|interlevel|prefixes\].** The **prefixes** keyword means to not advertise any prefixes. On IOS-XR, the logic is reversed. By default, interlevel and external prefixes are suppressed, and you can advertise them using the **advertise** keyword.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit#id-7a68f84e-51d3-46a2-8531-36a3563074af)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

R2 should no longer have ECMP routes to XR1. It should only be using R4 for transit. It will only use R3 for traffic R3 itself is advertising - its loopback and connected routes.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fve4DyaLV3RWKym8USsXU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4aeddbd6-6b14-4ae1-bc22-e9ca2b3e43dc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e12785cfb09038e8ecb0e101fb7ccb97&sv=3)

Note that the OL bit does not set R3’s metrics to max, as it works in OSPF. Instead, the OL means “don’t use me for transit.” The OL bit does not impact the actual link metrics. Also note that even if no other paths exist, a node with the OL bit set will _never_ be used for transit.

Neither R2 or XR1 have set the OL bit yet. They will on startup, and they will clear the bit once BGP sessions come up.

I tried to verify that XRv1 will wait for BGP, but it doesn’t seem to work. Instead, simply doing **on-startup** _**seconds**_ does work. The XRv will set OL=1 upon bootup, and will wait the specified amount of time before clearing the OL bit.

[PreviousHello padding](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-padding)
[NextLSP size](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/lsp-size)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit#id-744066d0-e8e0-45a8-9bdc-4bfb683e965b)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit#bd4e7ca4-7d99-4aa9-9192-5e985a13317c)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit#id-7a68f84e-51d3-46a2-8531-36a3563074af)
    

Copy

    #R2
    router isis
     set-overload-bit on-startup wait-for-bgp suppress external
    
    #R3
    router isis
     set-overload-bit
    
    #XR1
    router isis 1
     set-overload-bit on-startup wait-for-bgp

# LSP size | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/lsp-size.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Enable wide metrics everywhere. Configure R1 and XR2 so that their LSP is fragmented once is it bigger than 128 bytes.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/lsp-size#id-27cb9f9a-af44-4ec0-a403-8764cb2f3b99)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/lsp-size#a6ae56f2-fe8a-428d-b6ee-5386df0c9e63)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, an LSP is fragmented at 1500 bytes. We can control this by setting the **lsp-mtu**. When the router’s own LSP becomes larger than the specified MTU size, it is split into multiple LSPs.

LSP IDs are in the format <Sys ID>.<Circuit ID>-<LSP fragment>. For example, LSP R6.02-00 is R6’s pseudonode LSP on the LAN segment with circuit ID 02. For p2p circuits, the circuit ID is always 00. If a router needs to fragment its LSP, it increments the last portion. For example, R1.00-00, R1.00-01, R1.00-02, etc.

In ISIS, each LSP fragment is treated as its own LSP. It is flooded, has a seq number, etc. A router “combines” all LSP fragments from a single router in order to build the ISIS topology graph.

In our network, we should see two routers that have LSP fragments, R1 and XR2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrW1hGeFTncE2gWcpxNhy%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc717e1e1-53f2-47fc-809f-47ab91c03eee&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=aa57a8ecf5a4b242a36608336d6ea8df&sv=3)

The TLVs are simply distributed among the multiple LSP fragments in order to fit within the LSP-mtu size.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVmgwsqNbjGTo4bDnL0Ys%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddc4c3b5f-40e8-43d4-afff-3f22bbc2a2ef&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=600b5fea58eb1b50a9a74994ff9107d0&sv=3)

[PreviousOverload Bit](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/overload-bit)
[NextDefault metric](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-metric)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/lsp-size#id-27cb9f9a-af44-4ec0-a403-8764cb2f3b99)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/lsp-size#a6ae56f2-fe8a-428d-b6ee-5386df0c9e63)
    

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    router isis
     metric-style wide
    
    #IOS-XR
    router isis 1
     add ipv4 
      metric-style wide
    
    #R1
    router isis
     lsp-mtu 128
    
    #XR2
    router isis 1
     lsp-mtu 128

# Mesh groups | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/mesh-groups.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure R2 so that LSPs received on Gi2.12 are only forwarded out Gi2.24. LSPs received on Gi2.23 should only be flooded out Gi2.24 as well.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/mesh-groups#id-864808b9-bcf5-4c81-9f39-61d5c89fa36e)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/mesh-groups#adb6a7ac-5a75-4734-8200-b64cfe5b0e44)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Mesh groups allow you to control ISIS flooding behavior. By default, an LSP received on any interface will be flooded out all other interfaces. This can be an inefficient use of bandwidth in large scale, highly meshed topologies. To better scale ISIS, we can configure interfaces into groups for flooding. If an interface belongs to an ISIS mesh-group, any LSP received on that interface is only flooded out other interfaces that are _not_ in the same mesh group. You also have the option to completely block flooding on an interface using **isis mesh-group blocked**. No LSPs will be flooded out the interface.

To understand how mesh groups work, let’s first look at the default behavior when R2 receives an LSP from R1 on gi2.12. I shutdown lo0 on R1 to force R1 to update its LSP. We can see that R2 floods this out Gi2.23 and Gi2.24 by using **debug isis update-packets**. (Keep in mind these screenshots show Gi1 instead of Gi2).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPHLJ9uCKsMF6RoZfDznb%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6784f650-8836-45aa-ac35-eb1123919479&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f053c07e38d1516eace4b651854aaabe&sv=3)

Next, we configure Gi2.12 and Gi2.23 in the same mesh group and **no shut** the loopback on R1. Notice that now R2 only floods the LSP out Gi2.24. It doesn’t flood the LSP out Gi2.23.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FdTHZ7Z7RkKxSbwV2ugPf%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dedc288e5-9ae1-4030-9a03-1544bb5afa20&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=18394bbcd8fd64bbcc31e348d4aa73d2&sv=3)

Now let’s shut the loopback on R3 and verify that the LSP is flooded out only Gi2.24. This should be the case, because Gi2.12 and Gi2.23 are in the same mesh group, so an LSP received on either is not flooded out the other.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6Zi0vnRxrp8CmtMyHzXb%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da1d534c1-be9e-4dbe-8495-6bf88bb21f52&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0fb1655fbfa80b102783972ba5eeede0&sv=3)

Notice above that R1 only receives the LSP when it sees that R3.00-00 LSP has changed from R2’s periodic CSNP as the DIS. R1 then explicitly requests the LSP using a PSNP. The hold time of the LSP has decreased 7 seconds in this time period (from 1198 to 1191).

Mesh-groups are dangerous to use, because as you can see above, the only thing allowing R1 to eventually receive R3’s LSP is the periodic CSNP on the LAN. Not only did this severely impact R1’s convergence time, but R1 would never even learn of the new LSP if the network type was point-to-point.

[PreviousHello/Hold Timer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/hello-hold-timer)
[NextPrefix Summarization](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/mesh-groups#id-864808b9-bcf5-4c81-9f39-61d5c89fa36e)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/mesh-groups#adb6a7ac-5a75-4734-8200-b64cfe5b0e44)
    

Copy

    #R2
    int Gi2.12
     isis mesh-group 10
    int Gi2.23
     isis mesh-group 10

# Log Neighbor Changes | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/log-neighbor-changes.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure R1 so that when Gi2.12 is manually shut down, the following log message appears:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fh4mVtFYpV8XGIclWocjw%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2eb9ce58-56bc-4ebf-8521-201b26b7bf1d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0b5ddeacab865793297df3ed851bf784&sv=3)

Configure R2 so that when Gi2.12 on R1 is shut down, no log message appears at all.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/log-neighbor-changes#cd1a1040-cf0a-41d6-9ca0-ab7a1273420b)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/log-neighbor-changes#badb304c-9bca-494a-899e-286b484fb0d7)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, **log-adjacency-changes** is enabled. However, this only logs adjacency changes that are detected through the ISIS Hello. If the interface goes down, the adjacency is lost based on the interface, not the missing Hellos, so no log is generated. If we use the **all** keyword, it will log all adjacency changes, even those caused by non-Hello events.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FDahuCh7E39jsH1KLpZFm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D864028ca-cf97-4af9-9eab-0ceecfd4ede5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d2bd1c1fe45d42f77a739670317e1174&sv=3)

On R2, we will lose the R1 neighbor based on lost Hellos. The default setting on this version of IOS-XE appears to be **log-adjacency-changes**. So if we disable this, R2 will not see any log messages when any neighbors are lost.

[PreviousISIS Timers](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/isis-timers)
[NextTroubleshooting 1 - No routes](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-1-no-routes)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/log-neighbor-changes#cd1a1040-cf0a-41d6-9ca0-ab7a1273420b)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/log-neighbor-changes#badb304c-9bca-494a-899e-286b484fb0d7)
    

Copy

    #R1
    router isis
     log-adjacency-changes all
    
    #R2
    router isis
     no log-adjacency-changes

# Prefix Summarization | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization.md)
.

Load **isis.inter.area.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F3vYJWE3kfQQwtccTGWYn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D05b17ada-b203-4ee8-898b-53a77eee86d0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=edc1284013021b2de3f68534d6dab111&sv=3)

The topology has been changed so that there are three ISIS areas now.

*   Configure R3 and R4 to summarize R1’s loopback as 1.1.1.0/24 into Level 2.
    
*   Configure R4 to summarize R5’s loopback as 5.5.5.0/24 into Level 1. No other prefixes should be leaked into Level 1.
    
*   Configure XR1 to summarize XR2’s loopback as 20.20.20.0/24 into Level 2.
    
*   Configure XR2 to redistribute a new prefix, 20.20.200.20/32 into ISIS and summarize it as 20.20.200.0/24
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization#c567e9aa-46c1-443d-a5db-f72fe3fe351e)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization#c1cc2e82-1e9e-45f2-8a3d-f211ac59b500)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In ISIS, only L1/L2 routers can do inter-area summarization. This is similar to OSPF’s ABR doing summarization in type 3 LSAs. Like OSPF ASBRs, any ISIS router can be an ASBR and do external prefix summarization. But unlike OSPF, ISIS uses the same summary command for summarizing both inter-area and external prefixes.

When summarizing level 1 prefixes as they are advertised into level 2, you use the command **summary-address <prefix> <mask> level-2**. Optionally, you can leave the **level-2** keyword out, as level 2 is the default.

When summarizing level 2 prefixes as they are advertised into level 1, you must first ensure that the routes are being leaked into level 1 in the first place. Then you use the same command but specify **level-1**. The level is always the level you are advertising the prefixes into.

When summarizing redistributed routes into ISIS, you also use the same exact **summary-address/summary-prefix** command. We must specify **level-1** if we want to redistribute into level-1. By default, on both IOS-XR and IOS-XE, redistribution is only into level-2.

When adding a summary route, just like any other routing protocol, a null0 route is added to the RIB. In ISIS the AD for the summary route is still 115, unlike EIGRP which uses a lower AD for the summary route.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization#ae3c202f-ff22-4a80-b4ad-e7f697f9602a)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Verify that R1 and R2 know only 5.5.5.0/24 and no other L2 prefixes.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJWPtdbRmhNOXy2is9agU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D86804267-2f8e-4c93-a88f-93dd26edd3fb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=124d6f8320e00d065007278ba24a9d99&sv=3)

Verify that R5 knows 1.1.1.0/24, 20.20.20.0/24, and 20.20.200.0/24 instead of the specific /32 routes:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2rMN0zlg5YQeMcBOh7Oe%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D49c83007-bcae-4e0e-a236-4cd1d996a1a9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4d33e507ec1cafedb24e821be401b378&sv=3)

We can examine R3 and R4’s L2 LSP, and should see that both are injecting the 1.1.1.0/24 summary:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0U56XFEXRtm4MjTrWUDp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D64412806-77ab-4392-9e56-fffade21096b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f474e446dffba4e546198c22497ce9af&sv=3)

We can also see the summary route on any router preforming summarization:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FkZleI30FLPzJ9hvi1fo4%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db04f8fff-233a-4162-afe1-613b224ac393&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6e3206f05d81b4b5e82caa4dca1c20cf&sv=3)

[PreviousMesh groups](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/mesh-groups)
[NextDefault Route Preference](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-route-preference)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization#c567e9aa-46c1-443d-a5db-f72fe3fe351e)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization#c1cc2e82-1e9e-45f2-8a3d-f211ac59b500)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization#ae3c202f-ff22-4a80-b4ad-e7f697f9602a)
    

Copy

    #R3
    router isis
     summary-address 1.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 level-2
    
    #R4
    ip prefix-list LEVEL2_TO_LEVEL1 permit 5.5.5.5/32
    route-map LEVEL2_TO_LEVEL1
     match ip address prefix LEVEL2_TO_LEVEL1
    !
    router isis
     summary-address 1.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 level-2
     summary-address 5.5.5.0 255.255.255.0 level-1
     redistribute isis ip level-2 into level-1 route-map LEVEL2_TO_LEVEL1
    
    #XR1
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      summary-prefix 20.20.20.0/24 level 2
    
    #XR2
    int lo20
     ip add 20.20.200.20/32
    !
    route-policy LO20
     if destination in ( 20.20.200.20/32 ) then pass endif
    end-policy
    !
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      redistribute connected route-policy LO20 level-1
      summary-prefix 20.20.200.0/24

# Start | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/start.md)
.

These labs use INE's topology from their SPv4 workbook.

To begin, run the following command on your containerlab machine:

Copy

    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    containerlab deploy -t ine-spv4/ine-spv4.clab.yml --reconfigure

Once all nodes are started, run the following command to transfer the config files to all nodes. These files will be used to change between startup configs for subsequent labs.

Copy

    python3 transfer_configs_to_nodes.py

The script will prompt you for a directory name. Enter "ine-spv4".

Use the MTPutty session file located in **ine-spv4/ine-spv4\_putty\_sessions.xml** to quickly setup your SSH sessions to the nodes. Go to **Server - Import Tree** and browse for the file.

When you are done with the lab, use the following command to wipe it:

Copy

    containerlab destroy -t ine-spv4/ine-spv4.clab.yml

# LDP and ECMP | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-and-ecmp.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

ISIS is already pre-configured. Configure LDP on all routers using LDP IGP autoconfig.

Notice that R2 has ECMP routes in its RIB. How will R2 treat traffic sourced from 1.1.1.1 destined for 19.19.19.19 by default?

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-and-ecmp#id-19bc9259-1d81-4a2a-9705-608912514783)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-and-ecmp#id-7091f787-8a6b-4ae8-9458-c1a324f76062)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

LDP follows the IGP. So if there are ECMP paths in the IGP, both label bindings are installed in the LFIB.

We can check this by inspecting the LFIB entry for 19.19.19.19/32 on R2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FD5Ee7zu3zLUsJ2ErHWJI%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd251a8a5-79a5-4acd-bc82-76c2a3f2960e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1d3b0bd02b3979152c10c5319ca4f8e9&sv=3)

It just so happens that both R3 and R4 allocated the label 23 for 19.19.19.19/32.

We can verify which path will be used for traffic sourced from R1 using the following command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5QbTHry4NECxlPGoaOCW%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D91f624c7-bfc6-4528-bf75-b6ff6e5307bd&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=23abcbbe30786bd24ca6470b2dc62506&sv=3)

By default, the CEF load-sharing algorithm is **universal**, which only uses L3 information, but uses a hash so that each router makes a different hashing calculation. So when we traceroute from R1, we should see that all traffic is forwarded out Gi2.23 only.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzS45evAavkueHAMvAooQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddadf3bc5-fdb2-40b4-9154-3a3923ce4dcb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2b4bd7373690fce85bd10a01b290df3a&sv=3)

If we want, we can change the CEF load-sharing algorithm to include L4 flow information into the hash. This produces a different hop for each traceroute probe due to the different L4 port.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FIdDwQg7D0tW2qJzz3rDO%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1cd7789a-0f29-43a9-8ebd-34c0c4c6ddbd&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6bfdf1c90cd5fe81d57d213988226653&sv=3)

[PreviousTopology](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/topology)
[NextLDP and Static Routes](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-and-static-routes)

     mpls ldp autoconfig

# LDP Timers | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-timers.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

*   Configure LDP on all routers using LDP IGP autoconfig.
    
*   Configure R1 and R2 to use a hello/hold time of 1/3 seconds for the UDP discovery. The R2-R3 and the R2-R4 neighborship should continue using 5/15 seconds.
    
*   Configure XR1 and R6 to detect failure for the TCP session after 20 seconds. Configure only XR1 to achieve this.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-timers#id-77580364-c581-4366-89ea-0a62190c1d7b)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-timers#id-79fa12e6-fe6c-444d-b4c9-481b34ee51a2)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The discovery hello/hold time is only configurable globally. It is not configurable per-interface or per-peer. This poses a problem for us to achieve the 1/3 timers for R1/R2 but keep the default timer for R2’s other LDP neighbors. However, we can use the fact that LDP timers are negotiated to our advantage.

By default, the UDP discovery hello/holdtime is 5/15 seconds, and the TCP session keepalive/holdtime is 60/180 seconds. The targeted LDP discovery hello/holdtime is 10/90 seconds.

R1 configures the hello/hold interval as 1/3 seconds, and then advertises its local hold time in the LDP UDP Hello:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FSuuulX61LgnVX7H4FUgv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0bc8a7f2-061e-4733-8abc-25389c110311&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=62b4e7551595cac0e2768a14bbc241e4&sv=3)

R2 sees that R1’s hold time is lower than its own, so it negotiates down to R1’s value. We can see the discovery timers using the following command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnBDOcoX4VQWIEubvGxpo%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9d5d3d68-3352-476d-b360-6989dd7ca4c7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e91b0d09aa668a928302724872630795&sv=3)

We can also double check that R2’s other neighbors are still using the default discovery timers.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJzJkXLjmRb6nYNseg1ET%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3c8fa1c0-65ef-4f0b-9abb-ee6709ce8384&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=be4916827b7253fba21c6d0c274fa129&sv=3)

Likewise, the LDP TCP session timers are negotiated to the lowest value. On R6, we can see the TCP session timers using the same command. R6 uses the lower timer which XR1 advertised.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FQxkKEBKkhUzhTJPNAJ9X%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D38412493-31f0-49f0-af96-e992e55fd7ef&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2a7793b765f4a5481162dd5404cbeab3&sv=3)

The keepalive is always 1/3 of the holdtime. You cannot actually configure the session keepalive interval, only the session holdtime. So TCP keepalives are sent roughly every 6-7 seconds between R6 and XR1.

Note that the LDP discovery interval can be configured separately, and does not need to be 1/3 of the holdtime. For instance, if we configure R4 to use an interval of 2 seconds and a holdtime of 12 seconds, all of its neighbors will negotiate to 12 seconds for the holdtime and calculate an interval of 4 seconds, but R4 will use 2 seconds.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FH6CN1aTnzR1kiBeinVDm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D09996f17-fe22-43ae-b73e-169eeee8379f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2287ecf3519b54480c96abf5db8eeca8&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVqoMp60a0gyY5ydPEt8C%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db13544cc-68ed-4525-88ef-02567cf3dcc1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d277662960a7839f5abdc11760f2f88e&sv=3)

[PreviousLDP and Static Routes](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-and-static-routes)
[NextLDP Authentication](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-authentication)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-timers#id-77580364-c581-4366-89ea-0a62190c1d7b)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-timers#id-79fa12e6-fe6c-444d-b4c9-481b34ee51a2)
    

Copy

    #R1-R6
    router isis
     mpls ldp autoconfig
    
    #XR1
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      mpls ldp auto-config
    !
    mpls ldp

Copy

    #R1
    mpls ldp discovery hello interval 1
    mpls ldp discovery hello holdtime 3
    
    #XR1
    mpls ldp
     session holdtime 20

Copy

    #R4
    mpls ldp discovery hello interval 2
    mpls ldp discovery hello holdtime 12

# ISIS Timers | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/isis-timers.md)
.

Load **isis.inter.area.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Set R1 and XR2 to use the following ISIS timers:

*   Local LSPs should have a max lifetime of 600 seconds. These LSPs should be refreshed every 300 seconds.
    
*   Locally-generated LSPs should be throttled 500 msec after a change, 750 msec if occuring after an LSP was just generated previously, and a max backoff of 3 seconds.
    
*   SPF calculation should be throttled 250 msec after receiving an update, 500 msec if an SPF run has just occured, and a max wait time of 3 seconds.
    
*   Partial route calculation should use the same timers as SPF calculation.
    
*   During flooding, interfaces should pace LSPs at 20 msec intervals
    
*   During flooding, the router should allow for up to 3 seconds before retransmitting the same LSP. If LSPs do need to be retransmitted, these should be paced at 40 msec intervals.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/isis-timers#e7fa98cd-5cbd-4d4e-b6af-c6d2d38f7666)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/isis-timers#id-14b1764d-1cba-4d37-a071-e3761cc2fd51)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The **lsp-max-lifetime** command sets the lifetime on locally generated LSPs. By default this appears to be 1200 seconds. This defines how long an LSP is valid in the LSDB. A longer interval allows for less frequent refreshes, which saves some bandwidth in a large network.

The **lsp-refresh-interval** controls how frequently locally-generated LSPs are refreshed. This timer cannot be larger than the lsp-max-lifetime timer.

When an IGP topology change is detected, either via a local change or a received LSP, SPF should be delayed incase subsequent changes occur. The more you delay this, the more you can “batch” multiple topology changes together, but the less quickly the IGP will converge. The first parameter is the maxmium wait time. The second parameter is the initial wait time. The last parameter is the wait time between the first and second SPF run. Subsequent SPF runs will continue to backoff until reaching the max wait time.

Partial route calculation is any change that does not affect the topology. For example, if a prefix is removed/added from a node, the IGP topology has not changed, so an SPF run is not needed. Instead, a partial rotue calculation is used to more quickly update the RIB. The timers for PRC is configured in a similar manner to the SPF timers. This does not appear to be configurable for IOS-XR.

The interface-level command **isis lsp-interval** controls pacing during LSP flooding. During LSP flooding, you may want the router to send the LSPs at a slower pace to give the remote router a better chance of processing the LSPs. This command sets the delay between subsequent LSP transmissions on the interface.

During flooding, it’s possible that some LSPs are lost and need to be retransmitted. The amount of time to wait for an ACK to an LSP is controlled with the **isis retransmit-interval** interface command.

If many LSPs need to be retransmitted, these can be paced using a separate **retransmit-throttle-interval** setting. It may be the case that the router was pacing these LSPs too quickly at first, so retransmited LSPs can be paced at a slower timer.

[PreviousDefault Route Preference](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-route-preference)
[NextLog Neighbor Changes](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/log-neighbor-changes)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/isis-timers#e7fa98cd-5cbd-4d4e-b6af-c6d2d38f7666)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/isis-timers#id-14b1764d-1cba-4d37-a071-e3761cc2fd51)
    

Copy

    #R1
    router isis
     max-lsp-lifetime 600
     lsp-refresh-interval 300
     spf-interval 3 250 500
     prc-interval 3 250 500
     lsp-gen-interval 3 500 750
    !
    int Gi2.12
     isis lsp-interval 20
     isis retransmit-interval 3
     isis retransmit-throttle-interval 40
    
    #XR2
    router isis 1
     lsp-max-lifetime 600
     lsp-refresh-interval 300
     lsp-gen-interval initial-wait 500 secondary-wait 750 maximum-weight 3000
     !
     address-family ipv4
      spf-interval initial-wait 250 second-wait 500 maximum-wait 3000
     !
     int Gi0/0/0/0.1920
      lsp-interval 20
      retransmit-interval 3
      retransmit-throttle-interval 40

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    router isis
     lsp-max-lifetime <sec>
    
    #IOS-XR
    router isis 1
     lsp-max-lifetime <sec>

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    router isis
     lsp-refresh-interval <sec>
    
    #IOS-XR
    router isis 1
     lsp-refresh-interval <sec>

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    router isis
     spf-interval <max wait in seconds> <initial wait in msec> <min wait for 2nd run in msec>
    
    #IOS-XR
    router isis 1
     address-family ipv4
      spf-interval initial-wait <msec> second-wait <msec> maximum-wait <msec>

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    router isis
     prc-interval <max wait in seconds> <initial wait in msec> <min wait for 2nd run in msec>

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int Gi1
     isis lsp-interval <msec>
    
    #IOS-XR
    router isis 1
     int Gi0/0/0/0
      lsp-interval <msec>

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int Gi1
     isis retransmit-interval <sec>
    
    #IOS-XR
    router isis 1
     int Gi0/0/0/0
      retransmit-interval <msec>

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int Gi1
     isis retransmit-throttle-interval <msec>
    
    #IOS-XR
    router isis 1
     int Gi0/0/0/0
      retransmit-throttle-interval <msec>

# Default Route Preference | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-route-preference.md)
.

Load **isis.inter.area.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FiTxgc4tnJ7cB7yOsQRJE%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8354f8f6-700e-489d-a23d-5ecdfe36d154&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8a04dea29af870dfd3c011d377cf4ead&sv=3)

Configure area 49.1234 so that R2 prefers R3 for the default route, and only uses R4 upon loss of R3. Do not use metrics to achieve this.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-route-preference#id-8906312a-d34a-45ad-b14e-45f72cc89965)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-route-preference#id-3bb40c1b-d822-4711-b44b-6d2165b71701)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ISIS allows us to originate a default route just like OSPF. An L1 router will prefer an explicit 0/0 route that is advertised in the area over using the ATT bit.

By default, when a router uses **default-information originate**, the default is only injected into L2. To set L1 only, or L1/L2, we must use a route-map.

R2 now sees an explicit 0/0 route advertised from R3:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fe8mN9LqWb0e9XKV0o5as%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D43100a55-03ab-464e-9b94-ece126d20c33&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7a84091701abe7dd68ff73af78ce338b&sv=3)

Due to this, R2 only uses R3 as its default route:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPttgXbDzUoEw4G3BqHeN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6a23a184-6bf5-4052-b6a1-99f08efad84f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b902603fbb001be64ac924167773be38&sv=3)

We can see the ISIS RIB still has both 0/0 routes generated from the ATT bit set on R3 and R4, but the explicit 0/0 is preferred and installed:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FkFcaswDgCwClw7a3Qqe1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4f107f7d-5251-4f15-a7d2-52fd1eb7ad10&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8e2c040133a47827e4afbd44cf983643&sv=3)

[PreviousPrefix Summarization](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/prefix-summarization)
[NextISIS Timers](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/isis-timers)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-route-preference#id-8906312a-d34a-45ad-b14e-45f72cc89965)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/default-route-preference#id-3bb40c1b-d822-4711-b44b-6d2165b71701)
    

Copy

    #R3
    route-map SET_L1
     set level level-1
    !
    router isis
     default-information originate route-map SET_L1

Copy

    #R3
    route-map SET_L1
     set level level-1
    !
    router isis
     default-information originate route-map SET_L1

# IPv6 Single Topology | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/ipv6-single-topology.md)
.

Load **isis.ipv6.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.ipv6.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.ipv6.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

All routers have IPv6 link-local addresses enabled on their interfaces, and a loopback IPv6 address of 2001:db8::<router num>/128.

Without enabling wide metrics, configure IPv6 reachability between all routers on their loopbacks.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/ipv6-single-topology#da7e88de-588b-420e-a034-dd7ddad6821d)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/ipv6-single-topology#id-1b68dde3-d4d1-808b-b3da-e9d2dd18ccde)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is a disruptive change, because the network layer protocol ID field must match between routers in the ISIS Hello. When you enable IPv6 for ISIS on an interface, the router starts generating an ISIS Hello with two NLPIDs:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FIn98IC7oWkCgTY4vuvqe%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6a36dbdd-3859-41a7-8e15-c6371210ee2d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a8e4a4de4984c5ecd38054717571fcf0&sv=3)

The other router, which still has only IPv4 at this point, will reject the adjacency now.

Once all routers have IPv6 for ISIS enabled on all interfaces, you should have end-to-end IPv6 reachability.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FB62xt8RHC8VBFBpd158p%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D40743302-3b90-4796-a5b0-898779b45721&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6d7cee415105bf4fce4654f440752337&sv=3)

IOS-XE’s default IPv6 mode is single topology. In single topology, IPv6 “uses” the IPv4 topology. The IPv6 prefixes ride on top of the IPv4 topology and its adjacencies. IPv6 prefixes are simply advertised with TLV 236. This is used whether or not wide metrics are used. (Either can be used with single topology).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvCYcqm3AirP4wAmuJzGB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D611a1c28-27f1-4082-aaf9-dcec8a6096c4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6835dbe1e8160a90343dd44a2b58f7fe&sv=3)

The link-local address, used for the nexthop by the neighbor for IPv6 routes, is advertised in the Hello in the IPv6 interface address TLV (232).

On IOS-XR, we must enable single-topology under the AFI. By default IOS-XR uses multi topology, in which IPv4 and IPv6 each have a separate topology, and IPv6 is not required to be enabled on every interface.

In summary:

*   IPv6 can be used with either single topology or multi topology
    
    *   In single topology, IPv6 uses the IPv4 topology. IPv6 prefixes are advertised in a separate IPv6 reachability TLV (236)
        
    
*   Single topology is the default mode on IOS-XE
    
*   Multi topology is the default mode on IOS-XR
    
*   In single topology, every link must have both IPv4 and IPv6. If any router does not have IPv6 enabled, both IPv4 and IPv6 reachability is broken.
    
    *   This is because the adjacency requires all protocols be supported between both neighbors
        
    *   The exception is that you can use single topology and **only** IPv6. No IPv4 anywhere in the topology. In this case, the protocols supported TLV lists only IPv6 by itself.
        
    
*   Single topology can use either narrow or wide metrics. Multi topology requires wide metrics.
    

[PreviousTroubleshooting 2 - Adjacency](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-2-adjacency)
[NextIPv6 Single Topology Challenge](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/ipv6-single-topology-challenge)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/ipv6-single-topology#id-1b68dde3-d4d1-808b-b3da-e9d2dd18ccde)
    

Copy

    #R1
    int Gi2.12
     ipv6 router isis
    router isis
     add ipv6 unicast    ! Not strictly needed
    
    #R2
    int Gi2.12
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.23
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.24
     ipv6 router isis
    router isis
     add ipv6 unicast    ! Not strictly needed
    
    #R3
    int Gi2.23
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.34
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.36
     ipv6 router isis
    router isis
     add ipv6 unicast    ! Not strictly needed
    
    #R4
    int Gi2.24
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.34
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.46
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.45
     ipv6 router isis

    #R5

     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.519
     ipv6 router isis

     add ipv6 unicast    ! Not strictly needed
    
    #R6

    int Gi2.46
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.56
     ipv6 router isis
    int Gi2.619
     ipv6 router isis
    router isis
     add ipv6 unicast    ! Not strictly needed
    
    #XR1
    router isis 1
     add ipv6 unicast
      single-topology
     !
     int Gi0/0/0/0.619
      add ipv6 unicast
     int Gi0/0/0/0.519
      add ipv6 unicast
     int Gi0/0/0/0.1920
      add ipv6 unicast
     int lo0
      add ipv6 unicast
      
    #XR1
    router isis 1
     add ipv6 unicast
      single-topology
     !
     int Gi0/0/0/0.1920
      add ipv6 unicast
     int lo0
