# Conditional ATT Bit | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/conditional-att-bit.md)
.

Load **isis.inter.area.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXzMjLtro0rCaNxQoTCPa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D189ff671-f892-46dc-9a56-005f1454da33&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2925db34c3d868fe0d7cba96160472c2&sv=3)

Configure R4 so that it only sets the attached bit for area 49.1234 when the prefix 200.200.200.200/32 is present in the routing table.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/conditional-att-bit#id-454e6e1c-2128-4020-b825-74b7579f92ec)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/conditional-att-bit#bbe83d2a-5b28-4a1c-84b3-53d3aa5344ce)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The ISIS command **set-attached-bit** provides a way to control when the router sets the ATT bit in its L1 LSP.

Currently the prefix 200.200.200.200/32 is not present in the RIB, so R4 clears the ATT bit from its LSP. We can verify this on any L1 router in the area.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fc1jBrZ5yiJpOxQUyWP1D%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0bb53720-4ca5-466f-a45c-47d39207dde0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=274ca31873e5dd14053eb1a389b42dc1&sv=3)

If we inject 200.200.200.200/32 on any router, for example XR2, R4 should begin setting the ATT bit again.

On R4, the route-map now evaluates to “True,” so the attached bit is set again:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMBdyAOZTXaTAaHUW1AOT%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1d9310d6-26c9-4793-8a8b-0140162d276e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=537aece861d3e83cd95adf81860c9162&sv=3)

[PreviousAuthentication](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication)
[NextTroubleshooting iBGP](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-ibgp)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/conditional-att-bit#id-454e6e1c-2128-4020-b825-74b7579f92ec)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/conditional-att-bit#bbe83d2a-5b28-4a1c-84b3-53d3aa5344ce)
    

Copy

    #R4
    ip prefix-list LO200 permit 200.200.200.200/32
    !
    route-map ISIS_ATT
     match ip add prefix LO200
    !
    router isis
     set-attached-bit route-map ISIS_ATT

Copy

    #XR2
    int lo200
     ip add 200.200.200.200/32
    !
    router isis 1
     int lo200
      passive
      add ipv4

# LDP Inbound Label Advertisement Filtering | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)

.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

*   Configure LDP using LDP autoconfig under ISIS
    
*   Configure inbound label filtering on R1 and XR2 to filter out label bindings received from their LDP neighbors for all transit prefixes
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-inbound-label-advertisement-filtering#id-82b96419-0158-4e14-b7ac-d322bb979516)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-inbound-label-advertisement-filtering#cea49921-4c11-4f4f-93f1-b10f2d996998)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Inbound LDP advertisement filtering is much easier to configure than outbound advertisement filtering. In both IOS-XE and IOS-XR, we must apply an ACL on a per-neighbor basis to filter incoming LDP bindings.

On IOS-XE, we use the following command:

On IOS-XR, we use the following command:

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-inbound-label-advertisement-filtering#id-72976356-7a16-445d-90b8-e91a52fade3b)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On R1, since R2 is the only LDP peer, we can look at the LDP bindings summary for a quick check that the inbound filtering is working. Before implementing the filter, we see that we have one remote binding for every prefix:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2mxQOFgFypz64G7epkOF%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd9f6a11b-0761-4398-a9dd-cedab818857f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=81d61cf1fe9057e35bda747645a632cc&sv=3)

After implementing the filter, we should only see a remote binding for the /32 loopbacks, due to our standard ACL we are applying for R2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnfTHPkrB8KfxdwYQW43N%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De7b4475e-73d2-4ea1-aea9-98244ceb85da&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a06b78fc300de8d89bb9d0097492bca2&sv=3)

Likewise, on XR2, we can use the same command. First we verify that we are receiving one remote label (from XR1) for every prefix:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FxMgt2rtOh0Vmv55UOzjg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D599a7f77-a2cb-4073-a503-06f3e74d6695&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e48771664f5be2b0c5f1fae9f725f4a7&sv=3)

Next, we apply the inbound filter and verify that XR2 has discarded XR1’s bindings for non-loopback prefixes:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fi0hFSLhY8cI7cF7hfPEq%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1720b7ef-d8a8-4aa5-acc7-e3307db30234&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6198a42ea3ae0efe6152c62d0fee05f2&sv=3)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-inbound-label-advertisement-filtering#cea49921-4c11-4f4f-93f1-b10f2d996998)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-inbound-label-advertisement-filtering#id-72976356-7a16-445d-90b8-e91a52fade3b)
    

Copy

    #R1-6
    router isis
     mpls ldp autoconfig
    
    #R1
    ip access-list standard LDP_FILTER_IN
     deny 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
     permit host 20.20.20.20
     deny 20.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
     permit any
    !
    mpls ldp neighbor 2.2.2.2 labels accept LDP_FILTER_IN
    
    #XR1, XR2
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      mpls ldp auto-config
    !
    mpls ldp
    
    #XR2
    ipv4 access-list LDP_FILTER_IN
     10 deny ipv4 10.0.0.0/8 any
     20 permit ipv4 host 20.20.20.20 any
     30 deny ipv4 20.0.0.0/8 any
     40 permit ipv4 any any
    !
    mpls ldp
     address-family ipv4
      label
       remote
        accept
         from 19.19.19.19:0 for LDP_FILTER_IN

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    mpls ldp neighbor RID labels accept ACL

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    mpls ldp
     address-family ipv4
      label
       remote
        accept
         from RID:0 for ACL

# LDP Conditional Label Advertisement | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-conditional-label-advertisement.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

*   Configure LDP using IGP autoconfig on all routers
    
*   Configure R2 to only advertise labels for /32 routes to R1
    
*   Configure XR1 to only advertise labels for /32 routes to XR2
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-conditional-label-advertisement#id-9d0ba0e4-b5a2-4ad8-adef-159b05d7f1a7)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-conditional-label-advertisement#id-35538a27-d5e2-457a-a340-c7dd01bede4b)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

LDP Conditional label advertisement is very confusing. First, on any router we want to implement outbound advertisement filtering, we must disable the default advertisement which is for all prefixes. Without doing this, we will always advertise all label bindings to all neighbors, no matter what additional filters we add.

This posses a big problem when we go to advertise labels to only certain peers. For example, if we implement the following filter on R2 towards R1, we are also at the same time not advertising _any_ label bindings towards R3 or R4. (This is due to **no mpls ldp advertise-labels** command).

So instead, we must advertise the host routes to all peers, and then advertise all prefixes to _not_ R1.

Unfortunately, this logic does not work on XR1. On XR1, if we try this, XR1 will seem to match the SACL\_PERMIT\_ANY entry first, and not advertise _any_ label bindings to XR2. So instead, we implement something even more complicated. We have a second ACL which is ACL\_NOT\_HOST\_ROUTES which individually denies the loopback prefixes.

The above label advertisement indentifies two separate ACLs for advertisement:

*   ACL\_HOST\_ROUTES to any neighbors
    
*   ACL\_NOT\_HOST\_ROUTES (anything not to a loopback) to any neighbors besides XR2
    

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-conditional-label-advertisement#id-496aa6ae-7d60-40a8-b1f5-b06aec53f51f)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On R3, verify that R2 is still advertising a label binding for every prefix:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5Nu7XhrUw4ZfYsNJCDC5%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df9aea47e-5d71-4cd1-bb6a-f42deb90e3e4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2ba3bd79ecfeeadf09c2fbe2078dccba&sv=3)

We can see the same on XR1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKfbFXli5e6ziF9QkoZeS%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4b0c2e28-9c99-4f4d-950c-7b08152bac54&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=50e6bdfade1ed729f29f0f5675ed6603&sv=3)

Using this command, we can see why the logic we are doing on R2 didn’t work on XR1. Let’s move the XR1 advertisement filtering back to:

*   ACL\_HOST\_ROUTES to all neighbors
    
*   ACL\_PERMIT\_ANY to all neighbors besides XR2
    

Above, the ACL\_HOST\_ROUTES never gets matched. This appears to be because the ACL entries get re-ordered in the config:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2vM3JJ9mKUbohpChPEhL%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D42a36cb5-f98c-487f-85da-7e6fdc5a2aee&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=eb42daa15dd8b5d608935a595b001531&sv=3)

On R2, the SACL\_HOST\_ROUTES is first in the config, which might explain why it works. This actually seems very fragile. Could a router reload change the ACL order and break this on R2?

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FCfBJZnfF3Hd4eNBmfwPD%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D45804a78-cfe0-4d1b-8386-addc53fbb6e0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=06b6803eb3da3118b990eeff4e1c7e1b&sv=3)

Summary[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-conditional-label-advertisement#id-3ef3d44f-0036-43d5-bbaa-262bc0fce58c)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Outbound LDP label advertisement filtering is very complex. You are limited to using an ACL which makes it difficult to scale as well. In this lab, we would have to manually add ACL entries for every new router’s loopback that is added to the topology.

Additionally, there is the complexity of having to completely disable outbound label advertisements altogether, and create new outbound policies to re-advertise all label bindings to all _other_ neighbors. So in this situation, using local allocating filtering is _much_ better than trying to achieve a similar result using outbound label filtering.

I can see this feature only working well perhaps for a Unified MPLS type of setup, where the ABR is advertising label bindings for the “other” IGP. You could do outbound label filtering in that case. If, for example, you use 10/8 and 20/8 for each separate IGP, that might help scale the ACL management. However, it doesn’t matter if the ABR advertises these bindings, because the router will not have IGP routes for those bindings, and simply won’t use them. But perhaps a lab task could be to implement this feature for scalability. (You’re doing Unified MPLS to scale anyways, so why advertise all those label bindings unnecessarily too?)

    #R1-R6
    router isis
     mpls ldp autoconfig
    
    #R2
    no mpls ldp advertise-labels

    mpls ldp advertise-labels for SACL_PERMIT_ANY to SACL_LDP_ALL_OTHER_NEIGHBORS
    !
    ip access-list standard SACL_HOST_ROUTES
     permit host 1.1.1.1
     permit host 2.2.2.2
     permit host 3.3.3.3
     permit host 4.4.4.4
     permit host 5.5.5.5
     permit host 6.6.6.6
     permit host 19.19.19.19
     permit host 20.20.20.20
    !
    ip access-list standard SACL_PERMIT_ANY
     permit any
    !
    ip access-list standard SACL_LDP_ALL_OTHER_NEIGHBORS
     deny host 1.1.1.1
     permit any
    
    #XR1, XR2
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      mpls ldp auto-config

    #XR1

    !
    ipv4 access-list ACL_NOT_HOST_ROUTES
     deny ipv4 host 1.1.1.1 any
     deny ipv4 host 2.2.2.2 any
     deny ipv4 host 3.3.3.3 any
     deny ipv4 host 4.4.4.4 any

     deny ipv4 host 20.20.20.20 any
     permit ipv4 any any

# LDP Local Allocation Filtering | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-local-allocation-filtering.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

*   Configure LDP using IGP autoconfig on routers R1-R6 and XR1-2
    
*   On R1-R3 and XR1, allocate labels only for host routes using a prefix-list/ACL
    
*   On R4-R6 and XR2, allocate labels only for host routes _without_ using a prefix-list or ACL
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-local-allocation-filtering#eb63e9cd-9500-4f1e-9d3c-f8dc77248fab)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-local-allocation-filtering#id-21d76674-699c-441c-ab7f-52843f3a90b7)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, LDP will locally allocate labels for every non-BGP prefix in the RIB. However, generally LSPs are only formed on the loopbacks, so there is no reason to allocate labels for every transit prefix in the IGP. By allocating labels only for host routes, we can save some memory and better scale LDP.

To selectively allocate labels, we have two options. First, we can use a prefix-list/ACL to have granular control over what prefixes will be allocated a label.

The IOS-XR method is quite burdensome, because we cannot use a mask filter like we can with a prefix-list. This is the reason that we had to manually specify every host route in the ACL on XR1:

The second method is the built-in **host-routes** option. This instructs LDP to only allocate labels for /32 prefixes, and does not require any prefix-list or ACL.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-local-allocation-filtering#id-940a8fc5-f9cb-42e5-9445-38733b234ff6)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On any router in the topology, we should only see /32 prefixes in the LFIB and LIB. It does not matter which router we look at, because both the ACL/prefix-list method, and the built-in **for host-routes** method, have the exact same effect.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2d4B8AxgG0yn7V7dMdoA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1a312028-cc77-4b28-b499-e034d5990db1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b158961ab40d77e3c81aebcf48963c4a&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbyOLakGfjgoI25ktiPP5%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dbec36404-c80a-4c72-895f-2bd0b81e1e3a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1307809f91e19a2449d0a96a5a317782&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4iTU3ncB71MVyemm6WDT%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D880e7530-e1ef-4189-9bad-51559b141941&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d817c4ce648dde980937677897bf671c&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FohHYf5ELqJmVyqlxC6zn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6cc5897f-aa72-49c7-a690-0edd824b7b26&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=48f3f766de71c240067355a5e22550a7&sv=3)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-local-allocation-filtering#id-21d76674-699c-441c-ab7f-52843f3a90b7)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-local-allocation-filtering#id-940a8fc5-f9cb-42e5-9445-38733b234ff6)

     permit ipv4 host 1.1.1.1 any
     permit ipv4 host 2.2.2.2 any
     permit ipv4 host 3.3.3.3 any
     permit ipv4 host 4.4.4.4 any
     permit ipv4 host 5.5.5.5 any
     permit ipv4 host 6.6.6.6 any
     permit ipv4 host 19.19.19.19 any
     permit ipv4 host 20.20.20.20 any
    
    #XR2
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      mpls ldp auto-config
    !
    mpls ldp
     address-family ipv4
      label
       local
        allocate for host-routes

# LDP/IGP Sync (OSPF) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-ospf.md)
.

Load **ospfv2.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:ospfv2.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:ospfv2.cfg
    commit replace
    y

*   Configure LDP authentication for R2 on R3, using pass LDP23. Do not configure R2.
    
*   Configure LDP for all routers using autoconfig under OSPF.
    
*   Configure LDP sync so that all traffic from R1 to XR2 is always sent over R2-R4 instead of R2-R3 when LDP is not up between R2-R3.
    
*   Configure the R2-R3 link so that the IGP waits for LDP to be up for 20 seconds before reducing the metric.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-ospf#e1e52d41-250b-4825-b548-53b413d9c1e7)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-ospf#edc3146b-f5f3-4c40-bb03-7de9b1a5b347)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Although the feature may sound complex, LDP/IGP sync is fairly simple. The problem it solves is if the IGP converges before LDP converges (perhaps before LDP has finished exchanging labels), routing may find a best path that is temporarily unlabeled, breaking any LSPs and VPNs running over those LSPs. To solve this issue, the IGP advertises the link metric as the max value, and when LDP is fully converged, the metric is reduced to the regular metric of the link. This discourages the use of the link by the IGP until LDP is fully converged, hence the IGP is “in sync” with LDP.

LDP/IGP sync comes with two parameters that are important:

*   Sync delay timer
    
    *   Configurable on both IOS-XE and IOS-XR
        
    *   Controls how long the IGP waits to reduce the metric value once LDP is converged
        
    *   Default value is 0 seconds
        
    
*   Holddown timer
    
    *   Configurable only on IOS-XE
        
    *   Controls how long IGP will wait to hear LDP hellos before finally giving up and establishing an IGP adjacency, and then setting metric to max value
        
    *   Default value is infinite on IOS-XE
        
    *   Does not appear to be implemented on IOS-XR
        
        *   You could consider the default value 0 on IOS-XR
            
        
    

Naturally, LDP/IGP sync is configured under the IGP process as follows:

We can only configure the sync delay under each interface individually.

We set the holddown timer in IOS-XE globally:

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-ospf#a175d755-5321-4817-9f62-4964dc4959a2)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

First examine R2’s routing table and notice that no paths are via R3. R2 does not have an LDP session established with R3 due to the mismatched auth. This is a sign that the LDP/IGP sync feature is working.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FiFsNmQA5sMsePN4bYhfH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dde6b0181-3c48-4b4d-82c4-c4643107e95c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9b16c1c42cc1337ffdc76857034783ad&sv=3)

If we look at the OSPF interface cost, we see that the Gi2.23 cost is still 1, which is a little confusing. You might expect this to be 65535.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKw2EfUQPr72mfPpDiIeg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ded1c2a9b-47c7-451c-97ab-8290689b5dbf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f4d06034b8de3f1c4946233bd054b855&sv=3)

However, if you inspect the router’s Router LSA, you can see that the metric is indeed set to the maximum. The interface’s “regular” or “configured” cost is 1, which is what is reflected in the previous output.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsCIbgc6svWxX7WkUNphP%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D86415f66-2434-4305-a087-a7a320493ad9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ed1d7b39e8b5657f2ab25290915acbb0&sv=3)

A handy command for verifying LDP/IGP sync is **show mpls ldp igp sync**. We can see on R2 that Gi1.23 is currently in a status of “sync not achieved; peer reachable.”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FH1A1d5sMiHpe10F0SNDm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D30b1af76-94c7-4a57-83ec-0012cc23c140&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cffd532c3aa5fb356a056ddece971a7a&sv=3)

If we remove the authentication on R3, we should see that LDP is established. OSPF should then wait 20 seconds before changing the metric value back to 1. We can see this timer using the same show command as seen above.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTgTYUOXO8kxSMROTmrLp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D81440c95-c3e3-4842-8d7a-893fede6992c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2bafe33328e7e0c5dcd0eb59f738e86a&sv=3)

### Sync holddown[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-ospf#c4edc242-0557-410b-8dd1-17c65f280384)

Let’s breifly explore the sync holddown feature. This is only configurable on IOS-XE. This feature is kind of complicated, because it seems to only be in use when the interface detects no LDP Hellos at all on the other side. So to simulate this, we will need to completely remove LDP on R3 Gi2.23.

However, the other problem is that R2 has already formed an OSPF adjacency with R3. So we need to clear OSPF on R2 now.

Now we can see that R2 has no OSPF adjacency at all with R3:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTEpYvmpWOahbOSM9RRkH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3f9eaa4f-b3f8-42eb-8e22-1cdb5ada74bb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=67343dfc43ad6d49149b305b1a19ea34&sv=3)

If we look at the OSPF status for this interface, we see that the state is **DOWN (waiting for LDP)**. The interface is waiting to hear LDP Hellos. Without received LDP Hellos, the OSPF neighborship will never form.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FpPmCMkdMysEYAqriV18z%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5f8eecf0-8b96-4965-b6e3-4c0e570a5c06&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cd801261a7173cd181874838681cdb6e&sv=3)

If we change the holddown timer to something low, such as 10 seconds, we should see that eventually OSPF gives up and forms the adjacency anyways, albeit with max metric on the link. This seems better to me than waiting indefinitely, as that could cause a serious outage in production.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FmPcts3N6Zv5vM4yyMgBB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D03f48a72-823f-4bcf-89df-ec0d7b14101c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cbfbede0901645896d0d416ada13cdcf&sv=3)

Note that IOS-XR does not appear to implement this holddown timer. First, we can see that this parameter is not visible in the show output:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJNDcOXcZRo8K5Ee6UYt4%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc3db0e69-6a1e-4705-aa55-a2f357a1622a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4cbf2e3ef137776ab17dd4d5ee21ce46&sv=3)

Second, if we make the same change, we can see that OSPF still forms:

The sync status is “not ready”, meaning unsynchronized, but the OSPF neighborship still forms, unlike IOS-XE:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fx911BpTKRrmuDMRdLiZT%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df47a180c-71a2-41eb-8cd1-ee20e81efb35&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ed82cce40d964e7e930b5c881103502b&sv=3)

To me this seems better, because you can never cause an outage due to disabling LDP on IOS-XR when implementing IGP/LDP sync.

Copy

    #R1-R6
    router ospf 1
     mpls ldp autoconfig
     mpls ldp sync
    
    #R2
    int Gi2.23
     mpls ldp igp sync delay 20
    
    #R3
    mpls ldp nei 2.2.2.2 password LDP23
    !
    int Gi2.23
     mpls ldp igp sync delay 20
    
    #XR1-2
    router ospf 1
     mpls ldp auto-config
     mpls ldp sync
    !
    mpls ldp

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    router ospf 1
     mpls ldp sync
    !
    router isis 1
     mpls ldp sync
    
    #IOS-XR
    router ospf 1
     mpls ldp sync
    !
    router isis 1
     int gi0/0/0/0
      add ipv4
       mpls ldp sync

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int Gi2.23
     mpls ldp igp sync delay 20
    
    #IOS-XR
    mpls ldp
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
      igp sync delay on-session-up 20

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    mpls ldp igp sync holddown <msec>

Copy

    #R3
    no mpls ldp neighbor 2.2.2.2 password LDP23

Copy

    #R3
    int gi2.23
     no mpls ldp igp autoconfig

Copy

    #R2
    clear ip ospf proc

Copy

    #R2
    mpls ldp igp sync holddown 10000

Copy

    #XR2
    router ospf 1
     no mpls ldp auto-config
    
    #XR1
    clear ospf proc

# Troubleshooting iBGP | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-ibgp.md)
.

Load **isis.ibgp.tshoot.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.ibgp.tshoot.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.ibgp.tshoot.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMUKzKS3QffMxndzj6Bnh%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4fe0beb1-e75f-494f-8383-d779e95db850&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=673fbb79718bc7c6ff5b9f1592394f95&sv=3)

An iBGP session is configured between R1 and XR2. R1 is advertising a prefix (100.100.100.100/32). LDP autoconfig has been added so that traffic can be tunneled between R1 and XR2.

Explain why the iBGP session is not established, and find a way to fix it.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-ibgp#ee4fb440-75fb-4f20-ab60-d8abdfeab902)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-ibgp#id-4342ed97-973d-4793-b397-707132405b02)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Before making any changes, let’s examine the issue. First let’s look at the BGP neighbor on R1. Counter-intuitively, R1 states that it _does_ have a route to 20.20.20.20/32. However, this is very deceptive, because IOS-XE and IOS-XR cannot use the 0/0 route to establish a session with a peer.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FztKnOvkp5Y1plU20aeNY%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1d149a10-d80b-44cc-9419-ef20d5c8d2ff&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ab53dedcad65812b6f70a330c03d068c&sv=3)

If we simply debug ip bgp, we can see the issue. This seems to contradict the show output saying that “the RIB does have a route.”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbIrl88tVXpyTYchIhCoK%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D32ae833d-a825-4c7a-8435-60d5b4279d12&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2e2bddd7084454f13372db4755d846e7&sv=3)

IOS-XR gives us better output from the **show bgp neighbor** command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZFWhYnnxYnK0w2OFn3vR%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D889daf1c-7123-4f2e-a030-ccb9db9b91a2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=59abf3b3a312b68417ee7ef1bd734b94&sv=3)

One easy way to fix this is to leak L2 routes into L1. On R3 and R4, let’s leak 20.20.20.20/32 into L1. This should give R1 an explicit route to XR2.

The BGP peer now comes up. Only one side needed the explict route to initiate the TCP connection.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0r0f2tuYveXknBkPaRaA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D43f9da6b-aed8-47b2-bbe4-1789adcac1f2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d1d51efce4720466971669a20aa29cf3&sv=3)

However, a second problem now exists. On IOS-XR, a nexthop cannot be resolved through the 0/0 route.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPAhguKicKMkElLD1f8mm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9e5914aa-e94d-4fd7-a8ff-618ef03e653f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=50dee025fa7681f4afa0f5b8a4bcdf47&sv=3)

To demonstrate that this is not the case for IOS-XE, let’s inject a route on XR2, remove the L2 to L1 leaking on R3/R4, and only leak 1.1.1.1/32 on XR1.

Now XR2 can validate the nexthop for R1’s prefix:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsV2kXgGT4gG3PYFM3jJm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D009d7305-98f6-4770-b36e-20d06a75f945&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7fc958b586576340153f2208b35e76b6&sv=3)

Even though R1 is missing the /32 route for XR2, 200.200.200.200/32 has a valid nexthop.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FqXvMZDAlbU7ftczfSpA8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D68fc8dca-2c40-4faa-9ebd-7934f272aefb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e66373b2fb1f4717d06aa242c3ef7138&sv=3)

Right now, there is no reachability because R2 does not have 20.20.20.20/32 in its RIB, and doesn’t allocate a label for it, and then advertise this to R1. So the end-to-end LSP from R1 to XR2 is broken.

We can sort of get around this in a convuluted way by using static routing and static MPLS labels. On R2, make sure to find R3’s local label to use as the static output label.

Unfortunately, a static route is needed in order to make the MPLS entry valid. So we still had to provide some sort of routing for 20.20.20.20/32 on R1 to get this to work. It would obviously just be easier to leak 20.20.20.20/32 from L2 into L1 on R3/R4.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvuvYdjimfvA0ET9ZW5wa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5181e03d-91cd-4bc4-8e76-d1434341d5d7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1174287d1d2f4812dba0751aab5a9236&sv=3)

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-ibgp#ee4fb440-75fb-4f20-ab60-d8abdfeab902)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-ibgp#id-4342ed97-973d-4793-b397-707132405b02)
    

Copy

    #R3, R4
    ip prefix-list L2_TO_L1 permit 20.20.20.20/32
    !
    route-map L2_TO_L1
     match ip add prefix L2_TO_L1
    !
    router isis
     redistribute isis ip level-2 into level-1 route-map L2_TO_L1
    
    #XR1
    route-policy L2_TO_L1
     if destination in ( 1.1.1.1/32 ) then pass endif
    end-policy
    !
    router isis 1
     add ipv4 uni
      propagate level 2 into level 1 route-policy L2_TO_L1

Copy

    #R3, R4
    ip prefix-list L2_TO_L1 permit 20.20.20.20/32
    !
    route-map L2_TO_L1
     match ip add prefix L2_TO_L1
    !
    router isis
     redistribute isis ip level-2 into level-1 route-map L2_TO_L1

Copy

    #R3, R4
    router isis
     no redistribute isis ip level-2 into level-1 route-map L2_TO_L1
    
    #XR2
    int lo200
     ip add 200.200.200.200/32
    !
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 uni
      network 200.200.200.200/32
    
    #XR1
    route-policy L2_TO_L1
     if destination in ( 1.1.1.1/32 ) then pass endif
    end-policy
    !
    router isis 1
     add ipv4 uni
      propagate level 2 into level 1 route-policy L2_TO_L1

Copy

    #R1
    mpls label range 100 199 static 1000 1999
    mpls static binding ipv4 20.20.20.20 255.255.255.255 1000
    mpls static binding ipv4 20.20.20.20 255.255.255.255 output 10.1.2.2 2000
    !
    ip route 20.20.20.20 255.255.255.255 10.1.2.2
    
    #R2
    mpls label range 200 299 static 2000 2999
    mpls static binding ipv4 20.20.20.20 255.255.255.255 2000
    mpls static binding ipv4 20.20.20.20 255.255.255.255 output 20.2.3.3 30
    !
    ip route 20.20.20.20 255.255.255.255 20.2.3.3

---

# Backdoor Link | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/backdoor-link.md)
.

Load **isis.inter.area.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnqSZfUQV7o4oZ3dSXiSz%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df62b9cef-e9e2-49c1-ba3e-7c442af1ae44&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b8a7e4a0f95c616f781d7b0d572d1b3f&sv=3)

Configure an additional link between R1 and XR2, using vlan 120 with subnet 20.1.20.0/24. Configure this link so that area 49.1234 and 49.1920 can reach each other directly without traversing the L2 backbone. Do not let traffic destined for any other areas run over this link.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/backdoor-link#id-20b92a02-3c5a-4a31-aea9-bf179532a6c3)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/backdoor-link#b119a468-49a5-4f2e-a8f9-808106e22f65)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The backdoor feature configures a L1/L2 router to do two things:

1.  Not set the ATT bit in L1 LSPs
    
2.  Continue installing a default route via other L1 routers that have the ATT bit set
    

On IOS-XE this is configured with **is-type level-1-2 backdoor**. On IOS-XR this is configured using **attached-bit send never-set**.

It seems that this feature leaked L2 routes into L1 in past software releases, but this does not seem to happen by default on current software. Nevertheless we can manually do this with L2 into L1 redistribution on the two routers. We don’t need to worry about leaking any other L2 routes, because this is a completely separate, disjointed L2 adjacency, only between these two routers.

On R1, notice that it now has an L2 adjacency but it does not set the ATT bit in its L1 LSP. It is not _truly_ attached to the L2, it is just running a standalone backdoor link with another area.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKYt1ZJOBtWpgqbNLnLPz%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8107802d-4d95-4e28-99b1-9fc498e7d79b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3643ad0e93f3538dc5fdb1e8ce483b34&sv=3)

On R2, notice that it now learns L1 inter-area routes to area 49.1920 prefixes:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FcyAeahImFWalgCoBNwa7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5246b9e0-be03-4edc-93ea-015e6cef84da&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=dcf0cddc45f72dac938a4ad1b79be376&sv=3)

However, R3 and R4 do not learn these prefixes. This is because they are truly attached to the L2, so they reject L1 routes that have the Up/Down bit set.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FRNYaXRk6E3Dk7j09Dmxw%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D56853aef-a330-40bc-a19e-90977c77d310&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ed6dd8aee54257f3dd7961414032be39&sv=3)

Likewise, XR1 rejects the area 49.1234 inter-area L1 prefixes.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0Vj2V51uP7mjoh79mXLe%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1c10121e-aa26-4183-810e-4511d9a27de6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=18176040f39b483bb0bdddf4ffb11a58&sv=3)

However, L1-only routers in each area can use the backdoor link to directly reach each other.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Ff4A0dIjuFWHcM9XaXGqY%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De6fe9ae7-7a50-49de-b506-8aee60e61613&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6681d82a9d287939ede364f6cbfc17a4&sv=3)

[PreviousRoute Filtering](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/route-filtering)
[NextNon-Optimal Intra-Area routing](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/non-optimal-intra-area-routing)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/backdoor-link#id-20b92a02-3c5a-4a31-aea9-bf179532a6c3)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/backdoor-link#b119a468-49a5-4f2e-a8f9-808106e22f65)
    

Copy

    #R1
    int gi2.120
     encap dot1q 120
     ip add 20.1.20.1 255.255.255.0
     ip router isis
     isis network point-to-point
    !
    router isis
     is-type level-1-2 backdoor
     redistribute isis ip level-2 into level-1 route-map PERMIT_ALL
    !
    route-map PERMIT_ALL
    
    #XR2
    route-policy PERMIT_ALL
     pass
    end-policy
    !
    int gi0/0/0/0.120
     encap dot1q 120
     ip add 20.1.20.20/24
    !
    router isis 1
     is-type level-1-2
     add ipv4 uni
      attached-bit send never-set
      propagate level 2 into level 1 route-policy PERMIT_ALL
     !
     int gi0/0/0/0.120
      point-to-point
      add ipv4

---

# LDP Label Advertisement Filtering Challenge | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-label-advertisement-filtering-challenge.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

*   Configure LDP using IGP autoconfig on routers R2-R6 and XR1.
    
*   Configure all routers to only allocate labels for /32s.
    
*   In this topology, only R2 and XR1 are PEs. Configure R3 to obtain this output using inbound filtering:
    

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FwOYsSmCVAEBYKFmbY34X%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4e3505c6-4f25-4d6d-835d-043bcfd23558&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=962abba460fa8b8430fc302fd66af9d8&sv=3)

*   Configure the network so that R5 has this in its LFIB. Do this without configuring R5 itself:
    

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2ewjFlBt9sNukiZhCEMu%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4d1c9a5d-3ed6-44d3-a2c0-26ecac727220&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e3417c69ce55ed8f3bce571dc419f773&sv=3)

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-label-advertisement-filtering-challenge#id-56d2020b-0ad5-485c-92f6-764ef32f76e6)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Enable LDP and allocate only for /32s:

Verify that all routers only have /32 prefixes in their LFIB:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0OMJCjPvj6GHPA7WtNgW%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D454bcb61-0198-42b4-ab96-c4b71cd21576&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f592dec4d1e7f7e51a80a0b7e48f284a&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FC3cvvLGtVcLD7tz2xKW8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D20d4edf8-23d5-4de6-ad57-b2d2db10be9e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=13be74a4eaac78fb6742f693e159c59f&sv=3)

Configure R3 to filter all prefixes except for R2 and XR1’s loopback:

Note that you may need to clear LDP neighbors. R3 should now only have remote labels for 2.2.2.2/32 and 19.19.19.19/32

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOKUUVQBRi02j7ZMqjWRe%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2003d0ab-ae23-4c1f-908d-2129d9c538b5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=97365bcdae1ac07a47125230a7ba807d&sv=3)

Configure all of R5’s neighbors to only advertise labels for R2 and XR1’s loopback to R5:

R5 should now only have remote labels for 2.2.2.2/32 and 19.19.19.19/32

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FiuEJkni4RSVcrzVdwhCW%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D243c8432-545d-4703-a8cf-fca182d25cba&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ee8be57be2ae4c346a99667927c49b09&sv=3)

**NOTE:** Upon doing this lab again, I noticed that R4, R6, and XR1 are no longer advertising labels to any other peers besides R5! Instead I used a “to” ACL of any so that these routers advertise the PE loopbacks to all LDP peers, not just R5. We can also just omit the “to” portion and apply the advertisement filter to all peers by default.

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-label-advertisement-filtering-challenge#ec4db5e9-b0e1-4631-910e-38285412d0ce)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Before label allocation filtering was available, label control was achieved using inbound and outbound label filtering. As you can see, this is quite tedious, as you have to apply inbound filtering to every peer individually, or apply outbound filtering to a group of peers indentified in an ACL. Further, you are still left with several prefixes with no labels, because the router is still locally allocating labels. For example, on R5 we see local labels for 3.3.3.3/32, 4.4.4.4/32, etc., because it is allocating these locally, although it is not receiving any remote bindings for them.

Also remember that when using outbound label filtering, you must also turn off the default advertisement using **no mpls ldp advertise-labels** on IOS-XE and **mpls ldp label local advertise disable** on IOS-XR.

These days it is better to just use local label allocation. In this lab you allocated labels for host-routes, but you can also allocate based on a prefix-list (IOS-XE) or ACL (IOS-XR) using:

[PreviousLDP Inbound Label Advertisement Filtering](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-inbound-label-advertisement-filtering)
[NextLDP Implicit Withdraw](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-implicit-withdraw)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-label-advertisement-filtering-challenge#id-56d2020b-0ad5-485c-92f6-764ef32f76e6)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-label-advertisement-filtering-challenge#ec4db5e9-b0e1-4631-910e-38285412d0ce)
    

Copy

    #R2-R6
    router isis
     mpls ldp autoconfig
    !
    mpls ldp label
     allocate global host-routes
    
    #XR1
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      mpls ldp auto-config
    !
    mpls ldp
     label
       local
        allocate for host-routes

Copy

    #R3
    access-l 1 permit 2.2.2.2
    access-l 1 permit 19.19.19.19
    !
    mpls ldp neighbor 2.2.2.2 labels accept 1
    mpls ldp neighbor 4.4.4.4 labels accept 1
    mpls ldp neighbor 6.6.6.6 labels accept 1

Copy

    #R4, R6
    access-l 1 permit 2.2.2.2
    access-l 1 permit 19.19.19.19
    access-l 5 permit 5.5.5.5
    !
    mpls ldp advertise-labels for 1 to 5
    no mpls ldp advertise-labels
    
    #XR1
    ipv4 access-list R5
     10 permit ipv4 host 5.5.5.5 any
    !
    ipv4 access-list LDP_PREFIXES
     10 permit ipv4 host 2.2.2.2 any
     20 permit ipv4 host 19.19.19.19 any
    !
    mpls ldp
     address-family ipv4
      label
       local
        advertise
         disable
         for LDP_PREFIXES to R5

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    mpls ldp label
     allocate global prefix-list prefix-list
    
    #IOS-XR
    mpls ldp
     label
       local
        allocate for ACL

# Authentication | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication.md)
.

Load **isis.inter.area.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.inter.area.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fkej20q3WXtvEVVA7AOBH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da0fb641b-7705-416c-90ae-900af7515edc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=40c5d871662d3351d9606c8c4e3d51de&sv=3)

Configure area 49.1234 as follows:

*   R1-R2 should use HELLO123 as the hello password using the legacy syntax
    
*   R2-R3-R4 should all use HELLO234 as the password using MD5
    
*   The area should authenticate L1 LSPs and SNPs using “AREA1234” in clear text, but they should all be accepted if they do not contain authentication. Use the legacy syntax for this.
    

Configure area 49.0056 as follows:

*   R5-R6 should use HELLO56 as the hello password in plain text using the new syntax. Allow received Hellos to not contain authentication, or to contain wrong authentication.
    
*   The area should authenticate L1 LSPs and SNPs using “AREA56” in clear text. LSPs and SNPs should be accepted without authentication. Use the new syntax for this.
    

Configure area 49.1920 as follows:

*   XR1-XR2 should use HELLO1920 as the hello password using MD5.
    
*   The area should authenticate L1 LSPs and SNPs using “AREA1920” with MD5.
    

Configure authentication the entire domain as follows:

*   All inter-area L2 adjacencies should use the password “LEVEL2” with MD5
    
*   All L2 LSPs/SNPs shoud use the password “LEVEL2” with MD5, but all LSPs/SNPs should be accepted without authentication.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication#eab194fa-47dc-4914-8e30-56748efc63a5)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication#c18cc67a-193c-4e02-9207-5f31836df72a)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Authentication for ISIS can be quite configuration intensive. We’ll first go over authentication on IOS-XE.

### IOS-XE Authentication[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication#id-1c5c7d35-0b15-4738-89ba-1518aeb7e349)

To set the hello password using the legacy method, use the following command. This does not support MD5.

To set the hello password using the new syntax, use the following commands. This requires a key chain. It also supports MD5. Optionally, you can enable “send-only” which does not require the other side’s authentication to match or exist. You can also specify the level for each command. By default, both levels are used.

To set the authentication for L1 LSPs and SNPs, you can use the following legacy method. By default, only LSPs are authenticated. You use the **snp** command to enable SNP authentication, and use **send-only** or **validate** for the SNPs. LSPs will always be “validate” mode.

To set the authentication for L2 LSPs and SNPs using the legacy method, you essentially use the same command but with **domain-password**.

The newer syntax looks like the authentication for interfaces. You associate a key chain, and have the option of doing “send-only” for both LSPs and SNPs. You use **level-1** for area authentication, and **level-2** for domain authentication. It appears that both LSPs and SNPs are authenticated, and you cannot separate them (authenticating one but not the other).

### IOS-XR Authentication[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication#id-11ff72ce-67bf-4c5e-bde6-930e5ad6f230)

Authentication on IOS-XR is a bit more simple. You configure a hello-password as follows. The **accept** keyword is used to only accept incoming Hellos with that password, but not send Hellos with that password.

Area and Domain authentication work similarly to the new syntax for IOS-XE. Except you can authenticate LSPs without SNPs (which is the default choice). If you authenticate SNPs, it appears you must use the **send-only** keyword. Level 1 is used for area password, and level 2 is used for domain password.

[PreviousMulti Area](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/multi-area)
[NextConditional ATT Bit](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/conditional-att-bit)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication#eab194fa-47dc-4914-8e30-56748efc63a5)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication#c18cc67a-193c-4e02-9207-5f31836df72a)
    
*   [IOS-XE Authentication](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication#id-1c5c7d35-0b15-4738-89ba-1518aeb7e349)
    
*   [IOS-XR Authentication](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/authentication#id-11ff72ce-67bf-4c5e-bde6-930e5ad6f230)
    

Copy

    #R1
    int Gi2.12
     isis password HELLO123
    !
    router isis
     area-password AREA1234 authenticate snp send-only
    
    #R2
    int Gi2.12
     isis password HELLO123
    !
    int Gi2.23
     isis authentication mode md5
     isis authentication key-chain ISIS_HELLO
    !
    int Gi2.24
     isis authentication mode md5
     isis authentication key-chain ISIS_HELLO
    !
    router isis
     area-password AREA1234 authenticate snp send-only
    !
    key chain ISIS_HELLO
     key 1
      key-string HELLO234
    
    #R3
    int Gi2.23
     isis authentication mode md5
     isis authentication key-chain ISIS_HELLO
    !
    int Gi2.34
     isis authentication mode md5
     isis authentication key-chain ISIS_HELLO
    !
    int Gi2.36
     isis authentication mode md5
     isis authentication key-chain ISIS_HELLO_L2
    !
    router isis
     area-password AREA1234 authenticate snp send-only
     authentication mode md5 level-2
     authentication key-chain ISIS_DOMAIN_AUTH level-2
     authentication send-only level-2
    !
    key chain ISIS_HELLO
     key 1
      key-string HELLO234
    !
    key chain ISIS_HELLO_L2
     key 1
      key-string LEVEL2
    !
    key chain ISIS_DOMAIN_AUTH
     key 1
      key-string LEVEL2
    
    #R4
    int Gi2.24
     isis authentication mode md5
     isis authentication key-chain ISIS_HELLO
    !
    int Gi2.34
     isis authentication mode md5
     isis authentication key-chain ISIS_HELLO
    !

    #XR1
    router isis 1
     lsp-password hmac-md5 AREA1920 level 1

     !

     !

     !

     !

# LDP/IGP Sync (ISIS) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-isis.md)
.

Load **isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

*   Configure LDP authentication for XR2 on XR1, using pass LDP1920. Do not configure XR2.
    
*   Configure LDP authentication for R6 on XR1, using pass LDP619. Do not configure R6.
    
*   Configure LDP for all routers using autoconfig under ISIS
    
*   Configure LDP sync so that all traffic from R1 to XR2 is always sent over R5-XR1 instead of R6-XR1 when LDP is not between R6-XR1.
    
*   Configure the XR1-R6 link so that the IGP waits for LDP to be up for 20 seconds before reducing the metric.
    
*   Configure ISIS for wide-style metrics on all routers.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-isis#id-65e07f77-8335-4d05-ad9c-d720fb99f303)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-isis#b67ab131-6574-42e3-9dbd-46dd6298645a)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MPLS LDP/IGP sync for ISIS works very much the same as OSPF. The one small difference is that the max link metric for wide metrics is not (max-1), instead it is (max-2). This is because 16777215 has a special meaning in ISIS, which is that the link should be completely excluded from the graph. So instead, 16777214 is used as the “max metric.”

Also, note that when enabling LDP sync for ISIS on IOS-XR, we must apply this to each interface individually. This is a bit cumbersome. You could use an apply-group instead.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-isis#id-2a7d7292-5532-40cd-b293-759069ef31b5)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Currently, XR1 is not in sync with R6 or XR20 due to the LDP auth mismatch. We can verify this on XR1 using **show mpls ldp igp sync**.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Ft7duqL4ERAIuAPqDmym0%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D602af195-f4c3-450e-9dff-5f0576846b6d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2332531799c8cbdea77e2d0ebff6ea20&sv=3)

There are alternative routes to all prefixes, except for XR2’s loopback. XR2 is essentially a stub router. Notice that the metric is (max-2), not (max-1). The LDP/IGP sync feature will never make prefixes unreachable, it just discourages the use of links by setting the metric value as high as possible.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvU6HQUYmUlIbym5mRSDb%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D195da236-15e7-4e8c-aa57-897ecf019c72&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b51924b5087392c8ff1cfd0585783cab&sv=3)

16777215 (max-1) has a special meaning in ISIS, which is that the link should be considered unusable. IOS-XR allows us to set this metric manually using “maximum” and warns us that all routers will exclude this link from their SPF.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhQmuMQJPVyAqws4VyXXj%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df5b400ad-ed5a-4502-8aa5-e9b228c4a2e6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e3de0d5c9a3e46c97bc1746400b5b6ca&sv=3)

If we set this, the metric will still be 16777214 since LDP is not sync’ed yet. (Essentially, the rule is: If LDP is not synced, metric=(max-2)). If we bring up LDP on XR2, we can cause XR2 to become unreachable due to this (max-1) metric value on the link.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAUrwT57QZO5tUnFp1pLp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd8940a57-ba9f-430b-a2cb-a02a17623fba&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=49daa5c6c5151b3e202e0cfb365fe031&sv=3)

Now the prefix to 20.20.20.20/32 is not even present in the RIB:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fl9qZ84T4kbLv4jKcXRVg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddd873d3f-b6be-4a3e-87da-0432ddb1eff4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cfa6fe26648ca1ffd67b43c95cd80c30&sv=3)

Moving on to R6-XR1. Just like with OSPF, the ISIS interface metric for R6-XR1 is still configured as 10, so that is the value shown in the ISIS show output on XR1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPsHqSvTLJLIE2JybY0Or%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9ae600b7-7f7f-4cf1-b1d9-f800fb868ba9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=329d413332cff5236cef0df1e7a9b0f6&sv=3)

However, if we inspect the database, we see that the metric is actually (max-2) right now. Note that the link type is broadcast, and XR1 is the DIS.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhT1mh5hc8xT9CtPzzvr1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3eafc9f0-4492-47a9-ad0a-021d2fd28976&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6bd7f359e6d885d52b33e59bc3877b19&sv=3)

Let’s bring up the R6-XR1 LDP session and verify that the sync delay works on IOS-XR.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F10rl7bo813CX5QpNfDnp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dca19dd25-d987-49d4-aaa4-9fb1ef7b1e43&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1d1504cdbeb79ead10af6125a7d62dff&sv=3)

[PreviousLDP/IGP Sync (OSPF)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-ospf)
[NextLDP Local Allocation Filtering](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-local-allocation-filtering)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-isis#id-65e07f77-8335-4d05-ad9c-d720fb99f303)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-isis#b67ab131-6574-42e3-9dbd-46dd6298645a)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/ldp/ldp-igp-sync-isis#id-2a7d7292-5532-40cd-b293-759069ef31b5)
    

Copy

    #R1-R6
    router isis
     mpls ldp autoconfig
     mpls ldp sync
     metric-style wide
    
    #R6
    int Gi2.619
     mpls ldp igp sync delay 20
    
    #XR1
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      mpls ldp auto-config
      metric-style wide
     int gi0/0/0/0.519
      add ipv4 
       mpls ldp sync
     int gi0/0/0/0.619
      add ipv4 
       mpls ldp sync
     int gi0/0/0/0.1920
      add ipv4 
       mpls ldp sync
    !
    mpls ldp
     neighbor 6.6.6.6:0 password clear LDP619
     neighbor 20.20.20.20:0 password clear LDP1920
     int gi0/0/0/0.619
      igp sync delay on-session-up 20
    
    #XR2
    router isis 1
     add ipv4
      mpls ldp auto-config
      metric-style wide
     int gi0/0/0/0.1920
      add ipv4 
       mpls ldp sync
    !
    mpls ldp

Copy

    #XR1
    group ISIS
     router isis '1'
      interface 'GigabitEthernet.*'
       address-family ipv4 unicast
        mpls ldp sync
    !
    router isis 1
     apply-group ISIS

Copy

    #XR1
    mpls ldp
     neighbor
      no 20.20.20.20:0 password

Copy

    #R6
    mpls ldp nei 19.19.19.19 password LDP619

# Troubleshooting TE Tunnel | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-te-tunnel.md)
.

Load **isis.with.te.tshoot.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:isis.with.te.tshoot.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:isis.with.te.tshoot.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

A TE tunnel is setup on R1 with destination XR2. The tunnel is not coming up. Without making any changes to any other router besides R1, bring the tunnel up.

Do the same for the TE tunnel on XR2 with destination R1.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-te-tunnel#id-5d9a0452-ec88-425f-b382-30982909d9cb)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-te-tunnel#id-0eec46d9-b90b-4c28-b389-66225d4ac9b3)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On R1, we see that the tunnel is down due to no path to the destination. However, this by itself does not tell us all that much.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKZQUSQHyoYMfcIq2dUog%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da83631ec-ec98-4f7f-986b-7058e0ec5c4a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9cddec11298e305c1581012bf6c0d8c3&sv=3)

If we **debug mpls traffic-eng path lookup**, we still don’t get that much useful output. We see tha tthe path lookup simply failed - a path cannot be found.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FSGf1dxmxUz24Vd7eFwu2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9e3bb69e-4c3a-457a-b1fa-78c6a848e080&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e69884b4545d28dc6bf579e97accfb68&sv=3)

If we look at the TED, we come across a hint. The node R2 is marked with “no SPF.”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2KYxrHXJ8jDoK7zUz3pU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2758e0ad-b71f-43e9-9c2e-ec40b3c85ede&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7e613d7956849bb4cc138507d08110ac&sv=3)

The reason for this is that R2 has the overload bit set:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPoFQlZ4L56R0en00eOWN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfdba6c8e-5d1c-42df-890c-9f590cdfaa48&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d9be87181662b2d51f84116b57d21c8b&sv=3)

When a node has the OL bit set, it cannot be used in CSPF for TE calculation. Recall that an ISIS node with the OL bit set can never be used as transit for any prefixes (other than directly attached prefixes), so this makes sense that the node cannot be used in CSPF either. However, we can force the router to ignore the OL bit for TE tunnels using the following command:

By allowing mid nodes to have the OL bit set, the tunnel will come up on R1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fg9zFZiUTBcfVcSvh3tkd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D90bbddab-eb39-4184-977b-0a299e45ff42&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e9996ac80a92b0234b8536a2e8f3255d&sv=3)

### IOS-XR as the headend[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-te-tunnel#id-99c8243b-762a-4357-8447-05bb677c5b60)

Fortunately, IOS-XR gives us much better indication of the issue. We know that some transit node has the OL bit set, but not which node.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMemL8wYepXDUOx0inVEs%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D74f0d56a-aaab-4ad8-b5c0-5c0e48fc8ad9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d0563b2b21a1a58b3a1786e9f7cdb997&sv=3)

The TED on XR2 shows us that R2 is overloaded:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fq8mbf4HmvtQkdx4UiXRt%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da58e0fbe-2045-45f4-9693-1737807d19f8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=17814c8033d9cbd9c154ba21b0bc5d8a&sv=3)

A similar command allows us to still use overloaded routers for TE tunnels:

By ignoring the OL bit for mid nodes, we can get the tunnel to come up:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJyqSFFDhsRHG1Ib0foFn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D32e9ab90-2a63-4720-84c5-2ef0782e71be&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=aeddb8e68e28394a43eb1c0e5c3189f9&sv=3)

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-te-tunnel#id-5d9a0452-ec88-425f-b382-30982909d9cb)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-te-tunnel#id-0eec46d9-b90b-4c28-b389-66225d4ac9b3)
    
*   [IOS-XR as the headend](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/isis/troubleshooting-te-tunnel#id-99c8243b-762a-4357-8447-05bb677c5b60)
    

Copy

    #R1
    mpls traffic-eng path-selection overload allow middle
    
    #XR2
    mpls traffic-eng
     path-selection
      ignore overload mid

Copy

    #R1
    mpls traffic-eng path-selection overload allow head|middle|tail

Copy

    #XR2
    mpls traffic-eng
     path-selection
      ignore overload head|mid|tail

# Basic TE Tunnel w/ ISIS | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/basic-te-tunnel-w-isis.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.init.with.isis.cfg** or **mpls.te.init.with.isis.and.rsvp.cfg** (to skip enabling RSVP-TE)

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.init.with.isis.cfg
    ! or
    config replace flash:mpls.te.init.with.isis.and.rsvp.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.init.with.isis.cfg
    ! or
    load bootflash:mpls.te.init.with.isis.and.rsvp.cfg
    commit replace
    y

The basic IP addresses, L3VPN between XRv14 and XRv13, and ISIS has been pre-configured.

Currently traffic between XRv14 and XRv13 is not working because LDP is not running in the core. Configure an RSVP tunnel on the PEs, CSR8 and XRv11, that takes the following path (both forward and reverse):

*   CSR8
    
*   CSR9
    
*   CSR2
    
*   CSR10
    
*   XRv11
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/basic-te-tunnel-w-isis#faf106ab-8d29-4d93-9a33-679503d7b22a)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This lab is the same as the previous lab, except ISIS is used instead of OSPF. First we must enable MPLS-TE globally and per-link, and RSVP per-link. This step is skipped if you loaded **mpls.te.init.with.isis.and.rsvp.cfg**

Now we enable MPLS-TE on the IGP (ISIS)

We can use **show mpls traffic-eng topology br** on any router to verify that all routers have advertised their TE attributes and populated the TED.

Now we configure the TE tunnels as before.

Tracing between XRv13 and XRv14 verifies the path is correct:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFnfamiHq0VjrC7smMNXc%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd3af285c-1d1e-4561-91c8-c012a0bad24f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2bf05b4743299747389e4a5d097e2871&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2B4So5v0LeJ8f9jYuSWx%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D21ff5655-b611-40f3-8ec9-19ffed78ee05&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=47afc84cfcf1e82ff5b30dace7d3da0f&sv=3)

Theory[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/basic-te-tunnel-w-isis#edcc17b6-5d82-466d-9ada-5fb68a74a497)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

ISIS was easily extended to support MPLS-TE thanks to its implementation of TLVs. MPLS-TE uses sub-TLVs within the extended IS reachability TLV (22). This requires support for wide-metrics to be enabled.

We can see this in the ISIS LSPDB using the **verbose** keyword:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F16yi91vQ3lkfSuPfEuuu%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd22c07d3-4fa3-499d-967d-7b8b876b02c8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=eb4f2fc249ae1796b1588c000e9d0c5d&sv=3)

You can also see this same information with **show isis mpls traffic-eng advertisements**.

A pcap of the TLVs that enable MPLS-TE is shown below. The Extended IS Reachability TLV has serveral sub TLVs that advertise the TE metric, affinity, and bandwidth of each link.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FjvUb9p4lUvq65FV1VOHX%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D45d78699-ff9a-42b5-8806-ec0e537d82b3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4f9ba29691f88f97535d1952dde0ba3e&sv=3)
