# Tunneling LDP inside RSVP | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/tunneling-ldp-inside-rsvp.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.ldp.tunneling.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.ldp.tunneling.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.ldp.tunneling.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

The basic IP addresses, L3VPN between XRv14 and XRv13, ISIS, RSVP, and MPLS-TE has been pre-configured.

There is currently a TE tunnel between CSR9 and CSR10 that goes via CSR2. This is bidirectional. CSR8 and XRv11 have been modified via ISIS metric to use CSR9 and CSR10 as the bestpath to CSR8/XRv11.

Make the necessary configuration changes so that XRv14 and XRv13 can ping each other in their L3VPN. Do not add any additional TE tunnels.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/tunneling-ldp-inside-rsvp#a9b18bd0-feaa-48fb-a221-4f4264a95286)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

First we must enable LDP between CSR8↔CSR9 and CSR10↔XRv11:

You may think we have an end-to-end LSP between CSR8 and XRv11 at this point, however the L3VPN traffic is not working. Here’s what happens:

*   CSR8 pushes a label stack of { < CSR9’s label for XRv11> < VPN label> }
    
*   CSR9 pops the top label and pushes the TE label: { < TE label to CSR10 > < VPN label > }
    
*   CSR2 pops the top label and delivers to CSR10 with just { <VPN label> }
    
*   CSR10 drops the traffic
    

To solve this, we must run LDP within the TE tunnel, between CSR9 and CSR10. Then CSR9 will need to push two labels: the TE tunnel label and the LDP label for XRv11 learned from CSR10. Both functions are enabled simply by enabling LDP on the tunnel interface.

An LDP adjacency between CSR9 and CSR10 will come up. This is a targetted session. LDP is not actually running over the tunnel. Instead think of this as enabling LDP functionality on the tunnel. A targetted session is established, and the router will push the TE tunnel endpoint’s LDP label onto traffic forwarded down the tunnel.

Now the label stack outgoing from CSR9 looks like this: { <TE label> <CSR10’s LDP label for XRv11> <VPN label> }

Traffic between XRv13 and XRv14 is working:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FwSOL6s6J8xXRoF1UNV0Z%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1123dcfe-d635-4983-a3c6-65b9bd5198f7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=63bf5bb08b415ab8dc78be8691237c39&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FynshXWqNi0w5PoFE7yXt%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De6167195-0279-4473-b506-114b1ed8c2ac&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d4c8605dae14ac4fc51b0d719d41b27b&sv=3)

The **mpls ip** command on a TE tunnel instructs the router to form a targetted LDP session with the tunnel destination, and to push the tunnel destination’s LDP label as a second label when forwarding traffic through the RSVP tunnel. (The top label is the RSVP label learned from the downstream RSVP peer as usual).

Conclusion[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/tunneling-ldp-inside-rsvp#id-11fa9dfe-9e54-405a-82e3-8e356e016ad4)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

TE tunnels might be isolated to only the core between P routers. This could be done to provide FRR within the core, and help with scalability, because now you are not forming a full mesh of tunnels between all PE routers. However, you need to tunnel LDP within the TE tunnels so that the label is not prematurely popped, exposing the VPN label too early, which blackholes traffic.

Further Reading[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/tunneling-ldp-inside-rsvp#id-380da2e6-e0b7-49b7-ab18-81236cb6540a)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CSPF Tiebreakers | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cspf-tiebreakers.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure two separate TE tunnels from R8 to XR11, and two separate TE tunnels from XR11 to R8.

*   Each tunnel should reserve 200M of bandwidth.
    
*   The only path-option should be dynamic.
    
*   Find a way to ensure that the R8 → XR11 tunnels take the same path, and the XR11 → R8 tunnels take the same path. Do not manipulate TE/IGP cost in the network.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cspf-tiebreakers#fe98c550-4779-4838-b09a-52502c479c07)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cspf-tiebreakers#id-11acf9ce-df9c-45fa-b1ba-221214248e55)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

CSPF must always choose one single path. ECMP is never an option. When ECMP routes are found by CSPF, the following tiebreaker takes place:

*   Choose the path that has the least used bandwidth. This will balance TE tunnels among paths as each new TE tunnel is setup.
    
*   If there is still a tie, choose the path with the least number of hops.
    
*   If there is still a tie, choose a path at random.
    

We can control the first tiebreaker with the following command:

The default is **min-fill**. By using **max-fill**, we instead choose the path that has the _most_ used bandwidth. This will end up filling up a path with TE tunnels first, loading one path completely until putting new TE tunnels on a second path.

By using **random**, we bypass the bandwidth evaluation completely, not caring about how much available bandwidth is on the ECMP paths, and instead just always choosing one path at random.

To solve this lab, we can set the path-selection to use **max-fill**. This will cause all LSPs to always take the same path, if that path has enough bandwidth, because the router is trying to load a single path as much as possible before using alternate ECMP paths.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cspf-tiebreakers#aaefb4ea-8129-4818-8954-72b126667ea2)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

First, before changing the default path-selection, we setup the two TE tunnels one-by-one on R8. First tun1 is setup.

This tunnel was setup with the path: R8-R9-XR12-XR11

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FU7N0aR52Xpbi4Pcnfecv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D848bd9b1-5eef-4ee3-ad8f-f06bfea3e6b3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d7604367df9383b92677420725b54ca9&sv=3)

We’ll now setup tunnel2. By default, it should use a path with the least-filled bandwidth, so it should not go over R9 and XR12.

This second tunnel is setup over the path: R8-R6-R10-XR11. The reason is that R8 has two ECMP paths to XR11. The R9-XR12 path already has reserved bandwidth (200M), so 800M is available. The R6-R10 has 1000M available, so that path has the min-fill bandwidth.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FYxqMmcqm7qumV3dt00Ip%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5b22a46a-49aa-47ea-9af8-e47affec1c31&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5086c1d60eb3fc24d5bf03ea918062a5&sv=3)

We can change this by shutting down the tunnels, setting the tiebreaker to use **max-fill**, and re-signalling the tunnels.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FWCTf9HDymX0WQIRu0eII%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7497c2d5-90b9-4649-9fd5-78c8e4eecc50&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6db8f27258ee64120ea3efbb0d09ab14&sv=3)

Both tunnels now take the same path:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvvvOd66qpCIYBIjLbMEK%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D875c6913-2574-4141-9245-2b63441a1c0b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f1d5fe9b9a6b5c0995473849533415a8&sv=3)

We’ll now do the same on XR11. Before changing the default tiebreaker, we’ll setup tun1 and then tun2. First, we have to bring down the R8 tunnels, because the R9-XR12 path has very high bandwidth load.

Notice that IOS-XR has the same default behavior (min-fill). The two TE tunnels are balanced between two paths. First R6-R8 is loaded by random. Then for tunnel-te2, the R6-R8 path has 800M available, while the XR12-R9 path has 1000M available, so the XR12-R9 path is choosen due to least-fill.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fyfhgj8wVonMreoFVsq6d%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D64de7473-0d58-4e9c-a916-0fdc10408123&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e04e31fb2c2b6cd118245582df0da2b1&sv=3)

We can change this behavior by bringing down the tunnels and re-calculating them using max-fill.

Notice that the two TE tunnels now take the same path. First, R6-R10 is used by random. Then for tunnel-te2, R6-R10 has the most used bandwidth, so it is used again.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FoEgznVhn3K8IJ9aKKlOm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5fc4d43e-6fb5-4070-8d79-bac09da2e373&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d1d2bbb8ae8d4cd3e34c4f581cc2199b&sv=3)

### Shortest Hop Count[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cspf-tiebreakers#id-05ea9edd-3584-43a7-8aa0-46af1ae66dfb)

We can test the shortest hop count tiebreaker by artificially changing IGP metrics. The OSPF ref BW has been changed so that each link has a cost of 10. The link costs have then be manually manipulated to produce a 5 hop path from R8-R9-R2-R5-XR11 with cost 28, and a 4 hop path from R8-R6-R12-XR11 with cost 28.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5wrHq9pjI9zzNZD6VR7h%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfd94bdc2-754f-417a-9c04-924620bd14e2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=918a419c13c9afaa30ab9869348d7dd1&sv=3)

We have removed the max-fill tunnel-selection, so it is back to min-fill. When we signal the first path, it takes the R8-R6-XR12-XR11 path due to the shortest hop count.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FxykebOYcQxecfEZ9hqI9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1fda10be-25f2-4968-8990-f17e977618ee&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f80abd1f10810bffd4a56b60922aa6ae&sv=3)

Next, we signal tunnel2. It uses the R8-R9-R2-R5-XR11 path, because it is now less filled. Notice that the router shows that the R8-R6-XR12-XR11 path is still the “shortest” path, even though tunnel2 was signaled through the longer hop path through R2.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FtMd4xy1pkBCls2nswoTt%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D71503fc5-007d-4339-9514-3b749658beb6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cb848151d2be59285197ae9ea5dd254f&sv=3)

[NextTE Tunnel Preemption](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-preemption)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cspf-tiebreakers#id-11acf9ce-df9c-45fa-b1ba-221214248e55)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cspf-tiebreakers#aaefb4ea-8129-4818-8954-72b126667ea2)
    
*   [Shortest Hop Count](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cspf-tiebreakers#id-05ea9edd-3584-43a7-8aa0-46af1ae66dfb)
    

Copy

    #R8
    mpls traffic-eng path-selection tiebreaker max-fill
    !
    int tun1
     description R8_TO_XR11_PATH1
     tun destination 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 200000
    !
    int tun2
     description R8_TO_XR11_PATH2
     tun destination 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 200000
    
    #XR11
    mpls traffic-eng
     path-selection
      tiebreaker max-fill
    !
    int tunnel-te1
     description XR11_TO_R8_PATH1
     destination 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 dynamic
     signalled-bandwidth 200000
    !
    int tunnel-te2
     description XR11_TO_R8_PATH2
     destination 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 dynamic
     signalled-bandwidth 200000

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    mpls traffic-eng path-selection tiebreaker max-fill|min-fill|random
    !
    ! OR
    !
    int tun1
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-selection tiebreaker max-fill|min-fill|random
    
    #IOS-XR
    mpls traffic-eng
     path-selection
      tiebreaker max-fill|min-fill|random
    !
    ! OR
    !
    interface tunnel-te1
     path-selection
      tiebreaker max-fill|min-fill|random

Copy

    #R8
    int tun1
     description R8_TO_XR11_PATH1
     tun destination 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 200000

Copy

     description R8_TO_XR11_PATH2
     tun destination 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 200000

Copy

    #R8
    int tun1
     shut
    int tun2
     shut
    
    #XR11
    int tunnel-te1
     description XR11_TO_R8_PATH1
     destination 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 dynamic
     signalled-bandwidth 200000
    !
    !
    commit
    !
    !
    int tunnel-te2

     destination 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 dynamic

Copy

    no int tunnel-te1
    no int tunnel-te2

    !

# Start | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/start.md)
.

These labs use the XRd topology, called topology1. Note that I initially did these labs with XRv9K version 7.7.1. Almost everything is supported identically on XRd, except for L2 vlan rewrites. This is noted in the EVPN-VPWS lab.

To begin, run the following command on your containerlab machine:

Copy

    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    containerlab deploy -t topology1/topology1.clab.yml --reconfigure

Once all nodes are started, run the following command to transfer the config files to all nodes. These files will be used to change between startup configs for subsequent labs.

Copy

    python3 transfer_configs_to_nodes.py

The script will prompt you for a directory name. Enter "topology1".

Use the MTPutty session file located in **topology1/topology1\_putty\_sessions.xml** to quickly setup your SSH sessions to the nodes. Go to **Server - Import Tree** and browse for the file.

When you are done with the lab, use the following command to wipe it:

Copy

    containerlab destroy -t topology1/topology1.clab.yml

[PreviousSRv6](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6)
[NextTopology](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/topology)

# TE Tunnel Preemption | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-preemption.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.preemption.initial.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.preemption.initial.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.preemption.initial.cfg
    commit replace
    y

The basic IP addresses, L3VPN between XRv14 and XRv13, OSPF, RSVP, and MPLS-TE has been pre-configured.

Tun1 between CSR8 and XRv11 is pre-configured. Link affinities are set such that there is only one possible path from CSR8 to XRv11 on tun1.

Currently there is a tunnel setup from CSR8 to CSR5 using the same affinity with 700 meg of bandwidth. No shut tun1 on both CSR8 and XRv11. This tunnel requires 500 meg of bandwidth. Notice that it cannot be setup. Use tunnel priority, using the worst priority possible, so that XRv14 and XRv13 can reach each other.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-preemption#id-3a8a558f-d4d7-4dc9-938c-981097d16248)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Notice that when you try to no shut tun1, CSPF cannot find a valid path. This is because link affinity 0x1 is only on the path CSR8-CSR9-CSR10-XRv11, which currrently has a 700meg tunnel from CSR8 to CSR5 (CSR8-CSR9-CSR10-CSR5).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fis6IKkc4uqUBdQsctTwz%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3fa5e244-ecd0-480e-9681-7fa3269f6c0c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c97692f15170609f84b48e64a82b17eb&sv=3)

On XRv11 when we no shut the tunnel we see the same thing:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOMoJy0x9zQELNv8GdXKY%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D81b8da5d-0e53-449a-a809-70d2bf0d32d0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5522aa6b7a0e4f75298a046fb18f628d&sv=3)

First we’ll find the current priority of the CSR8↔CSR5 TE tunnel:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbZlbiMMjJGikBiKSjofv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd9a29133-bb0f-44e3-8119-7aab9fba677b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=afdb3acffe119d7932ce3e5fac4addca&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FClld7aNCwQmDmruadq0y%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D746da932-7b27-475d-9dc5-769c4e61bce1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cc5bafb12418d58c63425b9e92ceb948&sv=3)

We can also see this by using the TED and noticing that 700M of priority 4 bandwidth is reserved on nodes such as CSR9:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FWmb07yLdIQZsitkpqhWd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7c290685-29da-44ca-8e24-60c4b1cac82e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=219b5cb9e4033b2018e9669533c025ae&sv=3)

So to solve this, we must at minimum use a setup priority of 3 or better, because the tunnel’s hold priority is 4. This means that we must at minimum also use a hold priority of 3 or better. (Remember the setup prioroity cannot be better than the hold priority to prevent churn). Therefore the answer is to use a priority of 3 3 for the TE tunnel between CSR8 and XRv11.

Now the interfaces have only 500M reservered and it is as priority 3 bandwidth. The CSR8↔CSR5 tunnels have been preempted and gone down.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F7oGjWP250XqwqpLHyKL2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd3ee3af7-5635-43ba-9b88-c5bf0cfc91d2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2b9851cecc8e7084715faf306ee1a3b6&sv=3)

XRv13 and XRv14 should now be able to ping each other and trace over the correct path:

# Autoroute Announce Absolute Metric | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/autoroute-announce-absolute-metric.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.autoroute.announce.metric.xr.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.isis.cfg
    commit replace

Setup a dynamic TE tunnel from XR11 to CSR9. Configure autoroute annouce so that R8, R1, R4, and R9 are only reachable via the tunnel interface. But make sure that all destinations have the same exact IGP cost in the RIB.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/autoroute-announce-absolute-metric#id-5ea03718-fb2d-4da7-b0fc-e6123da48732)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The autoroute annouce absolute metric knob sets the static metric for the tunnel, and also uses this same metric for any destinations beyond the tunnel. Destinations beyond the tunnel do not increment in IGP cost.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FThTAz5pFOKua7L1OeScf%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D19de130b-1631-4bb9-a5b7-9329c97a414f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2e8ea81e7374467dc8cd3b09d9806932&sv=3)

Note that this metric change happens _after_ SPF has fully run. So for example, if we set this to 21, then the tunnel will not be used to get to R1, R4, and R8, even though those routes have a total IGP cost of 30. Additionally, the tunnel will not be used to R9 since the tunnel cost (21) is higher than the IGP cost to R9 (20).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FLFxpblBcVDe5Na7lszTr%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8c09998e-c7b5-4188-a89f-3ce1ca614803&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0a8ef48fb57d306c88ccef95600e1c09&sv=3)

Interestingly, setting this to 20 also removes any ECMP paths. This is because the IGP paths have a higher cost than the TE paths once the **metric absolute** command adjusts the TE paths from 30 down to 20.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FdEvcZZG7MduGvpkWCGaM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3fb8d6b7-13e7-43d1-a642-251082e71698&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c2b1072c21fd1c646beee4a2c58f3f27&sv=3)

Compare this to simply using **autoroute announce** with the default metric of 20:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F3SFNbcHGB7hEQH6xYS1N%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4b3d5c72-8569-4561-84dd-1a399218c5c2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=54a8ac7aecaa3598d94a538a5cb57ecb&sv=3)

# Forwarding Adjacency | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.forwarding.adjacency.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.forwarding.adjacency.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.isis.cfg
    commit replace
    y

A bidirectional TE tunnel is setup between CSR8 and CSR10 via CSR9. Use forwarding adjacency and IGP metric (if necessary) to force CSR2 to use only CSR10 to get to 8.8.8.8/32.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency#aedd1d0c-30c2-4624-9c30-6318ee7d2087)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Using forwarding adjacency announces the tunnel as an adjacency to the IGP. CSR8 lists an adjacency to CSR10 with the ISIS default metric (which is 10):

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrlBMMptoUcZcdSQBmtb7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1b53da26-6d09-4052-bb13-b08a4e476a71&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2b111f84ef24f35a072cdc795a0b0f5c&sv=3)

Likewise CSR10 announces the same adjacency to CSR8, and now all routers in the IGP include this link in the graph of the topology.

We will now see that CSR2 is doing ECMP to get to 8.8.8.8/32:

To force CSR2 to _only_ use CSR10’s tunnel, we can change the IGP metric of the tunnel or change the CSR2-CSR10 link cost. I thought we could change the TE tunnel’s isis metric but that doesn’t seem to work on CSR1000v. Instead I changed the link cost. (Note that on XRv, changing the ISIS metric of the tunnel _does_ work, by configuring it under ISIS just like any other interface).

CSR2 only uses CSR10 to get to 8.8.8.8/32:

                     [115/20] via 132.2.9.9, 00:00:09, GigabitEthernet2.529

# SRv6 uSID - Scale (Pt. 3) (UPA Walkthrough) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-3-upa-walkthrough.md)
.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FSZcXpYqvrAEHOBNVRqei%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Def17f94b-a29d-44cd-9739-976c8a1fec93&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2d7cd7c396e378b540e678fb060008e3&sv=3)

Although using a PCE for all end-to-end paths allows you to remove the leaking of loopbacks and locator prefixes into the L1 area, it is actually still not all that scalable. You will have a SRv6-TE policy per-PE per-color. If you are mostly using ODN policies that use the IGP metric, you will have many many policies that simply take the IGP shortest path.

The most scalable solution, in my opinion, is to use summarization of both the locator prefixes and the loopbacks. In fact, the loopback can be within the locator prefix, so the locator prefix summary alone can cover the loopback and resolve the BGP nexthops.

The problem then becomes: how do you implement BGP PIC? If a PE withdraws its loopback route in a remote L1 domain, the L1/L2 router hides this via the summarization. So BGP PIC cannot be triggered.

To handle this, the local L1/L2 router can leak the /128 or /48 prefix into the L2 with a max metric. This is called UPA (unreachable prefix announcement). This signals that the specific route is not available anymore. (Remember that the maximum possible metric value in ISIS indicates an unreachable route). To enable this, you use the following keyword on the L1/L2 router:

The router will leak the specific /48 or /128 alongside the summary prefix with an unreachable metric value. This route will only exist for a pre-determined amount of time. This is controlled using the following config:

You can also use the **unreachable-component-tag** keyword with the summary-prefix. This limits UPAs to components of the prefix that have that specific tag.

The ingress PE must have the following configuration in order to react to the ureachable prefix announcement. Any nodes along the path do not need this command, such as another L1/L2 router for a remote domain. This command notifies the RIB of the unreachable route, which triggers BGP PIC on the ingress PE.

Note that these commands were released in version 7.8.1.

[PreviousSRv6 uSID - Scale (Pt. 2)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-2)
[NextSRv6 uSID - Scale (Pt. 4) (Flex Algo)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-4-flex-algo)

Last updated 1 year ago

Copy

    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      summary-prefix fd00:0000:1000::/40 adv-unreachable

Copy

    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      prefix-unreachable
       adv-lifetime 1000          ! in seconds. Default is 180 seconds.

Copy

    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      summary-prefix fd00:0000:1000::/40 adv-unreachable unreachable-component-tag 100

Copy

    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      prefix-unreachable
       rx-process-enable

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-using-link-affinity.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg** or **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.and.affinity.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    ! or
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.and.affinity.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    ! or
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.and.affinity.cfg
    commit replace

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F21qEc87zwWXVQmdioVqi%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da51804ec-fa6b-4bfd-96fd-164a8a6f2588&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6becbb6a92585d94066d5d09978a232e&sv=3)

Configure link affinities as show in the diagram above. If you use the config file **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.and.affinity.cfg**, the affinities will already be pre-configured.

Create the following TE tunnels:

*   CSR8 to CSR5 without using orange links
    
*   XRv11 to CSR8 using only red links
    
*   CSR4 to XRv12 not using blue or green
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-using-link-affinity#id-6723914d-b8fa-41ce-b625-05ad510ed921)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

One router at a time, we set the link-affinity on the links themselves. Shown below is only CSR1:

On IOS-XR we can create affinity-maps and then assign colors to links:

Create the TE tunnels:

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-using-link-affinity#id-752beebf-a1ca-4d11-b592-7c4834ab0705)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

First we set link affinity on each interface individually. Each color is represented by a single bit. When set to one, that color is “turned on” or assigned to the link. When set to 0, the color is not assigned to the link.

To set multiple colors to a link we can simply add the values together. For example, for both red (0x1) and blue (0x4) we add them and assign the link 0x5. This is 0101 in binary.

We then create an affinity constraint on each tunnel. If we want the bit to _not_ match (”use links that are not orange”) we set that bit to 0 and the mask for that bit to one.

Let’s look in detail at how we can configure an instruction for “use links that are not orange.” Orange is 0x8, so we make sure affinity is 0XXX in binary. This is because we just need bit 4 to be zero in order to not use orange link. We make the mask match the four bit, so the mask is 0x1000. The rest of the bits are zero, because we don’t care if they are set or not. The tunnel affinity in hex becomes: 0x0 mask 0x8. This means “we care about bit 4, and the value must be zero.”

If we want the bit to match, we set the mask to 1 for that bit position. For example, to match all RED links, we use 0x1 mask 0x1. The affinity in binary is 0001, which is RED’s value. The mask is 0001 because we only care about the first bit matching for RED links. (We care about the RED bit being on).

With the mask we can only do AND logic. For example, match RED (0x1) and match _not_ BLUE (0x4): 0x1 mask 0x5. (The mask in binary is 0101 because we want to match the blue bit (4) as being 0, in addition to the first bit being 1 for RED).

We cannot do OR logic with a mask. You can’t say “match BLUE **or** RED” only “match BLUE **and** RED” / “match BLUE **and** not RED” / “match not BLUE **and** not RED” etc…

By default the tunnel affinity mask is 0xffff if you don’t specify it. The default affinity is 0x0 mask 0xffff if you don’t configure affinity at all. 0xffff means “match last 16 bits.” 0xffffffff would be “match all 32 bits.” This can potentially cause problems that might be hard to notice. If you color all your links and then don’t configure an affinity on the tunnel, CSPF may not find any path at all, because all links have some value in the last 16 bits and the tunnel is using 0x0/0xffff by default.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-using-link-affinity#id-16c2159f-3e54-4874-8d1c-25d38c959993)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can verify link affinity from any router in the area by inspecting the TED:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvacCmXcBghmecUYtElh5%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D593eb4b9-31f8-4e58-b381-2a0c72cf2224&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e915ad25ce7b4d63d8898a322e3aa4aa&sv=3)

The link affinity is advertised inside the opaque area LSA for each interface:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FR4KAnhTW85CEnQjCRnuz%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7ce388c4-3338-49ea-bb1d-7e994188ad90&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=fb7a2dc9ebf82a704ad257f699335a01&sv=3)

We can verify the affinity required on each tunnel, and verify the path the tunnel calculated:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2gqGNv2EHoFExLSk0vBA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ded4d70a7-a22e-4a53-9464-11e87829df87&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=100de111bce7492295b852cd079f5ff9&sv=3)

     ip unn lo0
     tunnel dest 5.5.5.5
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng affinity 0x0 mask 0x8   ! convert 1000 to hex 
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
    
    #XRv11 (to CSR8 using only red)
    int tunnel-te0
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel dest 8.8.8.8
     affinity 0x1 mask 0x1    ! convert 0001 to hex
     path-option 1 dynamic
    
    #CSR4 (to XRv12 not using blue or green)
    int tunnel0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel dest 12.12.12.12
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng affinity 0x0 mask 0x6   ! convert 0110 to hex
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic

# SRv6 uSID w/ Dual-Connected PE | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-dual-connected-pe.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.dual.pe.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.dual.pe.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.dual.pe.init.cfg

All routers are running both SR-MPLS and SRv6. The PEs are only using MPLS for the L3VPN.

Configure the PEs for dual-support of MPLS and SRv6. Use XR9 for MPLS VPN routes only, and XR10 for SRv6 VPN routes only. Once all four PEs are configured with support for both MPLS and SRv6, flip over to using SRv6 as the encapsulation instead of MPLS.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-dual-connected-pe#id-10fab814-8f7b-4c92-b394-3aadd35acd09)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-dual-connected-pe#id-87f31f15-9d00-4981-b207-fcea2849c576)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Instead of using an IWG, another option for migration from MPLS to SRv6 is to use dual-connected PEs. This reminds me of migrating LDP to SR. First LDP is enabled everywhere. Then you enable SR alongside LDP, but continue pushing only LDP labels. Then you change the label imposition to SR.

In this lab, SR-MPLS and SRv6 are already enabled. By default, BGP L3VPN will only use MPLS labels. To enable support for SRv6 _and_ MPLS, we must tell BGP to allocate an MPLS label, plus use SRv6 for the VRF:

When both MPLS and SRv6 SIDs are allocated, by default only the MPLS label is advertised. We also tell the router to use SRv6 SIDs as the encapsulation when advertising the VPN routes to XR10. When using a dual-connected PE for migration from SR-MPLS to SRv6, you typically want to have a separate RR for each encapsulation type to make the transition easier.

Lastly, we set LP lower so that the SRv6 routes are not used yet.

Now that step 1 is complete, we can verify that SRv6 SID advertisement is working correctly before we actually use it. We first see that all routes via the XR10 RR have a lower LP:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FR4Sh64L2LHyPYIS5QYAL%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db701fb94-d06e-41e9-8998-e3c7eaacf746&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7d342a737c858ee2ed96001cafd2608b&sv=3)

The VPN routes via XR10 have an SRv6 SID, while the routes via XR9 still only have an MPLS label:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FznDndSJJ6HGTD39tePgH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df9bdb504-a57e-4fd7-b6cd-2f3c6516a7f4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8c3dc63511fd946889de33a918f92ac6&sv=3)

All L3VPN routes still use MPLS encapsulation:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FCy1ellq81KqTBUfJCAvn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8cfae38c-d921-41a2-9b6a-db30c077c9a6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5ca00c42c1ddebc88c45ac64f1d91af3&sv=3)

Next, we set LP on the SRv6 routes to 110 to prefer them over the MPLS service routes.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FpoBqpVULnX1vf9mEYMej%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3401de3b-349e-47ae-bfb9-9b5b6baa92d3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cf1678948a3d8e79896aa29a1238f7ac&sv=3)

Traffic now uses SRv6 encapsulation:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXQBg8BxCExQM2H29fxMJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd5544bde-6ec8-4c19-8c9c-f08e23c449cb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=30cd214336cb81d0ce43576e4db3bc73&sv=3)

Similar to the LDP to SR migration, we can “flip the switch” and not incur any outage at all, as the control plane is fully setup for both SR-MPLS and SRv6 at the same time. If we needed to revert, we simply use LP to move back to using SR-MPLS encapsulation again.

[NextSRv6 uSID w/ Flex Algo](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-flex-algo)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-dual-connected-pe#id-87f31f15-9d00-4981-b207-fcea2849c576)
    

Copy

    # Step 1 - Enable SRv6 but still prefer MPLS by using LP
    #
    # XR5, XR6, XR7, XR8
    route-policy SET_LP($LP)
     set local-preference $LP
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 100
     segment-routing srv6
      locator CCIE
     !
     neighbor 2001:db8:200::a
      address-family vpnv4 unicast
       encapsulation-type srv6
       route-policy SET_LP(90) out
      address-family vpnv6 unicast
       encapsulation-type srv6
       route-policy SET_LP(90) out
     !
     vrf CUSTOMER
      address-family ipv4 unicast
       mpls alloc enable
       segment-routing srv6
        alloc mode per-vrf
      !
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       mpls alloc enable
       segment-routing srv6
        alloc mode per-vrf
    
    # Step 2 - Set LP higher on the SRv6 routes to prefer them over MPLS
    #
    # XR5, XR6, XR7, XR8
    router bgp 100
     neighbor 2001:db8:200::a
      address-family vpnv4 unicast
       route-policy SET_LP(110) out
      address-family vpnv6 unicast
       route-policy SET_LP(110) out

Copy

     segment-routing srv6
      locator CCIE

       segment-routing srv6
        alloc mode per-vrf
      !
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       mpls alloc enable

        alloc mode per-vrf

       encapsulation-type srv6
      !
      address-family vpnv6 unicast

# Forwarding Adjacency with OSPF | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency-with-ospf.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure a bidirectional TE tunnel between CSR8 and XRv11. Announce this TE tunnel into the IGP so that R5 will only use this TE tunnel to get to R8. Configure the tunnels so that when the tunnel goes down, the router waits 5 seconds before removing the tunnel from the IGP.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency-with-ospf#id-4f56002f-1b25-47ad-b0f4-1413713e74a6)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency-with-ospf#id-5494ef97-7e0f-49d3-b684-95b78edb0cda)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Using FA with OSPF has a few quirks on IOS-XE. First, if you configured the loopback interface for OSPF under the interface, you must activate OSPF on the tunnel explicitly. If you used the network command to activate OSPF on the loopback, then you don’t need to do this step.

Next, IOS-XE uses a very low bandwidth on the TE tunnel by default. This is the “physical line” bandwidth, not the RSVP signaled/requested BW for the LSP. This causes the OSPF metric to be extremely high. So you should set the OSPF metric manually.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsUDoLzeRdLS6rWJavyVd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df7149162-2472-44a0-b0d0-ba28368e3b5d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=03dfdd24c6b7f4ee34f9b0a127726799&sv=3)

IOS-XR doesn’t appear to have either of these problems. The TE tunnel’s bandwidth is 0, and the router uses an OSPF metric of 1 by default.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F06Afe0arJiQECsN0yudg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D089cd56e-88c7-470e-98dd-844ead994f95&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6b2277698695088b796fa216660b817f&sv=3)

The **holdtime** parameter is specified in msec. When the TE tunnel goes down, the router will wait for the **holdtime** interval before removing the link from the LSA or LSP. This allows the TE tunnel to briefly flap during path re-convergence without affecting the IGP.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency-with-ospf#id-92194846-e836-4292-a18f-b1bd3b70d674)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We should see the TE tunnel between R8-XR11 advertised as a link into the IGP. OSPF is not literally running over this link, so there is not actually an R8-XR11 adjacency that is maintained via OSPF Hellos. Instead, this allows routers in the area to use this link in their SPF calculations.

On R5, notice that R8 and XR11 report an adjacency with cost 1 between each other. To SPF on R5, this appears as just a regular link connecting them directly.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fwi9MfkGUnUHP0cziYbja%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da5fa5115-be02-441c-a8d1-8cd21de17c68&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c2625dbd12fb17c45a88e51e9862cd43&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FioyD09hB9SwzmwSb1j95%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da38acfa3-32b0-45dd-8d26-8585cec175ed&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=480e32359e8d49f0c6ba13b1d69dc602&sv=3)

R5 uses the TE tunnel as the primary path to R8 now, because the total cost is only 3 (1 to XR11, 1 for the TE tunnel, and 1 for the loopback of R8).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOYc0oRGirwl68bUxNPF8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D07e69ead-0e59-495b-8284-4ef9e10f26f5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6cacac80c5d56781a1dc04364f7be0ef&sv=3)

If the TE tunnel goes down, the routers will wait 5 seconds before removing their adjacency in the Router LSA. We can simulate this by running an extended ping on R5 to 8.8.8.8, and breaking MPLS TE on the R1, R6, and R9 links facing R8.

From this test, I see that R8 properly waits 5 seconds to remove the link to XR11, but XR11 removes the link immediately. Perhaps the holdtime functionality is not implemented in the XRv.

[PreviousForwarding Adjacency](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency)
[NextTE Tunnels with UCMP](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency-with-ospf#id-5494ef97-7e0f-49d3-b684-95b78edb0cda)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency-with-ospf#id-92194846-e836-4292-a18f-b1bd3b70d674)
    

Copy

    #R8
    int tun0
     tunnel dest 11.11.11.11
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng forwarding-adjacency holdtime 5000
     ip ospf 1 area 0
     ip ospf cost 1
    
    #XR11
    int tunnel-te0
     dest 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 dynamic
     forwarding-adjacency holdtime 5000

Copy

    #R8
    int tun0
     ip ospf 1 area 0

Copy

    #R8
    int tun0
     ip ospf cost 1

Copy

    #R5
    ping 8.8.8.8 repeat 100000000
    
    #R1
    int GigabitEthernet2.518
     no mpls traffic-eng tunnels
    
    #R6
    int GigabitEthernet2.568
     no mpls traffic-eng tunnels
    
    #R9
    int GigabitEthernet2.589
     no mpls traffic-eng tunnels

# SRv6 uSID | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.configured.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.configured.cfg

L3VPN for IPv4 and IPv6 is currently functional using SRv6 in the core.

Change the core to use uSID (microSID) instead. Use the block fd00:0000::/32 as the uSID block.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid#id-9b358110-0fa2-4d46-9c92-61514ea9881a)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid#id-7926eea5-51e5-4e95-a12e-dcca593bf25f)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

uSID (microSID) is an optimization for SRv6. uSID uses SID compression so that space in the IPv6 header is not wasted on duplication of bits (the common SID block and zero padding).

Let’s take an SR-TE policy that traverses five nodes, and ends with a function on the last node that has an instruction to decapsulate the packet and forward out an IPv4 VRF table. The SRH would look as follows. Remember that the zeroth index is the last segment, so this policy steers along the path R1-R2-R3-R4-R5, with a function on R5.

Notice that the the prefix is always the same (fd00:0000), and the zero padding is always the same. (Indexes 1 through 4 have all zeros after the third hextet). We can compress this SRH into a single 128-bit address by doing the following:

Each SID endpoint (R1, R2, R3, R4 and R5) must do a “shift and forward” operation to allow this to work. First, IPv6 routing carries the packet to R1 via the fd00:000:0001::/48 entry in IGP. R1 then sees that its own uSID is present, but the packet is not destined for itself. (There is no end-of-carrier (0000) following its own uSID, nor is there a local SID instruction (e000-ffff)). R1 deletes its own uSID, shifts the rest of the IPv6 address to the left 16 bits, and pads 16 bits of zeros at the end.

This process continues until the packet arrives at R5 with address **fd00:0000:0005:e0001::**. R5 has this entry in its FIB with a DT4 behavior.

The beauty of this compression is that MTU overhead is reduced, no SRH is needed (when using 6 or fewer uSIDs), and no change to basic SRv6 behavior needs to be made. There is no downside to using uSID compared to using “full” SIDs. Therefore most implementations of SRv6 these days use uSID from the beginning.

Cisco’s implementation requires a 32 bit uSID block and 16 bit uSID ID. A uSID carrier is a 128-bit SID that carries multiple uSIDs within it. Each uSID carrier starts with the 32 bit uSID block, and is followed by 16 bit uSIDs.

The 16 bit uSIDs can either represent a global node, or represent a local forwarding instruction (such as an Adj SID or a L3VPN forwarding instruction). In order to differentiate between global node uSIDs and local uSIDs, local uSIDs are always in the range e000-ffff. A local uSID must be proceeded by the node’s global uSID, just like we have seen with SR-MPLS. This allows the packet to be steered to the node which understands the local SID meaning.

To configure uSID, you simply use a ::/48 locator (32 bit block plus 16 bit ID). Additionally, you specify that the node will preform PSP and USD behavior. If the node is the penultimate endpoint (there is only one entry left in the SRH), it can perform PSP. If the node is the final endpoint, it can decapsulate the packet.

First, to accomplish this lab, we must remove the existing locator to be able to re-configure it for uSID. Then we re-define the SRv6 locator as a uSID locator.

There is also an option for **micro-segment behavior unode shift-only**, however this is not allowed to be committed on XRv9K. Presumably, this could be used for P-only routers, because they would only need to be SR-TE waypoints, and not decapsulate the header as an egress PE?

Just like with regular SRv6 using “full” SIDs, the locator is advertised into the IGP. This is already configured in this lab, so we don’t need to worry about this.

The nodes will advertise their locator into the IGP just as before, but now the END SID is a uN (microSID Node SID). The END.X SID is now a uA (microSID Adj-SID). The block length is now 32 bits, with the node ID length as 16 bits. Remember that this is not configurable. You must allocate the locator prefixes with this format in mind. This format is notated as F3216.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbwYLz8mkIF0pA7nRtPrl%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2f7d6c0f-8c29-430d-9c65-8660878a7eeb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ee70ca358136753b95c806678f39fb6d&sv=3)

In the SRv6 manager, we can see that the SID base block is actually a ::/24. This means we can configure multiple ::/32 locators but they must come from this ::/24. Typically the ULA space is used for uSID (fc00::/7).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fr45HGxukn2SI6b3822Sk%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5ba4c83b-0adc-465b-bdf3-f8f0e68095e4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=86fa6fca1ff83d71424f925d14642111&sv=3)

Notice that we can configure an additional locator with a block such as fd00:33::/32, but not fd00:1111::/32.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FIS4B6l2UfQox1N0foLAE%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1fcb1692-7b76-404c-8bb6-854e4f15b04c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e59aee1db0ce15bb7826286d0c4f0b23&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKnGJq7TsoNwU7Jej1fq0%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5e2c0446-06ee-4715-99d6-379f45211d53&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b9523608c2cb2086bbe4d152e57ab2e2&sv=3)

Each router will automatically begin allocating local uSIDs from the locator configured under the BGP services. For example, we can examine the local uSIDs allocated on XR5:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6q3Np0hJvQiUQtZnQd0D%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D09c8aaf4-081f-412c-9e61-18bd7b4376a4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1b748b22280101cefa2bbb87939be003&sv=3)

These are installed into the FIB, just as we have seen before with regular SRv6:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F93cd9aMbbKJrkoGf0pAi%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6aabe9c6-fa21-41a3-83ca-36e17d3be4c8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ea3a38374ee69f87f32666a114c12d63&sv=3)

Notice above that each uN SID has a ::/48 and ::/64 entry, and each uA SID has a ::/64 and ::/80 entry. When there are more uSIDs following the uN or uA, the ::/48 or ::/64 will be matched, respectively, and the node will only do shift and forward. When the end-of-carrier follows the ::/48, it will match the ::/64 or ::/80 entry (because the end-of-carrier is 16 bits of zeros). In this case, the PSP/USD behavior will happen instead of shift and forward.

All L3VPN services should still be working. Instead of a full SID, a uSID is advertised with the L3VPN route. The label now contains the local uSID (eXXX). Note that you need to ignore the trailing 0 in the label. For example, 0xe0020 is actually 0xe002.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvbevmMRKJYlACCSm3gwq%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6f7f46a4-cf89-4c31-a6a7-14486e136476&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3ce278f6fde97e4a2111418cf904857c&sv=3)

The detailed RIB entry references that the f3216 microSID format is used for encapsulating the customer packet and forwarding to XR7:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F3rxau6BnZKVLR06c9BM2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0f335078-985b-4ae8-935f-14bd9b1fc923&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0fb50d0cf8d7e7ef2912b5435afd67cc&sv=3)

Now that we have uSID configured, we can use SR-TE policies. We will see this in upcoming labs.

# SRv6 uSID w/ Flex Algo | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-flex-algo.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.flex.algo.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.flex.algo.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.flex.algo.init.cfg

Configure a new flex algo that minimizes latency.

*   Use flex algo #127
    
*   Use fd00:1::/32 for the uSID block
    

Latency values are already statically configured on all links.

Ensure that L3VPN traffic for the CUSTOMER VRF that is directed towards XR7 minimizes latency, by using flex algo #128.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-flex-algo#id-2fb9e60c-6d46-49a9-81e5-f22a678fc5b1)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-flex-algo#d4cce899-a26d-460c-8b95-a933a52ae2b3)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In link-state routing protocols, each router independently calculates a shortest cost path to every prefix. Because each router calculates this independently using the same algorithm, loop-freeness is ensured, and hop-by-hop routing works. (A circuit does not need to be established; routing is connectionless).

Flex-algo gives us the power to create a second topology by specifying a different optimization metric besides the IGP shortest cost, and also by specifying constraints. This allows us to gain TE capabilities without any state at all. (No SR-TE policies and no connection-oriented LSPs). This only works because every router in the IGP agrees that a given SID will use the associated algorithm for determining the best path. All routers in the IGP use the same exact algorithm for determining a SID’s best path, and hence the TE objective is realized without any state.

First we advertise the flex-algo definition into the IGP. Only one router must have this config, but for redundancy you should configure this on multiple routers. It’s no problem if every single router has this configuration.

This FAD (flex algo definition) is advertised into the IGP.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbKukHVTqWTbmtu6d7SXC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D47218bbf-e0f6-4a1b-acc3-9d3edcc4521d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=674e013442cd6b1f2ebcba26c1e1434a&sv=3)

If there are any conflicts in the definition for a given flex algo, the prioirty is used as the tiebreaker. The highest priority is best, and then the highest RID is best. We can see the results of the flex algo “election” using the following command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FX8oloEGl5x4PwZYdGNAy%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df743747b-ac86-4916-908f-b38b36bc3014&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cb4b8759b718e4788e84886c535d3fd0&sv=3)

Next we must create a SID that is associated with this flex algo. With SR-MPLS, we would simply add another prefix-SID to the loopback. With SRv6, we create a new locator.

The locator is advertised with algorithm 128 into the IGP:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMyTE3riNSyaNxiDbYcix%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd8035f2c-6085-49fd-aca1-fb4f16a60531&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ebecd81bafab1a464310092f31c3c17e&sv=3)

Now we can steer traffic using this locator. This will achieve routing based on lowest latency instead of lowest IGP cost, and it will do this without any SR-TE policies needed.

Although we have the ability to create an ODN policy that uses a particular flex algo, the SRv6 PCE cannot use flex algo as part of path computation. Normally we could do this:

However, the PCE will not successfully calculate a path. We can see this in the SRv6 SR-TE guidelines:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FcUNzkPZ7hpyLEKNRJgvy%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4aea46fe-fcb9-4b3f-8756-4b69bab88971&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d4c5edf5a746bd2fa758f3043e0fd2b0&sv=3)

Additionally, the headend can never compute its own dynamic paths. A PCE is always needed for dynamic SR-TE SRv6 policies.

Therefore, our only option appears to be to simply use the flex algo locator for the CUSTOMER VRF on R7. First we remove the global BGP locator and then set the specific locator for the address-families under the VRF:

Alternatively, we can leave the CCIE locator as the default locator under BGP, but specify the CUSTOMER VRF locator as the LATENCY locator.

Note that you can also control which locator is used on a per-prefix basis with an RPL:

We can see that XR7 now allocates a SID from the LATENCY locator instead of the CCIE locator:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJVgfXggRsGLmDte6x7Pd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D195b9c22-d42b-4d5d-a3df-5da197dfbd39&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7262a0e8e783fc773e5fb043c474b188&sv=3)

A traceroute to this SID gives us a sort of OAM verification. We can see that the path takes the lowest latency path to XR7:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzaddyN4HAbwqr5YGXvxh%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D99c71608-25b3-47f9-af20-476eb3bb71ce&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=129c7d9981e20bca948f2035a72e2a0a&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FUOz8Ar7jtak8O44X1LBs%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D41fff7c5-1976-407a-a87b-8a1b296b55c9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4e4b8b6cdb6b939a15c39e5370fc2262&sv=3)

The beauty of this is that there is no complex SID list needed for this. There is simply a single SID, which has the instruction to forward over the lowest latency path instead of the lowest IGP cost path. This essentially enables a multi-topology network.

[PreviousSRv6 uSID w/ Dual-Connected PE](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-dual-connected-pe)
[NextSRv6 uSID - Scale (Pt. 1)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-1)

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-flex-algo#id-2fb9e60c-6d46-49a9-81e5-f22a678fc5b1)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-flex-algo#d4cce899-a26d-460c-8b95-a933a52ae2b3)
    

Copy

    # All XR routers
    segment-routing
     srv6
      locators
       locator LATENCY
        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
        algorithm 128
        prefix fd00:1:<#>::/48
    !
    router isis 1
     flex-algo 128
      metric-type delay
      advertise-definition
     !
     exit
     !
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      segment-routing srv6
       locator LATENCY
    
    #XR7
    router bgp 100
     segment-routing srv6
      no locator CCIE
     !
     vrf CUSTOMER
      address-family ipv4 unicast
       segment-routing srv6
        locator LATENCY
      !
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       segment-routing srv6
        locator LATENCY

Copy

    router isis 1
     flex-algo 128
      metric-type delay
      advertise-definition

Copy

    segment-routing
     srv6
      locators
       locator LATENCY
        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
        algorithm 128
        prefix fd00:1:<#>::/48
    !
    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      segment-routing srv6
       locator LATENCY

Copy

    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      on-demand color 10
       srv6
        locator CCIE binding-sid dynamic behavior ub6-insert-reduced
       !
       source-address ipv6 2001:db8:200::5
       dynamic
       !
       constraints
        segments
         sid-algorithm 128

Copy

    #XR7
    router bgp 100
     segment-routing srv6
      no locator CCIE
     !
     vrf CUSTOMER
      address-family ipv4 unicast
       segment-routing srv6
        locator LATENCY
      !
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       segment-routing srv6
        locator LATENCY

Copy

    #XR7
    router bgp 100
     segment-routing srv6
      locator CCIE
     !
     vrf CUSTOMER
      address-family ipv4 unicast
       segment-routing srv6
        locator LATENCY
        alloc mode per-vrf
      !
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       segment-routing srv6
        locator LATENCY
        alloc mode per-vrf

Copy

    route-policy SRv6_POLICY
      if destination in (3.3.3.3/32) then
        set srv6-alloc-mode per-vrf locator LATENCY
      else
        set srv6-alloc-mode per-vrf locator CCIE
      endif
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 100
     vrf CUSTOMER
      address-family ipv4 unicast
       segment-routing srv6
        alloc mode route-policy SRv6_POLICY

# Start | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/start.md)
.

Note that XRd does not support any MVPN profiles. XRv9K only supports profiles which use P-PIM. You can configure profiles with mLDP and SR-P2MP, but they will not work in the data plane. The following labs were originally created with XRv9K nodes. However, these are very resource intensive, so I used XRd for this workbook. Profiles 28 and 29 cannot be fully validated with XRd, so keep this in mind while you work through these exercises. You may wish to use XRv9K for these exercises, but know that the dataplane will still not work.

To begin, run the following command on your containerlab machine:

Copy

    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    containerlab deploy -t topology1/topology1.clab.yml --reconfigure

Once all nodes are started, run the following command to transfer the config files to all nodes. These files will be used to change between startup configs for subsequent labs.

Copy

    python3 transfer_configs_to_nodes.py

The script will prompt you for a directory name. Enter "topology1".

Use the MTPutty session file located in **topology1/topology1\_putty\_sessions.xml** to quickly setup your SSH sessions to the nodes. Go to **Server - Import Tree** and browse for the file.

When you are done with the lab, use the following command to wipe it:

Copy

    containerlab destroy -t topology1/topology1.clab.yml

[PreviousMVPN SR](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr)

# FRR Link Protection (XE, RSVP Hellos) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-rsvp-hellos.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.frr.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

A TE tunnel using the path CSR8-CSR9-CSR10-CSR5 is setup on CSR8. Configure FRR link protection so that if the CSR9-CSR10 link goes down, traffic is rerouted around this failure and stitched back together on CSR10. Use RSVP Hellos to detect the failure. Set the interval to 500 msec and 5 missed ACKs.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-rsvp-hellos#b5e42054-8561-4ea8-900c-5d679cd3baf3)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-rsvp-hellos#f17e7903-cc34-40b9-9adc-f9f2460735d7)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MPLS-TE relies on fast failure detection. With Ethernet we are limited to the line going physically down, or using some sort of keepalive mechanism. Relying on line status is not reliable, because there could be multiple layer 1 devices in the path between two routers. So instead we must use RSVP Hellos, either with or without BFD.

In the previous lab we activated BFD, which is going to be a more common deployment, due to BFD being able to be offloaded into hardware. In this lab we explore using the RSVP Hello itself.

By default, RSVP does not use Hellos. When a path is setup, the neighbors are maintained using the PATH/RESV messages, not a separate RSVP Hello. To use RSVP Hellos, we must activate it at the global level and the link level:

RSVP Uses an activate/passive setup, in which one router is Active (sending requests), and the other end is Passive, simply acknowledging requests. Or both ends can be Activate. By default, when FRR is not configured on the interfaces of either neighbor, the Hello period is 2000 msec, and triggers failure when 4 ACKs are missed.

We can see this using the following show command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnXAChnWsssmLLCg6N7gs%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db1651e70-e3b7-4143-8e0d-feece2a8eb5f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3419643022d681f6f7d24a882e71cd66&sv=3)

When using RSVP Hellos _without_ using FRR, there is “ReRoute” protection instead of “Fast ReRoute protection”. This allows the router to send a PathErr to the headend upon detecting the neighbor down. However, usually you can just rely on your IGP for this, so it would not be a typical use case for RSVP Hellos.

Once we add the backup tunnel to this interface, the default interval changes to 200 msec. Additionally, the client changes to “Fast ReRoute.”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F9z8jL5GLL3WROHi1jGCT%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dea6de18f-e358-446f-a423-e08488829314&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8b606dae03e256e81db6cb2681f15bfa&sv=3)

Keep in mind that this is processd in the control plane, unlike BFD. To back off this interval a bit, we can change the interval and missed acks number via the following commands:

We can also control the DSCP value if desired:

Now when we shut down Gi2.590 on CSR10, we activate FRR on CSR9 within 2.5 seconds. This would be faster with BFD, but using RSVP hellos is the only other option if we cannot use BFD.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FGzOYP05ExwnlIL4EPvvZ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc99287ee-14eb-46e9-a242-59ce40950713&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8cb90fe23ecf967422161ee9ef96cfbf&sv=3)

Notice above that before we had an “Up” activce instance with CSR10. Then we had no active instances any more, and FRR had been activated.

[NextFRR Node Protection (XR)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-node-protection-xr)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-rsvp-hellos#f17e7903-cc34-40b9-9adc-f9f2460735d7)

    #CSR8
    int tunnel0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng fast-reroute
    
    #CSR9
    ip rsvp signalling hello
    !
    int Gi2.590
     mpls traffic-eng backup-path tun0
     ip rsvp signalling hello
