# FRR Node Protection (XR) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-node-protection-xr.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.frr.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

A TE tunnel using the path XRv11 - XRv12 - CSR9 - CSR1 - CSR4 is setup on XRv11. Configure FRR node protection so that if CSR9 goes down, traffic is rerouted around this failure at XR12 and stitched back together at CSR1. Test that the fast reroute works by shutting Gi2 on CSR9 and Gi0/0/0/0.592 on XRv12.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-node-protection-xr#id-92d7c96a-d58a-4b07-ab5e-3e0b3cf4b2e6)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Node protection is very similar to link protection, except the backup tunnel excludes the entire node rather than just a link address. This is sometimes called a NNHOP (next next-hop) tunnel because XRv12 is repairing the path at the next-hop of its own next-hop, which is CSR1.

XRv12 must learn CSR1’s label for the primary path. This happens via RSVP. When XRv12 request fast-reroute for node protection specifically, a label recording option is requested in the PATH message. The RRO in the RESV message contains the label at every single hop. This allows any NNHOP tunnel to be built along the LSP.

Note that requesting node protection specifically does not appear to be necessary. The label recording request happens whether or not node protection is requested. The **node** option, to me, appears to be an interoperability feature to work with non-Cisco devices in the MPLS-TE domain. The **node** option turns on the “node protection requested” flag in the PATH message. But on an IOS-XE or IOS-XR PLR, it does not appear to need this flag in order to provide node protection. The link or node protection designation is simply based on the backup tunnel’s destination.

Just like with link protection, we can see that XRv12 is ready to protect the primary tunnel.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FYYgxiAoocrHP8Qbtk58O%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1a92beab-b093-41f8-aea3-69e3dc902ed1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a3faf175609874bddcb3a141b128068f&sv=3)

The backup tunnel is taking the path XRv12-CSR6-CSR1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMh4Jq6SZct8dj7UV0Tqa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D446f53ce-b08a-48ba-91c3-92e76765c8a1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9192f55da26191937821b83052a9b791&sv=3)

We must bring down both Gi2 on CSR9 and Gi0/0/0/0.592 on XRv12. This is because XRv does not support BFD, nor RSVP Hellos. Once the interfaces are down, we can see the FRR status is “active.” This will stay in place permanently, because the primary path has only an explicit-path that must go through CSR9, which is now down.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FGg3CcWbFCPHonmeNxqWK%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8de36839-936e-4563-aa98-1cd98dd5bc73&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9b62fdbbabce6986c99b4302fde17e71&sv=3)

We can see at XRv11 it is in “reroute pending” although the tunnel remains up and connected.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FCeXSdcTqh5Kk9rT4X3VR%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da8461cb3-348e-4062-89be-d508df6140f8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b0017bb10fdaec245c8814779cc0d8e5&sv=3)

If XRv11 finds a new path, the FRR protection would go away on XRv12. On XRv11 we can see that the last error is from XRv12 which signaled a PathErr but that local repair was in place. This allowed XRv11 to try to do make-before-break.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJA5ALE8nHrFshMP2DZXa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D21f64e9f-1177-4f42-a631-68f51c187432&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8e5519afd1656e1c51a2fab27e6ef0b9&sv=3)

[PreviousFRR Link Protection (XE, RSVP Hellos)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-rsvp-hellos)
[NextFRR Path Protection](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-path-protection)

Last updated 1 year ago

Copy

    #XRv11
    int tunnel-te0
     fast-reroute protect node
     ! or
     fast-reroute
    
    #XRv12
    explicit-path name AVOID_CSR9
     index 10 exclude-address ipv4 unicast 9.9.9.9
    !
    int tunnel-te0
     destination 1.1.1.1
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 explicit name AVOID_CSR9
    !
    mpls traffic-eng
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.592
      backup-path tunnel-te 0

# SRv6 uSID w/ SR-TE Explicit Paths | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te-explicit-paths.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg

L3VPN for IPv4 and IPv6 is currently functional using SRv6 uSID in the core.

Configure an SR-TE policy on XR5 that uses an explicit SID list with uSID. The path should go via XR1, XR2, XR4 and then XR7. Color routes OSPF routes redistributed into BGP on XR7 to use this policy.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te-explicit-paths#ef965536-7a8e-4c9c-935d-1f50192e28ad)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te-explicit-paths#id-0fa97d53-1ce3-41ff-aca0-208ab3e14985)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

While SRv6-TE ODN policies are more scalable, it is still good to know how to configure SRv6-TE policies that use explicit paths. Using an explicit path with SRv6-TE requires several lines of configuration.

First we specify the SRv6 locator that is used to allocate a BSID. This is done when using an SRv6-TE policy (ODN or explicit paths).

Next, we configure an SRv6 SID list. We must specify that the SID list uses the f3216 format. (This is our only option). Remember _not_ to include the endpoint itself (XR7) in the SID list. This is because the BGP SID already will be steered towards the endpoint. (The SID comes from the egress PE’s locator block already).

Finally we apply the SID list to the policy as a candidate path. Make sure to enable SRv6 under the policy.

The policy should now be up. A BSID was allocated from the specified locator:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FevzPFGAUv0rLlNNEx5CB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8dc53418-d8fe-4d84-8719-fbe591edfafc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=dc66a00758811b927c0cb8c9e866080e&sv=3)

After XR7 colors the routes, traffic towards CE3 should take this SRv6-TE policy.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPAI9z5JPAnCPWYDa6cR2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dad2c55ae-6a31-4a32-95a3-f5ba7493af99&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b36fd29ba77eae6e062c883555afd91b&sv=3)

Taking a pcap of a ping from CE1 to CE3 shows the proper uSID container as the IPv6 destination address:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FW7fHQfJZCYwXSOxHMFLC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D99313727-e070-408b-9d9f-090459ea360b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9c04e2866a6ce498153e9ad6c1fc1064&sv=3)

CE1 receives ping replies:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Frv05lxtw5OxA1jHaoTKK%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfdafc75c-15af-4cd0-8c43-66feca1c7763&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3bd4ca7f254f7c0b21ae6bfb774edb71&sv=3)

[NextSRv6 uSID w/ L3 IGW](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-l3-igw)

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te-explicit-paths#ef965536-7a8e-4c9c-935d-1f50192e28ad)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te-explicit-paths#id-0fa97d53-1ce3-41ff-aca0-208ab3e14985)
    

Copy

    #XR5
    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      srv6
       locator CCIE binding-sid dynamic behavior ub6-insert-reduced
      !
      segment-lists
       srv6
        sid-format usid-f3216
       !
       segment-list LIST1
        srv6
         index 1 sid fd00:0:1::
         index 2 sid fd00:0:2::
         index 3 sid fd00:0:4::
        !
       !
      !
      policy POL1
       srv6
       !
       color 10 end-point ipv6 2001:db8:200::7
       candidate-paths
        preference 100
         explicit segment-list LIST1
    
    
    #XR7
    extcommunity-set opaque COLOR_10
      10
    end-set
    !
    route-policy SET_COLOR
      set extcommunity color COLOR_10
    end-policy
    !
    router bgp 100
     vrf CUSTOMER
      address-family ipv4 unicast
       redistribute ospf CUSTOMER route-policy SET_COLOR
      !
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       redistribute ospfv3 CUSTOMER route-policy SET_COLOR

# IGP TE Flooding Thresholds | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/igp-te-flooding-thresholds.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure R8 and XR11 to flood TED information upon the following **up** and **down** thresholds:

*   5 10 80 90
    

Configure R9 and XR12 to flood periodic TED changes which weren’t trigged by a threshold every 10 minutes.

Create bi-directional TE tunnels between R8 and XR11 that go through R9 and XR12 which reserve 100M. Which routers flood changes immediately into the IGP?

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/igp-te-flooding-thresholds#id-86686a83-3e32-4989-8aed-e824501f41a1)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/igp-te-flooding-thresholds#id-4a97cd9a-15f8-43c3-82f5-3e878ce72e13)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The TED must be kept up-to-date with all links in the topology and their associated available bandwidth, link affinity, and TE metrics. If many LSPs are reserved and torn down constantly, the available bandwidth values can change often, requiring lots of IGP flooding.

To minimize this flooding, but still keep the TED somewhat up-to-date, default thresholds are used to determine when to flood information upon changes in available bandwidth. By default, the following thresholds are used on IOS-XE and IOS-XR for both **up** and **down** changes in bandwidth:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAjCUFHdMhwrBz34vRNXY%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1c6aa06c-3a54-421f-9e88-b0b4654d4e2c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=458ef15195ddfcfb1c9509cea224feb5&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fo4JOFqKjgy8mBODa3Qlj%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4fbc08a2-e19c-423c-803b-ead4164ffe21&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=731affd383b14e3ac87f5be6721a3b34&sv=3)

When bandwidth consumed crosses one of the **up** thresholds, the IGP is flooded with the current bandwidth allocations. Likewise, when bandwidth consumed goes down and crosses one of the **down** thresholds, this information is flooded via the IGP.

We can set these values on a per-interface basis using the following commands on IOS-XE and IOS-XR:

If a change in bandwidth happens that doesn’t cross a threshold, then this information is flooded when the periodic flooding timer is triggered. By default, this is every minute on IOS-XE, and every 3 minutes on IOS-XR. We can control this globally using the following commands:

Also note that IGP flooding occurs when RSVP encounters an error due to path setup because of a lack of bandwidth. This must mean that the headend does not have an updated TED and thinks there is more bandwidth available than there actually is. So this triggers flooding on the router which encountered the error.

There is also a **bandwidth-hold** timer knob. This controls how long bandwidth is reserved on the interface during path setup. If the timer expires but the path setup has not been completed, the bandwidth allocation is freed up. By default this is 15 seconds.

IOS-XR also allows us to tune the **preemption-delay**. This appears to control how long to wait before preempting an LSP. The default appears to be 0 seconds.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/igp-te-flooding-thresholds#ffcde7a2-4278-4303-97ad-688605339dcc)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

First we’ll verify the thresholds on R8 and XR11. We’ll only check one interface for brevity.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsF5bGNRVUcilsWVN5pmG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc967ee8d-4394-4233-9647-7bcffe560093&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=078786ed88cf36a3a634c7c8ee2b92e3&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhUgZI6h5oVT2q78pQFNl%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd5747977-9675-40a4-835b-06fb34bfbed4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=393fb40daf18c40ef5b2b6a639b97a29&sv=3)

Next we’ll setup the paths between R8 and XR11 which each reserve 100M. Check the TED on any router in the topology, for example R5. We can see that R8 and XR11 have immediately flooded their new bandwidth values, but R8 and XR12 have not.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252ForGavdh2qxU8uZNjOECy%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd8515fce-0c00-4f10-9f85-3557a734d7b1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1a9b0adbd37d3cfef7decba289c94c69&sv=3)

R9 and XR12 have not advertised their updated bandwidth values yet because bandwidth allocation went up but did not pass the first 15% threshold mark. Once the periodic-flooding timer expires, we should see the updated information.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKTXGQxk9Qc9nXVq9Y4GQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1d193d13-c143-45b5-bb56-0aac0f172ce2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c457b3017334d43709994a5bb0414469&sv=3)

    mpls traffic-eng link-management timers periodic-flooding 600
    
    #R8
    int Gi2.518

     mpls traffic-eng flooding thresholds down 90 80 10 5
    int Gi2.568

    int Gi2.589

    !

     next-address 9.9.9.9

# FRR Multiple Backup Tunnels (Backwidth/Link Protection) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-backwidth-link-protection.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.frr.multi.bandwidth.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.frr.multi.bandwidth.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR (XR1, XR2 only)
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.frr.multi.bandwidth.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FueH0P2tWY2KA8Q7hpw1D%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D438f85d2-f0ff-4de2-a3b9-ea551f14731b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=52181baf0b7451d25117c85fd4bd8b70&sv=3)

There are four TE tunnels setup on the path CSR8-CSR9-CSR3-CSR2, each signalling 100M of bandwidth

*   Configure CSR9 for link protection, using two backup paths.
    
    *   One backup tunnel should use CSR9-CSR1-CSR3, and another should use CSR9-CSR10-CSR3.
        
    *   The path through CSR10 only has 100M available, so only one LSP should be backed up on this tunnel.
        
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-backwidth-link-protection#id-696f2da1-cb5f-41df-bbc7-eae3b9e0855f)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-backwidth-link-protection#c21cc976-5414-4998-8765-9e86ad3df7db)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When using multiple backup tunnels per interface, we also have the option of limiting how much bandwidth we want to use on each backup tunnel. This bandwidth is not signalled. Instead it is used to do admission control when permiting primary LSPs over backup tunnels.

This is controlled using the **backup-bw** command:

Because all primary LSPs are each signalling 100M of bandwidth, only one primary LSP can be protected by Tun1. We can verify this on CSR9:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXzi2ywpzVGupaIO4CVDD%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De95494fb-cf5c-4c2a-bc57-cedb1c3de972&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=422ecbc266d72e841684dbffd4f6701a&sv=3)

Notice that CSR8’s tun0 (the first one listed) has Tun1, while the other three have Tun0. There is a reason for this. When the router picks which backup tunnel to use for a given primary LSP, first the backup tunnels with limited backup-bw are evaluated. Tun1 had enough room, so it was used. The second through fourth LSPs then only had the option of Tun0, which has unlimited backup-bw. So the router will fill up backup tunnels that have limited bandwidth before filling up unlimited bw backup tunnels.

Note that we can also explicitly define unlimited backup-bw for a tunnel as follows. However, this limits us to either the global-pool or sub-pool.

If you configure this for the sub-pool, it means that no bandwidth is available for the global-pool.

On CSR9, all three LSPs that were using tun0 for backup have dissappeared. This is because Tun0 now has zero global-pool backup-bw.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FQ2aF7B6ItDTO67v4LLgp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1e1b6197-cd00-40da-9dba-64b14222fcae&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a931a2b8ad0beba51996822dd674fb71&sv=3)

Note that you can also specify backup-bw for DS-TE LSPs as well, using the sub-pool for traditional DS-TE, or class-type for IETF DS-TE.

Also, be careful when using this feature in general, as an LSP that requests no bandwidth cannot be protected by an LSP that has backup-bw. This seems a little bit like a bug, but appears to be how the feature is supposed to work. For example, if we remove the signalled bandwidth on CSR8’s tunnels, and add backup-bw to CSR9’s tun0, no LSPs will be protected.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMIFbu8TzKTIja2clQLMF%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1914ab86-6629-4c58-9831-f404563e3687&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=054976506ac519fe846d6968ca4a3924&sv=3)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-backwidth-link-protection#c21cc976-5414-4998-8765-9e86ad3df7db)
    

Copy

    #CSR9
    ip explicit-path name CSR9-CSR1-CSR3
     next-address 1.1.1.1
     next-address 3.3.3.3
    !
    ip explicit-path name CSR9-CSR10-CSR3
     next-address 10.10.10.10
     next-address 3.3.3.3
    !
    int tun0
     tunnel dest 3.3.3.3
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng 
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name CSR9-CSR1-CSR3
    !
    int tun1
     tunnel dest 3.3.3.3
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng 
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name CSR9-CSR10-CSR3
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw 100000
    !
    int gi2.539
     mpls traffic-eng backup tun0
     mpls traffic-eng backup tun1

Copy

    #CSR9
    int tun1
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw 100000

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int tun0 
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw global-pool unlimited

Copy

    #CSR9
    int tun0 
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw sub-pool 100000

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int tun0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 1 100000

Copy

    #CSR8
    int range tun0-3
     shut
     no tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth
     no shut
    
    #CSR9
    int tun0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw 1000000

# TE Tunnel Soft Preemption | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-soft-preemption.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.soft.preemption.initial.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.soft.preemption.initial.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR (XR11, XR12 only)
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.soft.preemption.initial.cfg
    commit replace
    y

There are two bidirectional LSPs:

*   XR11-CSR8 requesting 500M at priority 7
    
*   XR12-CSR8 requesting 750M at priority 6
    
    *   Currently shutdown
        
    

Configure XR11 and XR12 so that when XR12 brings up its LSP, it allows XR11 to do make-before-break.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-soft-preemption#id-4370dae6-e545-4c7a-aa6a-15ef3b8f9c57)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-soft-preemption#id-569c3206-a360-4373-bc45-098289902f49)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, when one LSP preempts another, the LSP that is being preempted is forcefully torn down. If a second path-option exists, it would be more graceful if the headend of the to-be-preempted LSP can do make-before-break and reserve a new LSP along a less-optimal path.

This feature is enabled using **soft-preemption**. It is only available on IOS-XR. When the preempting router “kicks off” the worse-priority LSP, the router signals to the existing headend that this is about to occur so that it can do make-before-break and gracefully establish a new path. The router does this using a PATH ERROR message that contains code 34/1, which means reroute/flow soft-preempted. This is different from the normal PATH ERROR message which is 2/5 meaning policy control failure/flow was preempted.

Note that I could not get this to work correctly on XRv. Perhaps the feature isn’t implemented fully? Also this is not mentioned in Russo’s study guide, so it’s possible I’m not using the feature correctly too. When XR12 preempt’s XR11’s tunnel, I get packet loss between XR13-XR14, and I see XR11 forcefully tear down the LSP in response to XR12’s error 2/5.

[PreviousTE Tunnel Preemption](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-preemption)
[NextTunneling LDP inside RSVP](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/tunneling-ldp-inside-rsvp)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-soft-preemption#id-4370dae6-e545-4c7a-aa6a-15ef3b8f9c57)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnel-soft-preemption#id-569c3206-a360-4373-bc45-098289902f49)
    

Copy

    #XR11, XR12
    mpls traffic-eng
     soft-preemption
    !
    int tunnel-te 1
     soft-preemption

# SRv6 uSID w/ L3 IGW | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-l3-igw.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.igw.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.igw.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.igw.init.cfg

The PEs XR5/XR6/XR7 are SR-MPLS only. They only use XR9 as the RR.

XR8 is SRv6 only, and only uses XR10 as the RR.

Configure XR2, which belongs to both the SR-MPLS and SRv6 domains, to be the interworking gateway (IWG), translating between SRv6 and SR-MPLS for both L3VPNv4 and L3VPNv6.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-l3-igw#de4480ea-29aa-435a-81c8-ebfdf9fc3406)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-l3-igw#f9c9f6fb-57b8-4e00-aa1f-7d23da454961)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When an operator wants to transition from MPLS to SRv6, there may be a transition period in which there are domains that only use MPLS and some domains that only use SRv6. Or it might be the case that two domains are merged together, and you must support interworking betwen an SRv6-only domain and SR-MPLS or LDP-only domain. An IWG (interworking gateway) is needed to translate between the MPLS domain and SRv6 domain.

This sounds complex, but the operation is fairly straightforward. The IWG simply inserts itself in the middle of all flows, somewhat performing option A inter-AS functionality. Every customer VRF must be defined on the IWG. The IWG will advertise routes learned from the MPLS domain into the SRv6 domain with an SRv6 SID. Likewise, it will advertise routes learned from the SRv6 domain into the MPLS domain with an MPLS label. The IWG simply translates between these two domains by advertising these routes from itself and performing a routing lookup upon received traffic.

First we must define the VRF on the IGW. The **stitching** RTs are the SRv6 RTs. The normal RTs are the SR-MPLS RTs. Currently, XR5, XR6 and XR7 use 100:1, and XR8 uses 100:2.

We enable SRv6 for BGP, and enable SRv6 under the VRF. The mode will automatically be a per-VRF mode, as the router will need to do a table lookup when stitching traffic coming from the SRv6 side onto the SR-MPLS side. Additionally, we enable MPLS label allocation for the VRF as well, as the VRF will be allocating both MPLS labels and SRv6 SIDs.

Next we configure the stitching on the SR-MPLS side. This is done under the neighbor statement. R9 is the RR for the SR-MPLS domain, and R10 is the RR for the SRv6 domain. We peer with R9 and use three special commands:

*   **import reoriginate stitching-rt** means to import routes as normal (using the normal 100:1 RT), and then reoriginate them with the stitching RT
    
*   **route-reflector-client** is needed, because the IGW needs to reflect routes learned from the SRv6 RR to the SR-MPLS RR
    
*   **advertise vpnv4 unicast re-originated** means to advertise the VPN unicast routes that have been re-originated from SRv6. These will use the normal RT (not the stitching RT) when they are reoriginated, because the **stitching-rt** keyword is not added.
    

On the SRv6 side, we use a similar configuration:

*   **import stitching-rt reoriginate** means to import routes with the stitching RT (100:2) and then reoriginate them using the normal RT
    
*   **route-reflector-client** is needed as above, to reflect routes between the RRs
    
*   **encapsulation-type srv6** is required so that the router advertises the VPN routes with only the prefix SID, not an MPLS label. (We have previously allocated a normal MPLS label under the VRF).
    
*   **advertise vpnv4 unicast re-originated stitching-rt** means to advertise the VPN unicast routes that have been re-originated from SR-MPLS, and use the stitching RT when re-originating them.
    

Note that you can use the same RT for the normal and stitching RT. This works without any issue. For example, I've changed R8 to use the same RTs as the SR-MPLS PEs:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FcZF1MrqHKlmLsltdyWQC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9c1c1a67-09d3-40b8-923f-a09b393ad28f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ae7ecf98f0e87139e42be3e297d7fa51&sv=3)

The IGW now uses the same RT for both the normal RT and stitching RT:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FjgoNPcztTp0TM1M65YCg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D59c463af-da98-4aa1-bb94-897be3b9a21b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9379e95cc8230eb1c980dc5aed98547d&sv=3)

Whether you are using the same or different RTs for SRv6 and SR-MPLS, traffic shold now be working between CEs on the SR-MPLS side, and CE4 (on the SRv6 side):

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FUWYEkf8iWFLAkV1lDd4L%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1c4259b1-a175-49d7-a793-b9bb724a4d03&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=14dfe1beb70ab8e883f16f657e088395&sv=3)

Within each domain, each PE believes that the IGW is the “true” PE for routes in the other domain. For example, within the SR-MPLS domain, XR5 believes that XR2 is the PE for 4.4.4.4/32.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fh1u84ITbWXCPZWl4NWJH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dffef5c02-198a-431d-8feb-1386eec1b33b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3594c994f8fd47254bbe84afd4fea413&sv=3)

XR8 believes that XR2 is the PE for 1.1.1.1/32:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5rgW9WPGaZUW6oIg9Tx4%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddd706f8e-9dd5-48c0-967b-2b9f5fbb1208&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a60760b08a832f9bd087c2410e11f5b1&sv=3)

XR2 simply does a stitching operation in each direction using normal routing procedures. The packet arrives either via the MPLS label or SRv6 SID, and XR2 does a routing table lookup. The route points to the other domain, so the packet is forwarded either with an SRv6 encapsulation, or MPLS label.

The per-VRF label 24003 simply means “do a table lookup in the CUSTOMER VRF”:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FtxP1DT9nVuqiywiKTqxg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dda1d2ca7-354d-4b8f-abed-167e4cd696ec&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3afb2dd24dc52196b5f7334dba1d1a26&sv=3)

Likewise, the SRv6 SID fd00:0:2:e004:: means to do a table lookup in the CUSTOMER VRF:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FItUqqtZe2yGW1tnt7gye%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcb1cf285-f32c-44ec-8996-d3ab85f3b36f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=09df6fcead4339057acced3cc916b023&sv=3)

XR2 performs a table lookup, and then preforms normal ingress PE functionality by sending the packet either down the SR-MPLS LSP or encapsulating it with an SRv6 SID.

### EVPN and L3VPN Reminder[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-l3-igw#ef4ff81a-4088-4189-b8e0-cbe4070629fc)

It is useful to compare this to interworking for EVPN and L3VPN. The commands for SRv6/MPLS interworking appear to be borrowed from EVPN/L3VPN interworking.

With EVPN/L3VPN stitching, VRF routes learned via VPNv4/v6 are re-advertised into the EVPN domain as type 5 routes. The DCI router (a sort of IWG for EVPN/L3VPN) has two sets of RTs:

*   Normal RTs for the VPNv4 L3VPN domain
    
*   “Stitching” RTs for the EVPN domain
    

Using the same commands we have just used in this lab, the DCI router will import the stitching RTs in the EVPN domain, and re-originate them into L3VPN:

The DCI router also must advertise the L3VPN routes into the EVPN domain as type 5 routes. The router imports routes from VPNv4 and re-originates them with the stitching RT. Then it advertises these re-originated routes with the stitching RT into EVPN. The **stitching-rt** keyword in the **advertise** command essentially means “advertise re-originated routes from VPNv4 but change the RT to the export stitching RT.”

See this post for more details on EVPN/L3VPN interworking: [https://xrdocs.io/ncs5500/tutorials/bgp-evpn-and-l3vpn-interworking/](https://xrdocs.io/ncs5500/tutorials/bgp-evpn-and-l3vpn-interworking/)

    #XR2
    vrf CUSTOMER
     address-family ipv4 unicast
      import route-target
       100:1

      !

       100:2 stitching

# SRv6 uSID w/ SR-TE | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg

L3VPN for IPv4 and IPv6 is currently functional using SRv6 uSID in the core.

*   Configure XR9 and XR10 as PCEs and XR5, XR6, XR7 and XR8 as PCE clients.
    
    *   The PCEP session should use IPv6.
        
    *   Configure XR9 as the primary PCE.
        
    
*   Configure the XR1-XR3 link with high latency.
    
*   Color BGP routes received from CSR3 for low-latency ODN SR-TE.
    
    *   The policy should be calculated via PCEP.
        
    
*   Traffic from CSR1 to CSR3 should take the path CSR1-XR5-XR1-XR2-XR4-XR7-CSR3
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te#cc8fb17f-ebb0-4ee0-9e32-7fe68819e9a2)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te#id-43d99181-a28f-4e0e-a1e3-33f0ab62b34f)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Using SRv6 with uSID allows us to use SR-TE which we are already familiar with. Everything works very similarly to using SR-TE with SR-MPLS. The main difference is that you must define the locator for the policy, and specify that the router will allocate a SID with behavior uB6-insert-reduced SRH.

Otherwise, everything else should already be familiar. First we configure PCEP. R9 will be primary PCE by giving it a lower precedence value.

If we forget whether a higher or lower value is best, we can use the below show command to verify which PCE is being preferred:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FtJ4e6VxVoYddSEp4tFEB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6ad3f0cd-7be8-4693-b7bc-a7be70950c2e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6695d533aeb7152ca6f0cc1fa11702d7&sv=3)

On the egress PE, we set the color on the VPN routes. CSR3 is running OSPF as the PE-CE protocol, so XR7 sets the color as the routes are redistributed from OSPF into BGP.

We also set the latency value on the XR1-XR3 link to be high. Even though no other links have latency configured, the TE metric appears to be substituted for the latency value, so the policy will still be able to be calculated.

Finally, we set the ODN policy on the ingress PEs.

XR5, upon receiving the colored route, asks the PCE to calculate an associated policy. This is successful, as we see on R9:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fras0cOSKnwokDthWVpPN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1ab9b012-e4cd-43ab-88cb-dd48ac9b2f53&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4c524d8e4702aba7fd4dcb946bf29ebf&sv=3)

The details show us that the first SID is R2, and last is R7:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVDkgZTT5V8flHpM0TXnD%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da77b783a-efc7-4d11-8628-70a7a281de9f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c539fd23460fe5501f6de1a25583d134&sv=3)

XR5 allocates a Binding SID for the policy, and reports it to both XR9 and XR10 (for redundancy).

There does not appear to be a way to verify the actual carrier SID that will be produced by this policy. In the CEF table we can see that the ultimate encapsulation uses fd00:0:7:e003, with the SRv6 SID fd00:0:2:: being inserted:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FutjWneDpk0D5OwmYeIvp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcc09892e-ecae-4b13-821c-61d43f236ef4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c5bcddf4f134956dd88154e91e384441&sv=3)

By taking a pcap, we can see that the destination address is the correct compressed CSID:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FL6ow0QWv061j8dE4C0uI%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5f6abbc0-722b-4e62-8a29-d232f1f541bd&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=458879e9811f84ac1ba52d97219f4c4b&sv=3)

### Further exploring the ODN policy[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te#c524c29d-8f47-40d6-8613-3146ac37f247)

I found that the following config does not work.

The ODN policy does not come up until I specify **srv6** under the ODN policy. It appears that without **srv6** under the ODN policy, there is no way for the router to know that it is not an SR-MPLS policy.

Alternatively, I can just define the locator directly under the ODN policy itself.

[PreviousSRv6 uSID w/ EVPN-VPWS and BGP IPv4/IPv6](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-evpn-vpws-and-bgp-ipv4-ipv6)
[NextSRv6 uSID w/ SR-TE Explicit Paths](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te-explicit-paths)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te#cc8fb17f-ebb0-4ee0-9e32-7fe68819e9a2)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te#id-43d99181-a28f-4e0e-a1e3-33f0ab62b34f)
    
*   [Further exploring the ODN policy](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te#c524c29d-8f47-40d6-8613-3146ac37f247)
    

Copy

    #XR9
    pce
     address ipv6 2001:db8:200::9
    !
    router isis 1
     distribute link-state
    
    #XR10
    pce
     address ipv6 2001:db8:200::a
    !
    router isis 1
     distribute link-state
    
    #XR5, XR6, XR7, XR8
    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      on-demand color 10
       srv6
        locator CCIE binding-sid dynamic behavior ub6-insert-reduced
       !
       dynamic
        pcep
        !
        metric
         type latency
      !
      pcc
       source-address ipv6 2001:db8:200::<R#>
       pce address ipv6 2001:db8:200::9
        precedence 100
       !
       pce address ipv6 2001:db8:200::a
        precedence 200
    
    #XR1, XR3
    performance-measurement
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.3013
      delay-measurement
       advertise-delay 1000000
    
    #XR7
    extcommunity-set opaque COLOR_10
      10
    end-set
    !

# SRv6 uSID w/ EVPN-VPWS and BGP IPv4/IPv6 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-evpn-vpws-and-bgp-ipv4-ipv6.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.services.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.services.init.cfg

SRv6 uSID is already preconfigured in the core.

Configure an EVPN-VPWS service between CSR1 and CSR3 using SRv6 as the underlay.

*   CSR1 is configured for 10.0.0.1/24 on Gi2.3311
    
*   CSR3 is configured for 10.0.0.3/24 on Gi2.3333
    
*   This will not work in the data plane on XRd
    

Configure BGP IPv4/IPv6 in the global table between CSR2 and CSR4 also using SRv6 as the underlay.

*   The BGP peerings are already setup in the global table
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-evpn-vpws-and-bgp-ipv4-ipv6#id-5761a4b3-a9eb-4376-884c-c6565dac0dca)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-evpn-vpws-and-bgp-ipv4-ipv6#id-58cac120-853f-412b-9c5e-c917b9c15684)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SRv6 can be used as the data plane for EVPN-VPWS and global IPv4/IPv6 unicast. It does not appear to be supported for bridged EVPN. But bridge-domains are not configurable on XRv9K anyways.

For EVPN-VPWS, we must do two things. First, we configure the locator that EVPN will use:

Next, we configure the encapsulation as SRv6 on the xconnect:

Alternatively, we can specify the locator on the individual p2p xconnect. However, we still must activate SRv6 under EVPN:

The SID advertisement works the same as we have seen with L3VPN. The SID is advertised within a Prefix SID Sub TLV. The label field contains the function bits.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTgcu98tJHuYDV0fCGtji%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D36cba6e3-b74b-4f2d-b577-75c4e3679be6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=00ae12e9347ca7c3312781638db4582f&sv=3)

The PE installs this ::/64 SID into the FIB with a uDX2 instruction, which means to decapsulate and cross-connect for a layer 2 service.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FLyoKP5wkhVTg9SSode3u%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc5a54d70-5379-40bb-b757-deec944c2cfa&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2615294367d98b6933927fab6ef29189&sv=3)

Note that on XRv9K, this L2 service works in the data plane. However, on XRd, it seems that the node cannot do vlan rewrite operations, so this is not working in the data plane.

Next, we configure BGP IPv4/IPv6 unicast in the global VRF for SRv6. This is just like 6PE, in which global IPv6 unicast is tunneled across an MPLS core by advertising a service label with the ipv6/unicast prefix. To configure this, we first need to fix an issue. The PEs are not setting next-hop-self on the routes. This causes the RRs to not select these prefixes as best because the nexthop is inaccessible. When these were VRF routes, the PE automatically sets next-hop-self for the VPNv4/v6 route, as the PE is technically the router originating the VPN route.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4hyiCEd92LLHP4E9B4Rp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8fcfd018-6d84-4ea9-89d0-0416f46e79e7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3ce047551d08d6ec9dc11e10518a4c0e&sv=3)

We fix this by setting next-hop-self:

Next, we enable SRv6 for BGP the same as we did for L3VPN. We can also configure the locator to be used by default:

We must do two other things. We must set the SRv6 alloc mode under the global AFIs, and we must set the encapsulation type as SRv6 under the iBGP neighbor statements.

Now the global prefixes have a SID associated with them. The difference with global IPv4/IPv6 unicast is that BGP-LU is not used, so there is no label field to place the function bits inside. This is just an optimization to better pack BGP updates, so it is not a major drawback.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJF90IhsGR9PjgvrmkFfD%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddc634415-da75-4e78-bc5f-2d0d6bb40a76&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0f670fffb1a602f16c480b32664dc468&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FxRb7Jdu2n1VtApFfQboa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D62db493e-aa53-4d33-b96c-59def892558c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=98f3d4ec3f53bd7220e8d70bbcb79652&sv=3)

Traffic between the two pairs of CEs should now be working:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FmtpPdR5JKT2doMWJM4T3%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D35953662-f7ac-4b77-afeb-34d43c2cc8f1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=259b333883def85450c32fa4ed74d6c8&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOYwPJnX4VYRxRPPfNLgZ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7879386b-fcf3-4c99-aa13-6298b0698612&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=50791939ad90a4725d389af5bf31a1d1&sv=3)

[PreviousSRv6 uSID](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid)
[NextSRv6 uSID w/ SR-TE](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-sr-te)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-evpn-vpws-and-bgp-ipv4-ipv6#id-58cac120-853f-412b-9c5e-c917b9c15684)

# FRR Multiple Backup Tunnels (Node Protection) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-node-protection.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.frr.multi.node.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.frr.multi.node.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR (XR1, XR2 only)
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.frr.multi.node.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FIDh5Pi6BLMx7gYKfw878%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D46a0f8cd-9e48-46c1-93ad-044b3b8a69ef&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=069723cb6ab17638e70eab6ee18747d7&sv=3)

There are two TE tunnels setup:

*   CSR8-CSR9-CSR3-CSR2-CSR5
    
*   CSR8-CSR9-CSR3-CSR10-CSR5
    

Configure CSR9 for node protection, protecting both LSPs when the link to CSR3 fails. The tunnels on CSR8 already request FRR protection.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-node-protection#id-90b86683-3274-4f78-8e21-cdfdd4d568b3)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can also apply RSVP Hellos to better detect failure:

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-node-protection#f13c7266-428d-4400-97e7-33d8dd6da6a5)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The PLR can have multiple backup tunnels applied to a single interface. When the tunnels have the same NHOP, primary LSPs are round-robined across each backup tunnel. Each LSP is only associated with one backup tunnel though. When the backup tunnels have different destinations, the router is smart enough to understand which backup tunnels are available/applicable to which primary LSPs. When both a NNHOP and NHOP backup tunnel exist, the router prefers the NNHOP tunnel, as that protects both the link and the node.

On CSR9, we can see that both LSPs have their appropriate backup tunnel assigned. Tun0 has a destination of CSR2, and Tun1 has a destination of CSR10. CSR8’s Tun0 goes through CSR2, and CSR8’s Tun1 goes through CSR10, so this is correct.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FI1Z0oyF5oQsAdaoHeVFB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0fcb0788-532a-410f-b6e0-71ba70f2f731&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ed55f87136a0f90db473072b3116910b&sv=3)

When the CSR3-CSR9 link goes down, CSR9 will activate both at the same time:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FqTIOomzeXv8wKMn35IMC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D090378fa-f296-4786-9e30-2984dcb9cb37&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=fab5573987a6d7064131acdaa9f8cbbe&sv=3)

[PreviousFRR Path Protection](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-path-protection)
[NextFRR Multiple Backup Tunnels (Link Protection)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-link-protection)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-node-protection#id-90b86683-3274-4f78-8e21-cdfdd4d568b3)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-node-protection#f13c7266-428d-4400-97e7-33d8dd6da6a5)
    

Copy

    #CSR9
    ip explicit-path name AVOID_CSR3
     exclude-address 3.3.3.3
    !
    int tun0
     tunnel destination 2.2.2.2
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name AVOID_CSR3
    !
    int tun1
     tunnel destination 10.10.10.10
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name AVOID_CSR3
    !
    int gi2.539
     mpls traffic-eng backup tun0
     mpls traffic-eng backup tun1

Copy

    #CSR3, CSR9
    ip rsvp signalling hello
    !
    int gi2.539
     ip rsvp signalling hello

Copy

    #CSR3
    int gi2.539
     shut

# Autoroute Announce Backup Path | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/autoroute-announce-backup-path.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.isis.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.isis.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.isis.cfg
    commit replace

Configure a TE tunnel from R8 to R10 going through R3. Use autoroute so that this TE tunnel is only used in the event that the R9-R10 and R6-R10 links go down.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/autoroute-announce-backup-path#id-1d0bc641-2fb7-4b4c-8e34-5b0781f79668)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/autoroute-announce-backup-path#d5ed1b52-f2bf-4175-81e8-676b7b1045a2)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, a TE tunnel uses the IGP cost of the best IGP path to the destination. In our case, if we don’t change the autoroute metric on the TE tunnel, the cost will be 20 even though the TE path itself goes R8-R1-R3-R10.

For example, remove the autoroute metric and notice that the TE tunnel replaces the IGP paths to R10:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fmk670tGJmDrljCgfR5O9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De285b6a1-a816-405e-a8d5-55fb6473a735&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7e3a0627974abe86098561106f6e7102&sv=3)

We’ll now add the metric back in, and the TE tunnel should no longer be used:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FxiGoLQrKKO1nvNTr3i4W%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9387dcc5-4236-478a-b7e1-179f75835fae&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b1b7e507093bd6a90d57ef2df290eb63&sv=3)

What we have now is essentially a backup TE tunnel path. If we lose the two shortest IGP paths to R10, we force traffic to go via R3 instead of via XR12. To simulate failure, we’ll shut down the R9-R10 and R6-R10 links:

R8 now uses the TE path to R10. Due to the metric of 21, it is better than other remaining paths which have a metric of 30.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FL9iG8igtSA64Nfdeihf1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4e55073f-7007-470d-8e41-15fa4bd3b8d8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=fc3226fe7dd4d0d718a185a1ed541044&sv=3)

[PreviousAutoroute Announce Absolute Metric](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/autoroute-announce-absolute-metric)
[NextForwarding Adjacency](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/forwarding-adjacency)

# Start | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/start.md)
.

To launch the lab, you must have already installed containerlab and cloned the git repo.

To begin, run the following command on your containerlab machine:

Copy

    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    containerlab deploy -t mvpn/mvpn.clab.yml --reconfigure

Once all nodes are started, run the following command to transfer the config files to all nodes. These files will be used to change between startup configs for subsequent labs.

Copy

    python3 transfer_configs_to_nodes.py

The script will prompt you for a directory name. Enter "mvpn".

Use the MTPutty session file located in **mvpn/mvpn\_putty\_sessions.xml** to quickly setup your SSH sessions to the nodes. Go to **Server - Import Tree** and browse for the file. This requires you to use the same management IPs for your nodes as I did. If you changed your management IPs, you must edit the xml file first before importing it into MTPutty.

When you are done with the lab, use the following command to wipe it:

Copy

    containerlab destroy -t mvpn/mvpn.clab.yml

# Full Mesh Dynamic Auto-Tunnels | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-dynamic-auto-tunnels.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Using the full mesh dynamic auto-tunnel feature, configure CSR4, CSR5, and CSR8 for a full mesh of TE tunnels. Do not use an ACL to specify the tunnel destinations on the routers. They should dynamically learn of the TE tunnel endpoints.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-dynamic-auto-tunnels#id-336cd891-bed9-4494-b8b2-e5392258561c)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-dynamic-auto-tunnels#id-2527b04d-e307-4a84-80c1-735ab421147e)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Using auto-tunnel mesh with OSPF is even more scalable than regular auto-tunnel mesh. With “regular” auto-tunnel mesh, we must specify the tunnel destinations using an ACL. This ACL is referenced by the auto-template tunnel destination.

IOS-XE supports doing dynamic discovery of auto-tunnel mesh endpoints using OSPF. XRv does not support this. This feature is also not supported in ISIS. The router advertises a type 4 Opaque-Area LSA (router information) that includes the mesh-group and its loopback IP address. Any other routers that have an auto-template using the mesh-group number as a the tunnel destination build a dynamic tunnel to the specified IP address in the LSA.

For example, we can see R8’s advertised type 4 Opaque-Area LSA which advertises the mesh group (10) and Lo0 address:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVA9ajBcN2jLJUw7NwwAN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd982e2b9-2404-4579-9f79-bf3f6f5126a5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9c21c009cbf3de6b693d7d86a308e324&sv=3)

This is very similar to BGP auto-discovery of VPN endpoints, for example for VPLS or EVPN.

We can prove that IOS-XR does not support this feature because it cannot decode the TLV in R8’s Router Information Opaque-Area LSA:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbJl5vDkX0lqqUXPb0Q02%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2b03ed69-2128-4b78-a335-9f69fc3575b0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9c1295137f6277e13ab5e81d0f80095a&sv=3)

CSR4, CSR5, and CSR8 should now have a full mesh of tunnels. We were able to use the exact same config template on all routers, which is extremely scalable from a configuration standpoint. (Although not very scalable in terms of state in the network for a full mesh of TE tunnels). But the drawback is that this is not supported on IOS-XR.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FUWQRBQ6UmboEO2CVcPzM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D11005e86-2b6c-42c2-bbe5-9032d6a72310&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=eb85342b44aecfaa807bf1fa27d9b80a&sv=3)

[PreviousFull Mesh Auto-Tunnels](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-auto-tunnels)
[NextOne-Hop Auto-Tunnels](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/one-hop-auto-tunnels)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-dynamic-auto-tunnels#id-336cd891-bed9-4494-b8b2-e5392258561c)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-dynamic-auto-tunnels#id-2527b04d-e307-4a84-80c1-735ab421147e)
    

Copy

    #CSR4, 5, 8
    
    mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel mesh
    !
    interface Auto-Template1
     ip unnumbered Loopback0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel destination mesh-group 10
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute announce
    !
    router ospf 1
     mpls traffic-eng mesh-group 10 lo0 area 0

# TE Tunnels with UCMP | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure two TE tunnels from R8 to R2. One must go through R4, and one must go through XR12. Using signalled-bandwidth, configure a 2:1 load share ratio so that R4 receives twice as much traffic.

Do the same for R2 to R8, creating two TE tunnels. One must go through R1, and one must go through R6. Without using signalled-bandwidth, configure a 2:1 load share ratio so that R1 receives twice as much traffic.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp#dbcfb58c-05c9-47da-bd95-6a1e0db025b3)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp#id-59eb178a-a941-4567-b3c0-121300d051dc)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

With TE tunnels you can easily preform UCMP. By default, UCMP will happen using signalled bandwidth. We can see this on R8. TE tun1 has twice as much signalled bandwidth as TE tun2. Both tunnels have **autoroute announce** configured. Tun1 receives a 2:1 load share:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2uA5f1IJ7nw088PjQscV%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd56301fd-cf2a-44d2-baf3-1fb8fcfd6081&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=47f0e1cd11261a0dadc3cde5159ce0f1&sv=3)

If you do not want to use signalled BW on the TE tunnels, or you want to override the signalled BW, you can use the **load-share** option. We can see this on R2.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2IFEoBoQTNNN4GCpLDQA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D423c47ba-1492-452c-9ec1-5fddcbd366ff&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d80edbb7f2fa7a797c9e7d58b4b2be17&sv=3)

This should also work on IOS-XR, but on XRv it will give you a commit error if you try to use **load-share** on a TE tunnel. You can use unequal signaled-bandwidths on XRv, but it will not produce UCMP in the RIB.

Caveats[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp#id-87160e54-0ae2-4bcb-97c8-de844ce38258)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If you have multiple tunnels with signalled BW, but one tunnel has no signalled BW, all tunnels revert to ECMP. We can see this on R8 if we add one more tunnel to R2 but without any signalled BW.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FWy9FXDuzqwDiZKvVbAPV%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D31413f7b-8f98-4a51-9499-6bb4c3861488&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b4c270210acf521fb28b6c3dd5fc0180&sv=3)

When the **load-share** option and a signalled BW option are both on the tunnel, only the **load-share** option is used. We can test this on R2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzurSGzufqfQt9D0hdACE%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da3ac517d-fec8-4f7b-a7ae-acff28dbe09e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7bbd7da846e112f5f6520b161415222d&sv=3)

If we add a third tunnel to R2 that only uses signalled BW, the signalled BW is counted as a load-share value. Below we simply use a BW of 5 kbps. This gets added to the RIB as a 5:2:1 ratio with the two existing TE tunnels (which use **load-share**).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F9n4D7Vns5595GbrrdqFX%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D718d6651-3dfe-4468-ad68-63422e9a8de6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bc3f7f76740201f34df5add50668dab5&sv=3)

[NextAuto-Bandwidth](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth)

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp#dbcfb58c-05c9-47da-bd95-6a1e0db025b3)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp#id-59eb178a-a941-4567-b3c0-121300d051dc)
    
*   [Caveats](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp#id-87160e54-0ae2-4bcb-97c8-de844ce38258)
    

Copy

    #R8
    ip explicit-path name VIA_R4
     next-address loose 4.4.4.4
    !
    ip explicit-path name VIA_XR12
     next-address loose 12.12.12.12
    !
    int tun1
     description R2_VIA_R4
     tunnel dest 2.2.2.2
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 2000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name VIA_R4
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute announce
    !
    int tun2
     description R2_VIA_XR12
     tunnel dest 2.2.2.2
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 1000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name VIA_XR12
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute announce
    
    #R2
    ip explicit-path name VIA_R1
     next-address loose 1.1.1.1
    !
    ip explicit-path name VIA_R6
     next-address loose 6.6.6.6
    !
    int tun1
     description R8_VIA_R1
     tunnel dest 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng load-share 2
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name VIA_R1

     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng

     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name VIA_R6
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute announce

Copy

    #R2
    int tun1
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng load-share 2
    !
    int tun2
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng load-share 1

Copy

    #R8
    int tun3
     description R2_NO_BW
     tunnel dest 2.2.2.2
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute announce

Copy

    int tun1
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng load-share 2
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 1000
    !
    int tun2

     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 5000

# Profile 27 w/ FRR | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-frr.md)
.

Coming from the previous lab, configure the Tree SID to use FRR TI-LFA.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-frr#fd8b9b3e-1815-4cb1-a576-b0e022e929b4)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-frr#id-0406bf94-d2d1-45e7-831e-a2f9d3a1fdb1)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

To be able to use LFA with P2MP Tree-SID policies, we must first enable TI-LFA everywhere. This is done easily using the above group configuration. TI-LFA is added to every Gigabit interface.

Next we simply enable FRR LFA on the policy. Since this is a static policy, we do this on the PCE.

Let’s look at a transit node such as XR1. Before making this change, the outgoing interface is explicit. The nexthop is the router’s IP address on the link. These are both signs that FRR is not in use for this P2MP policy.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrLJ1L7qEQcDenMQAB3Sh%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D23d41321-c318-438c-b951-77e53175db7a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=70cf5c1ced641f17bc21747c22fba3a2&sv=3)

After making the change, we can see on the PCE’s policy that FRR is enabled. All of the nexthops now have an exclamation point, indicating that FRR is in use.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6FEB66coslXtV5ZUHK99%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc0aa4cc4-37d5-409c-a416-48238eb99a86&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9228ca97916d6824580904baba5392c1&sv=3)

On XR1, we now see no outgoing interface. The nexthop is now the node’s RID, and it has an exclamation point. This indicates that the IP FRR for the nexthop dictates the outgoing interface now.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5lLZLNp7BgIvnrhZXUtw%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Def679250-b186-4902-b67d-50780b8143ca&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=10612973740ab9f3296f39681bbee37b&sv=3)

Under normal circumstances, the direct link to R3 is used. But under FRR protection conditions, the multicast traffic is tunneled to R3 via the link to R2 (Gi0/0/0/0.3012).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FDw0Z5NigQAMNUFng08qB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db59e2d48-7e6c-4d52-b53c-24bf3642b4c2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c7c40f874e07ad8b542e01849c51a99d&sv=3)

The backup path will push two labels on top of label 15001: {16004/16003}.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAkOKkXlxbeDr4wS8xtfG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd2422f4a-0d8c-4903-8a49-a756f44436f9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d0b0431e123cef21af69a4368ccdc0c6&sv=3)
