# Full Mesh Auto-Tunnels | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-auto-tunnels.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Using the full mesh auto-tunnel feature, configure CSR8 and XR11 so that they have TE tunnels to each other, plus CSR4 and CSR5. Do not configure CSR4 and CSR5. They will not have any headend TE tunnels. Use a tunnel ID range of 1000-1999 on CSR8 and XR11.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-auto-tunnels#cfcfd470-fa76-4f09-9a82-e9066fc9ced0)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-auto-tunnels#c524a94f-104c-4a8e-848c-439c515c6730)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Full mesh auto-tunnels allow you dynamically create tunnels to all endpoints in an ACL using a template tunnel interface. This allows you to to more easily create a full mesh of TE tunnels with less configuration overhead. Additionally, adding a new TE tunnel to a new PE is simply a matter of adding an entry to the ACL.

The auto-mesh feature requires an ACL be defined to determine the tunnel endpoints. On IOS-XR you use a prefix-list. You can define the local PE itself in the ACL or prefix-list, it doesn’t hurt anything. This can allow you to copy+paste the ACL/prefix-list on every PE.

Next, you create a template tunnel interface. On IOS-XR you instead create an attribute-set which contains the attributes of the template tunnel interface. On IOS-XR we are limited to only doing a dynamic path-option. This cannot be specified. IOS-XR’s attribute-set seems limited to things like affinity group.

Finally, on IOS-XE we activate the feature globally and optionally define a tunnel ID range.

On IOS-XR, we define the tunnel ID range under the **mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel mesh** section. Also remember to globally define the MPLS-TE unnumbered loopback.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-auto-tunnels#b481fbdb-2dc4-4198-a7e6-766741d9e457)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On CSR8, we can verify the auto-tunnel mesh config and the generated tunnel interfaces using the following command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FswFHR3NRA8FdHFc5Voua%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D61a92be4-4fab-4518-b65f-35de68b15dc8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ff7509fe4fcbbf61533a3732911d4ca0&sv=3)

The dynamically created tunnel interfaces cannot be viewed in the running config, but they can be view using **show derived-config**.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FaRIvP53EFwx5sVxroUmq%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9b90fa17-1efe-424c-a259-b43918f984f8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=af59dfb55b01c5ea8136a07600d8a1c1&sv=3)

You can see how this feature is actually fairly simplistic. The router just takes every valid entry in the standard ACL and builds a new tunnel interface with that entry as the destination.

Using our standard show command we can verify the status of the tunnels.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6tCpFgITu8p9ZxaHQLRB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfd1ac98f-69d9-4706-96e9-ee354ce2ad77&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b6a2594c5146a213b1ffc9597d8f9361&sv=3)

We can also verify that autoroute is working.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FGS5iom8Fr3nJL7PU1W8f%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D269c0000-55d5-42df-b69a-fa7bef0b8e95&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e045d82232eeceff8eec7625f48b6ab5&sv=3)

We can preform this same verification on XRv11. Note that I had previously used a 0.0.0.0/0 le 32 prefix-list entry on XRv11, which created 13 total tunnels. These have been removed, which is indicated by the output at the bottom (cumulative counters).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FcK3nh4pnbk1DJ4oIsWat%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4da3e644-cd4d-4fbf-acd8-8eff436cf460&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=96aed21a3f047a1649420fc78c9841eb&sv=3)

We can see that the default and only path-option on these auto-tunnels is dynamic.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJKqYCOMlsCbmA4ULIiIX%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D631de28b-cbad-4484-9f54-3ba4b955e54d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ad146ec507da3120d4f55a940a4bd28f&sv=3)

**show mpls traffic-eng tun br** gives us an indication of which tunnels were auto-created by the auto-tunnel feature using the **+** symbol.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FgDcbM8i3m50UdIzEzhWA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9eb5e2bb-b186-4f6c-a368-9b6c889400b5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4addc36f7ac534464a9d14ff32a8d482&sv=3)

Finally, we should be using these tunnels for routes to the endpoints due to autoroute.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4T3klR9EjzUtihY4RP35%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db2003100-29e5-4b14-a89d-0267da3bd533&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c458a4fa20d14549b98e285c316721ee&sv=3)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-auto-tunnels#cfcfd470-fa76-4f09-9a82-e9066fc9ced0)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-auto-tunnels#c524a94f-104c-4a8e-848c-439c515c6730)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-auto-tunnels#b481fbdb-2dc4-4198-a7e6-766741d9e457)
    

Copy

    #CSR8
    mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel mesh
    mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel mesh tunnel-num min 1000 max 1999
    !
    interface Auto-Template500
     ip unnumbered Loopback0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel destination access-list 10
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute destination
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
    !
    access-list 10 permit 5.5.5.5
    access-list 10 permit 11.11.11.11
    access-list 10 permit 4.4.4.4
    access-list 10 permit 8.8.8.8
    
    #XRv11
    ipv4 unnumbered mpls traffic-eng Loopback0
    !
    ipv4 prefix-list TUNNEL_ENDPOINTS
     permit 8.8.8.8/32
     permit 4.4.4.4/32
     permit 5.5.5.5/32
     permit 11.11.11.11/32
    !
    mpls traffic-eng
     auto-tunnel mesh
      group 10
       attribute-set MESH_ATTRS
       destination-list TUNNEL_ENDPOINTS
      !
      tunnel-id min 1000 max 1999
     !
     attribute-set auto-mesh MESH_ATTRS
      autoroute announce

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    access-list 10 permit 5.5.5.5
    access-list 10 permit 11.11.11.11
    access-list 10 permit 4.4.4.4
    access-list 10 permit 8.8.8.8
    
    #IOS-XR
    ipv4 prefix-list TUNNEL_ENDPOINTS
     permit 8.8.8.8/32
     permit 4.4.4.4/32
     permit 5.5.5.5/32
     permit 11.11.11.11/32

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    interface Auto-Template500
     ip unnumbered Loopback0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel destination access-list <STANDARD ACL>
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute destination
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
    
    #IOS-XR
    ipv4 unnumbered mpls traffic-eng Loopback0
    !
    mpls traffic-eng
     auto-tunnel mesh
      group 10
       attribute-set MESH_ATTRS
       destination-list TUNNEL_ENDPOINTS
     !
     attribute-set auto-mesh MESH_ATTRS
      autoroute announce

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel mesh
    mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel mesh tunnel-num min 1000 max 1999

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    ipv4 unnumbered mpls traffic-eng Loopback0
    !
    mpls traffic-eng
     auto-tunnel mesh
      tunnel-id min 1000 max 1999

# FRR Path Protection | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-path-protection.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.frr.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

A TE tunnel using the path CSR8-CSR9-CSR10-CSR5 is setup on CSR8. Configure FRR path protection so that if the primary path goes down, traffic is rerouted around this failure using a pre-signaled path of CSR8-CSR1-CSR3-CSR2-CSR5. Test by shutting down the CSR9-CSR10 link.

Additionally, configure TE-tunnel 0 on XR11 for path-protection, simply using a dynamic path for the standby LSP.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-path-protection#c93ea3c9-6b4e-4eaa-8d51-d93f66d24030)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Path protection involves pre-calculating and signalling a secondary path option from the headend. Upon receiving notification that the primary path is no longer up (via RESV tear, local detection, etc), the headend will immediately switch traffic onto the backup TE tunnel. This is a completely separate TE tunnel that is already signaled from the headend to the tailend, using a separate path-option.

Path protection is not nearly as fast as link or node protection, because the protection is not always happening at the PLR (unless the headend itself is the PLR). If the link down event happens 5 nodes away, this has to be detected, then signaled to the headend which is not guaranteed to happen within 50 msec. The only thing path protection helps you with is not having to run CSPF again and signal the new path.

When using path protection we need to make sure to **not** use **tunnel mpls traffic-eng fast-reroute**. We aren’t really using FRR on the primary path itself, instead the headend is creating a separate TE tunnel and will locally switch to that tunnel.

Note that path-protection on IOS-XR is enabled as its own command. A path-option is not explicitly associated with the protection. Instead, IOS-XR appears to be smart enough to calculate a completely path divert backup path to use as its standby LSP. You can also use an explicit-path as your backup path-option if desired.

Note that the following syntax also appears to work:

Verification - CSR8[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-path-protection#id-375a130e-44e8-4e21-95b6-292de1db1d8b)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

You may need to shut/no shut the tunnel. You should see that the backup tunnel has been pre-signaled and shares 0 common nodes:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FYNrsookQhhUNQC9mwjxa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd1ffdffc-aa2f-4c6d-b579-c23611cf4194&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c41ce94bbe65579123e5b1d88b316a8e&sv=3)

Add the parameter **protection** to see more details. We an see the primary LSP path and protection LSP path.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FffEtrr5xxQBb0lnQSk6m%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D981e7c55-2523-4fb3-81d3-f64394bea9b1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=10a7da92f3475359ef0172c44ddf271c&sv=3)

We can also see on any node along the protection LSP that the TE tunnel is fully signaled:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0joPPjEnQoSH9CLiYzYl%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6d4fc184-51cc-4665-8b4c-bb0f9f8d6068&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5fed9ae594a6bc285109792521412093&sv=3)

If we shut down Gi2.590 on CSR9, we should see that the backup LSP is now in use on CSR8.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F1drGhZFNtSvLy1RJEIQN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D84e799d4-e1f4-4d16-b92c-300fdad46fd3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=70c04a56333f3f4ef948d7cf612a35b9&sv=3)

This will last indefinitely, as CSR8 cannot satisfy path-option 1. However, if it was able to find a new LSP that satisfies the original path-option, we would see that the path protection would only be temporary.

Also note that if the backup path option is not valid, you will see “Path Protection: Requested” - it has been requested but could not be fulfilled. This appears to be the case when you use a path-option number that is not the same as the normal path-option.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FSY5EthEqsU6sWZYwO8WF%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5f4adfe8-651b-41a9-94ea-87aaa9b56c7b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cf355e17d43816ec9468e5948a90c92f&sv=3)

If we change the primary path-option to 2, it appears to work.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAD7x3DpNSLitRlb5Z2KR%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D38b11043-2c6d-407c-89f5-50cfecd02427&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=764237a587455425981c869b5b29cfb7&sv=3)

If the protected path is not valid, that will also cause path protection to only show “Requested.” Here I shut down the CSR3-CSR2 link. Now the strict explicit path-option cannot be satisfied:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F3StngM022pJy0NQ0Lvg6%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D57fb2b45-9cd1-45bb-8ba2-17d9026d45eb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a8616806cbd1b903a2754666e407828f&sv=3)

If I change the explicit-path to use loose next-addresses, it can now be setup.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F1vi9zdUZSy3klKPpV15D%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D64463503-639a-4290-a0af-a718431bae72&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3a5798a6e4b278d8704ba6922905ead1&sv=3)

Above, the protection LSP goes CSR1-CSR3-CSR2, but actually takes the path through CSR10.

Verification - XR11[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-path-protection#c2f20f2a-a8c3-4266-8b16-64561d3b7a62)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Path-protection on IOS-XR is fairly simple. The feature is enabled under the TE tunnel, and you must give it an additional path-option to use as its standby LSP.

We can see that the router now has two separate LSPs for the tunnel:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fn7f9VeWFpbGezhg3dQjs%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddf5b940e-faf8-4482-bced-c51623afaf66&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=787f342e1d15aba443ad5b2cf54a6efb&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXD50vL29j5agvj9W1Mbx%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dce78fbec-4bfc-4fb7-b779-72e969cb5066&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=449a0c74a6eb29e2d5c0c113a85d54ef&sv=3)

Path option 1 is what is actually used for setup, and path option 2 is used for the standby LSP. This LSP is fully signaled. For example, we can see that the LSP is up on R3:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F3RUlr17l2hsyIPZy0bYI%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D41326b09-3e02-4433-8170-2252407e6039&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=23763341c12e16e4e9d46bfac099ea8a&sv=3)

If we bring down the XR12-R9 link, we should see this LSP becomes active:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FT1smpskmsVxfiADhb1Ln%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da3e7d9e7-3e84-4e3c-9af8-36426b2c72b8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e70ef3cc3c51e70150549cf67740f790&sv=3)

Above, XR11 immediately switches over to the standby LSP and then generates a new standby path. We can see this second path below:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FpfuKyQhquLQrYq9Ied4x%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da7325ce6-66ae-4b96-b222-a642d2458378&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b0a8a8ae9da54fdb58c21e9730608184&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F59nhu21G37RC9q12UtSY%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2971784a-8855-4a51-8527-c4d6dad5dc68&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0e35e4afdca9d15f3b81a64d9518429d&sv=3)

Could we use a single dynamic path-option with the **path-protection** command?

Unfortunately this does not work. It seems that the router needs a second option in order to calculate and setup the standby LSP. The router appears to be able to only use a single path-option for both setup and standby LSPs when the primary LSP path-option has failed.

It could be in this lab that there is not a secondary path that is completely distinct from the primary path? However in this topology, there should be a valid secondary path.

# FRR Backup Auto-Tunnels with SRLG | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-backup-auto-tunnels-with-srlg.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.frr.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

A TE tunnel using the path CSR8-CSR9-CSR10-CSR5 is setup on CSR8. Configure automatic FRR link protection on CSR9 so that if the CSR9-CSR10 link goes down, traffic is rerouted around this failure and stitched back together on CSR10. Ensure that the backup tunnel does not use the links to XR12, CSR2, or CSR6.

Additionally, there is a TE tunnel from XR11 to CSR4 that passes through XR12-CSR9. Configure automatic FRR link protection on XR12 with a backup path that does not use the link to CSR10.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-backup-auto-tunnels-with-srlg#id-323b42dc-6f8f-4478-9a5a-772e63615ac0)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-backup-auto-tunnels-with-srlg#id-074cd0cd-a351-49fc-9855-504500c5cfc6)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SRLG (Shared Risk Link Group) is a mechanism for marking interfaces that should be grouped together because they share the same fate. An example of this is links that all share the same conduit, or links that use different wavelengths of the same fiber. If one fiber is cut, it is very likely other fibers in this conduit would be cut.

If your backup path ends up using a fiber that is in the same conduit as the primary path, then you have a good chance of both your primary and backup path going down at the same time, and therefore not providing fast reroute protection. To solve this, you can assign links that share the same fate to the same SRLG group. Then you tell the router to calculate auto-tunnels using SRLG in either preferred or force mode. In preferred mode, the router tries to calculate backup paths that don’t use links in the same SRLG, but if it can’t find any paths, it still calculates a backup path anyway. In force mode, the backup path will not come up unless it is a path which strictly does not contain a link in the same SRLG group as the primary link. (It is srlg-disjoint).

To assign an SRLG to a link, you use the following commands:

This information is flooded into the IGP as another attribute on the link, just like TE metric, affinity, and available bandwidth. We can see the SRLG information of links in the TED as follows:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FEqDrVLlTOUtyP6aLdXNt%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D50a77188-46d2-4466-ad29-783776b58cf2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3b0b1767d1d7a3384e6d5b867d67ad89&sv=3)

We can also see all SRLG values and their links in the topology using this command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FA2xXn68YoDZZwdchpGuY%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Defd42817-435b-4704-86cc-bfdb594c0c97&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8a75d48c346f9c7e911c4bace065195c&sv=3)

The **force** and **preferred** keywords for SRLG protection for auto-backup tunnels requires a closer look. On IOS-XE, you must specify either **force** or **preferred**.

On IOS-XR, the default is **force**, and optionally you can override this using **preferred**.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-backup-auto-tunnels-with-srlg#bc1cd51b-bbb5-460b-8cc5-36ea603637c5)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On CSR9, we should see that the CSR9-CSR10 link is protected for the CSR8-CSR5 LSP, and that it is using CSR3 for the backup path. All of CSR9’s directly connected neighbors which are themselves also directly connected to CSR10, are in the same SRLG. Also, since we specified **nhop-only**, the router is not allowed to calculate node-protecting backup paths. This leaves CSR9-CSR3-CSR10 as the best possible backup path.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFsW7LwZquI1OA7dgH2zY%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D588213cb-2d50-4646-aa3e-60f8111554d5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6220623b7fe92cf5536f28f52ab0e40d&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FGbo8rJrL35eXJPQ07jWH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddae4d816-5cb0-4593-a362-cd0cb264aa90&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=98d4fd7606f2633b61ce2621d1838386&sv=3)

On XR12, we have a similar situation. We must use a **nhop-only** tunnel, and the XR12-CSR9 and XR12-CSR10 links are in the same SRLG, leaving XR12-CSR6-CSR9 as the best link-protecting backup path. However, this actually can’t be used, because the CSR9-CSR6 link is also in SRLG 10. If you happened to make the SRLG group IDs different on CSR9 and CSR10, then that would be a valid solution and you would see XR12-CSR6-CSR9. However, I instead see XR12-CSR6-CSR1-CSR9.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXY59yXFAin4sQ9845JLE%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D311bf943-4ba2-456a-9645-bdfe675548ce&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=17052122726a0aba4a0bbc77e4eeaceb&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FHxsxDbd0AZyrNmRy4VNv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1ec3c565-b901-450c-b3b8-32d40e322ffa&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=eb637babd8234dd2bb77d1472cc9c948&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FSnYpzeMH2WsV9X9kA9UM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2c650602-b26f-49b4-bf93-4fda5a82e89b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=748225ff24b13482ef57907dcf45cf4c&sv=3)

So as you can see, the router takes into account not just the local SRLG values, but the SRLG values for other routers in the topology. Essentially, SRLG is just another possible constraint that you can use, and it is flooded with all TE information as admin weight and affinity.

Note that IPFRR (LFA and TI-LFA) do not take into account the SRLG values of other routers in the topology. The router can only use local SRLG values for srlg-disjoint LFA/TI-LFA backup paths.

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-backup-auto-tunnels-with-srlg#id-074cd0cd-a351-49fc-9855-504500c5cfc6)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-backup-auto-tunnels-with-srlg#bc1cd51b-bbb5-460b-8cc5-36ea603637c5)
    

Copy

    #CSR8
    int tun0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng fast-reroute
    
    #XR11
    int tunnel-te0
     fast-reroute
    
    #CSR9
    int GigabitEthernet2.529
     srlg gid 10
    int GigabitEthernet2.592
     srlg gid 10
    int GigabitEthernet2.569
     srlg gid 10
    int GigabitEthernet2.590
     srlg gid 10
    !
    mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel backup nhop-only
    mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel backup srlg exclude force
    
    #XR12
    ipv4 unnumbered mpls traffic-eng lo0
    !
    srlg
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.502
      1 value 10
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.592
      1 value 10
    !
    mpls traffic-eng
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.592
      auto-tunnel backup exclude srlg
      auto-tunnel backup nhop-only
     !
     auto-tunnel backup tunnel-id min 100 max 199

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int GigabitEthernet1
     srlg gid <value>    ! Where gid is "global ID"
    
    #IOS-XR
    srlg
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
      1 value <value>    ! Where 1 is the index number

Copy

    CSR9(config)#mpls traffic-eng auto-tunnel backup srlg exclude ?
      force      Backup tunnels MUST not use SRLGs of protected interfaces
      preferred  Backup tunnels try to avoid using SRLGs of protected interfaces

Copy

    RP/0/0/CPU0:XRv12(config-mpls-te-if)#  auto-tunnel backup exclude srlg ?
      preferred  SRLG exclusion is preferred but not mandatory
      weighted   If SRLG is shared admin weight of the SRLG is added to link metric
      <cr>

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-4-flex-algo.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.multi.area.part4.init.cfg** in the XRv9K topology in CML.

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.multi.area.part4.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.multi.area.part4.init.cfg

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fs3Q4NI08EkB9jpt8tIai%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd8ec7624-42c4-47d7-98d0-c9bb49fc02ff&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=75ac7b84dcbc994a8cc20a34c2b77307&sv=3)

The leaking and summarization of loopbacks has been added back in.

Add a new locator that uses flex algo 128. This should optimize latency. Ensure that prefixes are summarized at the L1/L2 routers and propagated to all L1 areas. Use **fd00:1::/32** for the prefix block, using the same formula for the node ID (XXYY, where XX is the domain, and YY is the node number).

Static latency values have been added to all links, as shown in the diagram above. If a latency value is not specified, it is statically set to 10.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-4-flex-algo#id-7be862e9-8cd9-4372-8afb-38bf1559a0ba)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-4-flex-algo#id-400c16c7-e4fe-494f-85f6-03d02778252b)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Using flex algo with prefix summarization uses the same configuration you are familiar with from the previous summarization lab, but with a slight twist to ensure that the algorithm is included in the prefix summary.

First we configure the Flex-Algo Defintion (FAD), the locator, and advertise the locator in ISIS:

Next, we add the ::/32 to the RPL that is used to control route leaking from L2 into L1:

Finally we add the prefix summarization. We must include the **algorithm** keyword so that the flex algo is included on the summary prefix. Without this, the prefix will simply be a normal IGP summary.

To demonstrate the issue, let’s remove the algorithm from the prefix summarization on XR3 and XR4:

XR3 and XR4 add a fd00:1:7800::/40 IPv6 external prefix to their L2 LSP. They supress the more specific SRv6 locator advertisements for fd00:1:7807::/48 and fd00:1:7808::/48:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FDau5cigywsLElCSn2HUm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3438e86c-5006-455c-8fb5-3409ca40d1c8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9d88cd8d56e6cc203dadc018dbd42345&sv=3)

The problem is that to XR1, this simply looks like a normal IGP prefix. So essentially, the default algo #0 is used.

A traceroute from XR5 to XR1 follows the IGP path XR5-XR1-XR3-XR7.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTBaYOG4KzWD2xFBtqQ8c%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9ffa445e-b8ad-43c8-8d39-9e8bd308bd1c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=22ab6a47dfe6e0f14ddafefff2d6c6df&sv=3)

Let’s add the **algorithm** keyword back onto the prefix summary:

The prefix has been removed as a normal IPv6 external prefix, and is now an SRv6 locator with an associated algorithm:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FHN4KsE6HyC3kbU1BfenG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D268b399c-a945-4b1e-a7a7-c5aa5f47c83e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=29a3dcf856aa01bb2cef19b9adb60103&sv=3)

XR1 now uses its delay values for the metric instead of its IGP costs, as it sees that the prefix is associated with algo 128, not the default algo 0. XR1 has a best path via XR4 due to lower latency values. Additionally, XR1 passes this prefix from L2 into L1 as an SRv6 locator, not an external prefix. So you only need to set the algorithm at the local ABRs which do L1 to L2 propagation.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FULpcTSSq4saxTR8U53pP%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D84297d9a-0753-4f37-b948-179c5cb6e22b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4920ad0d012605e9c91211f2a381e3ee&sv=3)

A traceroute from XR5 to XR7 now takes the lowest latency path:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FWvwcUSSQqRqufvgErMG2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da82b4316-b2cc-4dd5-95dd-b3a4ab209647&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0f9d64845d8969a9d4e92cea375841b3&sv=3)

Note that there is also optional **explicit** knob that can be used on the summary advertisement. This means that only SRv6 locators that have the specified algorithm attached will be candidate contributing prefixes towards the summary.

We also saw in the previous article that the **adv-unreachable** knob should be used as well. This enables UPA (unreachable prefix advertisement) so that upon failure of a contributing prefix, the L1/L2 router will leak the contributing prefix with an unreachable metric to allow PEs to correctly do fast reroute (BGP PIC).

While this UPA for each flex algo summary is enabled on the XR docs design guide, I don’t quite know if this is really necessary. The BGP service routes should all be via the loopback, so simply using UPA for the single loopback should be all that is necessary. The flex algo summary will only be used for the SRv6 SID, not BGP nexthop reachability.

### The need for a PCE[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-4-flex-algo#id-25330f3a-a5f8-4dd6-a92f-0550c38e9da7)

Notice that a traceroute from XR7 to XR5 does not take the lowest latency path. Why is this?

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJGoeglqrbPNQz34wez2H%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da81d617c-e691-45b1-afaa-5044353ca3c4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=963b8d16cfb5b0e8300135cdc9339711&sv=3)

The reason is the inherent rules for L1/L2 redistribution in ISIS. XR7’s lowest latency path is through XR3. However, XR3 has two routes for fd00:1:5600::/40. It knows this via L2 from XR1, and via L1 from XR4. The L1 path via XR4 has a lower metric (latency), but XR4 has set the down bit as the prefix is propagated from L2 into L1, so XR3 cannot use this route for risk of looping. Therefore, XR3 must use its L2 route via XR1.

Notice that XR7 actually calculates the correct metric of 60 for the path:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FX0f6wyaMz6J5qc1ehwPz%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D51163a47-1c52-4b9c-aefb-11855c66c8a3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1c71e35381c7bf9b63a12bcc68446409&sv=3)

However, XR3 has a metric of 110 because it must use its L2 route:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzrSRQCGW41nbtDW9P95O%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De43b42d4-a0f1-4ffe-82d4-c4d04778abcb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=40b5c8181e86ab6cc967dee6ba2e8ac6&sv=3)

The best solution to this is to use a PCE for end-to-end inter-area path calculation.

[NextSRv6 uSID w/ TI-LFA](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-ti-lfa)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-4-flex-algo#id-400c16c7-e4fe-494f-85f6-03d02778252b)
    
*   [The need for a PCE](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-4-flex-algo#id-25330f3a-a5f8-4dd6-a92f-0550c38e9da7)
    

Copy

    #XR1-XR10
    router isis 1
     flex-algo 128
      metric-type delay
      advertise-definition 
     !
     exit
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      segment-routing srv6
       locator LATENCY
    !
    segment-routing
     srv6
      locators
       locator LATENCY
        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
        algorithm 128
        prefix fd00:1:YYXX::/48   ! Where YY is the domain, and XX is the router number
    
    #XR1, XR3, XR4
    route-policy L2_TO_L1
      if destination in (fd00::/32 ge 40 le 40) then
        pass
      endif
      if destination in (2001:db8:200::/40 ge 128) then
        pass
      endif
      if destination in (fd00:1::/32 ge 40 le 40) then
        pass
      endif
    end-policy
    
    #XR1
    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      summary-prefix fd00:1:5600::/40 algorithm 128
    
    #XR3, XR4
    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      summary-prefix fd00:1:7800::/40 algorithm 128

# SRv6 uSID - Scale (Pt. 1) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-1.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.multi.area.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.multi.area.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.multi.area.init.cfg

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fjca6LWV5hGxV6V9OIj0E%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddd599ea2-a179-484c-bd2b-a35747c13396&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6ed80140a57cafad0c6575d85e96f7a3&sv=3)

Configure SRv6 uSID using fd00:0000::/32 as the locator block on XR1-XR8.

*   Use a node ID of XXYY, where XX is the domain, and YY is the node number.
    
    *   Use domain 00 for XR1-XR4
        
    *   Use domain 56 for XR5 and XR6
        
    *   Use domain 78 for XR7 and XR8
        
    

At the L1/L2 routers, summarize the locator prefixes so only one prefix is present in the RIB of L2-only routers for each domain.

Ensure that L3VPN fully works for the CUSTOMER VRF.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-1#id-4e196e0f-1d20-4e8b-b4fd-7fdf6562d561)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-1#de5d65d2-b29b-4cc3-b4fa-35885267e569)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SRv6 uses the IPv6 destination address as the SID. Nodes simply need IPv6 reachability towards SRv6 SIDs, so we can summarize these prefixes just like any other IP prefix in order to achieve scalability.

By summarizing the SRv6 locator blocks in each L1 area, we can have 100s or even 1000s of ISIS L1 areas and keep the core routing tables at their minimum entries. Only one prefix will exist per L1 area.

First we use a particular addressing scheme to support unique locator blocks per-area that are easily summarized. We must use the same 32 bit block within the IGP altogether, but we are left with 16 bits to use for the node. In this lab, the first 8 bits are the area, and the last 8 bits are the node ID.

For example, a core router such as XR1 is fd00:0000:0001::/48. An L1 PE such as XR5 is fd00:0000:5605::/48, where 56 is the area and 05 is the node ID.

At the L1/L2 routers, we must manually inject summary prefixes for these locator prefixes. On XR1 we summarize fd00:0000:5600::/40, and on XR3/4 we summarize fd00:0000:7800::/40:

We should have reachability between locator SIDs now. For example, XR5 can trace to XR7’s END SID. We first find XR7’s END SID using the following command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FmH1GBKRFZM7yyijn172R%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D99149162-86d6-4c3e-a1ea-de329c647bfd&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0b7458e4fe70ff51dff318d8ae9d8512&sv=3)

XR5 can trace to this:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FH01hD5MNhPmz9FO7Aodx%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dafed7fc0-1a03-4c1d-8300-39bd8861aa5f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7f6b6b818b81f6b0de427d1686df073f&sv=3)

XR5, as an L1-only node, simply follows its default route to the closest L1/L2 router, which is XR1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbCANAHLd4X82vJZNJUba%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df4dbd884-8443-41d0-b9dd-fdd69502bc70&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0a2cfdb8d9236c169ac398d06b487a5d&sv=3)

XR1 follows the summary ::/40 prefix it has learned in L2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2WvuhcBB3zB5VN6vmgtM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D849a05e8-99e7-411e-a2ca-62c2457567d7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e1c7870493094e5a938d7052e3331539&sv=3)

XR3 follows the ::/48 prefix that R7 has advertised:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FUEy3nvSHeIomYQhza6rU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db0d129ff-f0e8-48ed-b48f-452152950e55&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e177502fec04313e0577141a26387382&sv=3)

As you can see, this is just basic IP forwarding principles. Because the SRv6 SID is simply an IPv6 destination address, simple summarization can be used to scale SRv6.

Next we must ensure the L3VPN services are working. First we need to specify the locator for SRv6 under BGP:

Right now we notice a problem: Each PE is only marking the routes from the other PE in its own L1 area as usable:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fhx9I6MQ7BPyU58qrMjBc%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D572b097f-ce63-41f0-988e-a0f19cd70d75&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e75e35bf937ec1e1869e08c4b8ed8274&sv=3)

We can see the problem by inspecting any single prefix. Notice that the nexthop is inaccessible:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FJ7PSp0787xMAcBocGJlQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De9e640d2-5642-4376-8742-cf0a8cb6834c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=74c0488ead56a4db475b65bf5946341b&sv=3)

The BGP nexthop cannot be reachable via a default route (::/0). To fix this we have a few options. We can simply leak all prefixes from L2 into L1, or we can leak a summary route that covers the loopback prefixes. To make this easier, let’s leak all /128 loopback prefixes into L1.

The VPNv4 paths are now marked as bestpath:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FLOmXClq49SdzhpB9cCSc%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D656e097d-87f1-4cff-98c4-f18095f68061&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4e35a33b652ac22be687c34835e84c71&sv=3)

However, we still have a problem. A CE can reach another CE in connected to a PE in the same L1 domain, but not a CE connected to a PE in a remote ISIS domain. For example, CE1 can reach CE2 but not CE3:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Ft12V7EralG09jyBRqva1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4bad5f69-766b-4e14-b053-843e9e2f754a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9bd8a1643dd8963ae2be9361e7ffb94c&sv=3)

Looking at the detailed route on XR5, we see that the SID list is correct:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzO6OB7YHQ4bzyMac8v1S%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9db56ad2-efd6-4415-a8df-4e00833f0464&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d4863a06f951ef21f18bef8668f6476c&sv=3)

However, in the CEF table, we see a clue:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F17k2oeLDUj6BZjHRKzSe%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4a7fed3a-0888-4ab1-852e-754d98ed1504&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=58d123cf76b176c9d5c329993dcf6cb5&sv=3)

In L3VPN with MPLS, we must resolve the BGP nexthop to a /32 route. In L3VPN with SRv6, we must resolve the SID to a route in the FIB. It cannot match the ::/0. Currently the route to the SID fd00:0:7807:e002:: simply matches the default route:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FmALscGrpO2pgxUSGDOM6%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D940311f1-971d-452b-ba3a-9351cfe4b027&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e3c7fa0926f8f58183eee3ae066eef62&sv=3)

In addition to leaking the loopbacks into L1, we must leak the locator prefix blocks:

Now XR5 has the summary ::/40 for the SRv6 SID:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FoUqJlhJDK7cZPi2Dbtf7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df01ffd77-4a64-43b6-bc5b-c79919114bca&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=212727dd1c9e28a0f06878a7430e0a14&sv=3)

The CEF entry is now resolved:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZFXaweV3pKKcvAzY1aUJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3e261440-d1ee-4519-8e23-34196908afe9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e3e7f247323c2182bb8729bdc87e59f7&sv=3)

Traffic is now working:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F49ERcmx5UyD1pEIBhJj7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da26a4c4b-7c15-4550-a121-376b8d1681a9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=213f560e62b70477eccbafb38340fb08&sv=3)

In summary, we use ISIS levels to achieve high scalability with SRv6. This allows us to easily summarize locator prefixes at each level boundary. However, we must be careful to make sure that the BGP nexthops and SRv6 SIDs are resolvable through a route that is more specific than the default route (::/0).

Copy

    #XR1-XR8
    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      segment-routing srv6
       locator DEFAULT
    
    #XR1-XR4
    segment-routing
     srv6
      locators
       locator DEFAULT
        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
        prefix fd00:0000:<R#>::/48
    
    #XR1
    route-policy L2_TO_L1
     if destination in (2001:db8:200::/48 ge 128) then pass endif
     if destination in (fd00:0000::/32 ge 40 le 40) then pass endif
    end-policy
    !
    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      summary-prefix fd00:0:5600::/40
      propagate level 2 into level 1 route-policy L2_TO_L1
    
    #XR3, XR4
    route-policy L2_TO_L1
     if destination in (2001:db8:200::/48 ge 128) then pass endif
     if destination in (fd00:0000::/32 ge 40 le 40) then pass endif
    end-policy
    !
    router isis 1
     address-family ipv6 unicast
      summary-prefix fd00:0:7800::/40
      propagate level 2 into level 1 route-policy L2_TO_L1
    
    #XR5-XR8
    router bgp 100
     segment-routing srv6
      locator DEFAULT
    
    #XR5
    segment-routing
     srv6
      locators
       locator DEFAULT
        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
        prefix fd00:0000:5605::/48
    
    #XR6
    segment-routing
     srv6
      locators
       locator DEFAULT
        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd

    #XR7

    #XR8

     srv6

        micro-segment behavior unode psp-usd
        prefix fd00:0000:7808::/48

# SRv6 uSID w/ TI-LFA | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-ti-lfa.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.usid.configured.cfg

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FeQUwIGQR2AjVLxIfimtw%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd093f8f9-54c0-4d47-b409-978bf95ed42b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=12dd2d5dde36477bcf4eaba65df5caa2&sv=3)

Increase the XR2-XR4 link (vlan 3024) metric to 100.

Enable TI-LFA so that a link-down event for vlan 3013 on XR1 causes fast-reroute using vlan 3012.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-ti-lfa#id-5379c407-d254-4f8f-aa17-4b33f06ebcf6)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-ti-lfa#id-8eea06a7-f3f0-4326-a214-d3205ad7884a)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

TI-LFA for SRv6 works the same as with SR-MPLS. Instead of an MPLS label stack that is pushed, an SRH is pushed ontop of the packet.

We enable TI-LFA for SRv6 the same way as SR-MPLS. We simply use two commands: **fast-reroute per-prefix** and **fast-reroute per-prefix ti-lfa** under the interface under the AFI.

Let’s examine the backup path for XR7’s locator prefix, which is fd00:0:7::/48. Under normal circumstances, this would be an LFA via XR2. However, we’ve increased the metric of the XR2-XR4 link, so a separate P and Q node exists:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FxHQCv3jx9reRtLEuv5wI%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd074ddc2-f6fa-4a50-91c0-04b98ad6a3da&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=28c3394611414a052e77d18f5b591470&sv=3)

The RIB shows us that the SID list for the backup path is XR2’s Adj-SID (uA) for XR4. XR4 will then release the packet to XR7.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZJWgZoxYCwnT2vgmZTA6%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8ccadb82-6bcb-4727-a4cc-46edb5889d2f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d7c1337ece4fa9b7a796dcac19196df2&sv=3)

If we shut down Gi0/0/0/0.3013 and take a pcap on Gi0/0/0/0.3012, we see that XR1 inserts the SRH into the existing IPv6 header in order to provide fast-reroute protection. The behavior is **H.Insert.Red**, not **H.Encaps.Red**, so the existing IPv6 header is retained. (The SRH is inserted, instead of encapsulating the packet with a brand new IPv6 header).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fr5R7X5QlTgejK8HBWxIO%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D04e55492-fd86-4ac4-8fe1-68cdb08efc54&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=fb9e916fa361992e42b58517c72318fb&sv=3)

XR2 should perform PSP, placing the fd00:0:7:e001:: SID in the destination, removing the SRH, and forwarding out the interface towards XR4.

[PreviousSRv6 uSID - Scale (Pt. 4) (Flex Algo)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-scale-pt.-4-flex-algo)
[NextMulticast](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-ti-lfa#id-5379c407-d254-4f8f-aa17-4b33f06ebcf6)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/srv6-usid-w-ti-lfa#id-8eea06a7-f3f0-4326-a214-d3205ad7884a)
    

Copy

    #XR2, XR4
    router isis 1
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.3024
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       metric 100

Copy

    #XR1
    router isis 1
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.3013
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       fast-reroute per-prefix
       fast-reroute per-prefix ti-lfa

Copy

    #XR1
    router isis 1
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.3013
      address-family ipv6 unicast
       fast-reroute per-prefix
       fast-reroute per-prefix ti-lfa

# Auto-Bandwidth | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure a TE tunnel from CSR8 to XR11, and from XR11 to CSR8. Use a dynamic path option. Ensure the routers install a path to the destination through the TE tunnel.

Configure auto-bandwidth on both tunnels using the following parameters:

*   Use the lowest application timer
    
*   Set the min BW as 10 kbps and max as 50 mbps
    
*   Set the initial bandwidth as 5 kbps
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth#id-6942f064-1381-428e-9486-baa4433a9cce)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth#id-83f89643-786d-4628-9890-1718ebcba00e)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Auto-Bandwidth is a feature that automatically adjusts the signalled-bandwidth of a TE tunnel based on how much traffic is actually being forwarded out the tunnel. The idea is that, in times of low utilization, less bandwidth is reserved in the network, allowing for more LSPs to be created. However, if a tunnel starts utilizing a lot of bandwidth, the actual RSVP control-plane signalled-bandwidth matches the data plane bandwidth. This allows higher priority tunnels to take precendence in times of congestion.

Auto-Bandwidth essentially works by just watching the output traffic rate of the tunnel over a given amount of time (the collection interval). The highest bandwidth usage seen is configured on the TE tunnel every application interval. You will literally see the signalled-bandwidth on the TE change in the running config for IOS-XE.

The collection frequency is how often the output rate is inspected. This is 5 minutes and does not appear to be configurable. The application frequency is how often to take the highest value seen from every collection period, and apply it to the TE tunnel’s signalled-bandwidth. This is by default 24 hours but can be adjusted as low as 5 minutes.

Besides setting the min and max values, and the application frequency interval, as we did in this lab, you can also set the **adjustment-threshold**, which gives a percentage threshold that bandwidth on the tunnel must exceed before making a change. You can also set **collect-bw** which simply collects the bandwidth information without actually making a change to the tunnel.

You can also configure an **overflow threshold** which triggers an early bandwidth update if a percentage threshold is exceeded. On IOS-XE you use the following command, where X is the number of consecutive samples exceeding the threshold, and Y is the percent threshold which triggers the early bandwidth update.

On IOS-XR, the syntax is just reversed:

IOS-XR also gives us an **underflow** parameter we can use, which allows an early bandwidth update if the bandwidth falls below a given percentage threshold.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth#id-2db497ce-a8e8-41f1-ae6c-796b0630f5a1)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

After running a full size ping for several minutes on each router, we can see that the auto-bw feature manually applied a signalled-bw to the tunnel.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZpIQzsXBf7i9saXpWg4n%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5b724fde-cee4-428f-b9d1-759b4009045a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=05a990331fbb23065d53ce3ca369bf8a&sv=3)

Using the familiar **show mpls traffic-eng tunnels** command, we can see some statistics about auto-bw:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F1YPO3GozlPFYJwMi4F1P%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2c78b781-33c1-4c50-aab9-055b489e64a5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7392746ebc3e866515f84d25b3addab8&sv=3)

*   300 is the application frequency (in seconds). This is how often the signalled-bandwidth is applied to the TE tunnel.
    
*   225 is the time remaining (in seconds) until the application of the bandwidth to the TE tunnel is triggered.
    
*   191 is the current value of the bandwidth requested by the TE tunnel
    

We can also see this on XR11. However, the bandwidth does not appear to be literally applied to the tunnel in the show run config.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FRcc8I9zuAPS0lqmRA9Gx%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D992d8222-4c51-4948-88eb-e6781c30488d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b0e6fd32b29fee302a7327060fe180c6&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTC89pUPk616iW0KMKySO%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcf379b5b-20fe-4a56-8958-3b9bea5010a1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3df280f2370a2b7e167de13ca7bfccaa&sv=3)

However, we can see that even though the configured bandwidth is 5kbps, the actual requested bandwidth is currently 760 kbps:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFGObptuaxMClNrXzWYdn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D07278e29-9f1a-4e91-b783-3a2029431d2d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=35d9a32b6a58b9696a1c4fa366bf59dc&sv=3)

Using Auto-BW with path option lockdown[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth#b602da7d-2f3c-4517-8437-eb296dd01dda)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On IOS-XE, if you have a path-option in effect that has the **lockdown** keyword, the path is still re-signalled every time the auto-bw feature applies the new bandwidth.

On IOS-XR, the bandwidth is not applied because of the **lockdown** keyword on the path-option. If we lockdown the dynamic path-option, notice that the Auto-bw section says “no BW application because Tunnel is in lockdown”:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F9c1jdkHjAJScEmBrGtuS%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcd114fee-b6be-4e1c-83ef-10093def72d4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ebc2dd63d7c9bf5b3842096daab46d32&sv=3)

Instead you would need to apply the bandwidth to the TE tunnel using a manual exec command:

Now we see the highest-seen BW is actually applied to the tunnel, even though it is in lockdown. Note that I had to do this twice. The first time, it only applies the minimum bandwidth, (10 kbps in my case). The following time, it applies what it has seen as the highest bandwidth in the previous collection period.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F3qJ4ofhWF1ch1b1FQGl6%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc0fe5f8f-3a98-4c3b-98c4-96dc462977b1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e47210c4bad36d7d6581b519b1707106&sv=3)

[PreviousTE Tunnels with UCMP](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/te-tunnels-with-ucmp)
[NextFRR Link Protection (XE, BFD)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-bfd)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth#id-83f89643-786d-4628-9890-1718ebcba00e)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth#id-2db497ce-a8e8-41f1-ae6c-796b0630f5a1)
    
*   [Using Auto-BW with path option lockdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth#b602da7d-2f3c-4517-8437-eb296dd01dda)
    

Copy

    #R8
    int tun0
     tunnel dest 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 5
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng auto-bw frequency 300 max-bw 50000 min-bw 10
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute announce
    
    #XR11
    int tunnel-te0
     dest 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 dynamic
     autoroute announce
     signalled-bandwidth 5
     auto-bw
      bw-limit min 10 max 50000
      application 5
     

Copy

    #IOS-XE
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng auto-bw overflow-limit X overflow-threshold Y

Copy

    #IOS-XR
     auto-bw overflow threshold Y limit X

Copy

    auto-bw underflow threshold Y limit X
    !
    ! or
    auto-bw underflow threshold Y min kbps

Copy

    mpls traffic-eng auto-bw apply tunnel-te 0

Continuing on from the previous lab, configure the default MDTs to exclude RED links and use FRR. Color the XR1-XR3 link red.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-28-w-constraints-and-frr#id-019684ea-5ee6-4de9-b4cd-a4d81e9c40b8)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In profile 27 (static p2mp policies), the policy was configured directly on the PCE, so the constraints and FRR was configured there as well.

In profile 28 and 29, FRR and constraints are configured on the PEs. These affect only the p2mp policies for which they act as a root. (The PE only asks the PCE for path computation for p2mp policies for which it is the root).

To configure constraints, you must create a normal on-demand SR-TE policy, and then associate that color with the default MDT. Additionally, FRR is enabled on the default MDT.

This lab asks us to avoid link color RED. On the PEs, we must add an ODN policy as follows. Any color can be used. Also note that we could have choosen another metric type besides igp.

This color is associated with the default MDT for SR. Additionally, FRR is enabled for the default MDT.

If we look at the policy on the PCE, we can see that FRR is enabled, and the affinity constraint was signaled. Note that all the nexthops have an exclamation point, indicating FRR is in use.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FCfN2QE9uoDMtU2XJHUHm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D20c45b79-3764-47db-90a3-59ea1ec65c9c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=efdf5aef6fa0739f2657e99dfd09b839&sv=3)

This is also reflected on the PE. Note the outgoing interface is “none” as TI-LFA is used to find the outgoing interface now.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKYzVah7i9JDPyOoC33YW%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5acbce7c-66c1-4c9d-97cf-b67251b66c40&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6a0e3e52e297032c82476da0545c403d&sv=3)
