# FRR Link Protection (XE, BFD) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-bfd.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.frr.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.frr.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

A TE tunnel using the path CSR8-CSR9-CSR10-CSR5 is setup on CSR8. Configure FRR link protection so that if the CSR9-CSR10 link goes down on CSR9, traffic is rerouted around this failure and stitched back together on CSR10. Use BFD to detect the failure.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-bfd#id-0778779b-c5c9-4e5d-884d-c16a2cd3400b)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-bfd#id-77c206bf-e5e0-4b17-aea5-950822ab9a01)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MPLS-TE FRR (fast reroute) allows for sub-50 msec convergence times during link or node failures in the network. Without this, the TE path would have to be explicitly torn down, the IGP would signal the change, which updates the TED, and then the headend would calculate a new path via CSPF, and set it up via RSVP. This would cause a noticeable, although brief, outage to drop-sensitive traffic.

Using FRR, backup tunnels are precalculated. The backup tunnels are applied to the interface of the protected link, or the interface facing the protected node. When this link goes down, the local router immediately switches traffic for the protected LSP onto the backup LSP.

In link protection, the backup tunnel terminates on the NHOP itself (the router on the other end of the link). The PLR (point of local repair) learns the NHOP’s label for the primary LSP simply because the PLR is directly connected to the NHOP. The PLR pushes two labels when protecting the primary LSP: the top label is the label for the repair tunnel, and the second label is the NHOP’s label for the primary LSP. The penultimate hop of the repair tunnel will naturally preform PHP, exposing the NHOP’s local label for the primary LSP. Thanks to the global label space, this label can arrive via any interface, which allows FRR to function properly.

In node protection, the backup tunnel terminates on the NNHOP, which is the NHOP’s nexthop. The PLR learns the NNHOP’s label for the primary LSP via the label record option in the RSVP RESV message. We will see this in action in the next lab.

In both link and node protection, link failure is either detected physically, or via RSVP Hello. If relying on the RSVP Hello, you will likely want to use BFD. This allows you to quickly reconverge. Without BFD or RSVP Hellos, you would need to wait about two minutes for RSVP to detect the failure by default, due to the LSP refresh failing. Note that RSVP Hellos are not used by default. To use them you need to activate RSVP Hellos globally, and at the link level:

If you wish to use BFD, you simply add the **bfd** keyword to the end of both commands.

FRR uses three main steps:

*   The headend must request FRR protection on the LSP.
    
    *   This allows some LSPs to use FRR and some not to use FRR, which lets you to protect only important LSPs in case your backup paths run over links that would not have enough bandwidth to protect _all_ LSPs.
        
    *   When you activte FRR protection on the LSP, the RSVP PATH message contains two flags: Local protection requested, and Label recording requested. Label recording is only necessary for node protection, however it always appears when requesting FRR protection on the LSP.
        
    
*   The PLR must configure a backup tunnel and apply it to the protected link.
    
    *   If using link protection, the backup tunnel terminates on the NHOP, and should use an explicit-path avoiding the link.
        
    *   If using node protection, the backup tunnel termiantes on the NNHOP, and should use an explicit-path avoiding the node.
        
    
*   The PLR must detect the failure, either physically, via RSVP Hellos, or via BFD
    
    *   RSVP Hellos are not sent by default. You must activate them explicitly. You can optionally use BFD with RSVP, which we have done in this lab.
        
    

Once the PLR detects failure it does a few things:

*   Protects the primary LSP by switching data traffic onto the backup tunnel
    
*   Informs the headend that a fault has occured, but that the tunnel is undergoing protection using a PathErr message
    
    *   The headend knows not to tear down the tunnel in this case. Instead it can try to reoptimize the tunnel and preform make-before-break so that there is no outage.
        
    
*   Changes the primary tunnel’s SENDER\_TEMPLATE in the PATH message used for refreshing to its own IPv4 address. This forces the NHOP’s RESV messages to arrive back at the PLR, and allows the primary LSP to continue being refreshed over the backup tunnel.
    
    *   If the primary LSP cannot find an alternate path, it will remain signaled over the backup path indefinitely.
        
    

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-bfd#a557f098-4d82-4b80-8d2d-d4681153e561)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

First, CSR8 must request FRR protection on the TE tunnel. We can verify this at CSR8 itself:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOEPFXhUrk7QibTLR8KVH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D04334ee9-18df-43f1-80ef-8a3f3380ce5c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=71abeab823dcdac43bca30748ae86405&sv=3)

We can also see at CSR8 that the record route option has already recorded each hop’s label (in parathesis):

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fr1h9jqlX5tXbFHU3VT9k%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc2b491bc-ba9f-4ba7-9095-f57ac012bb47&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f5117a8772229993d488ab24415e9e6a&sv=3)

Next, CSR9 and CSR10 will run BFD, with FRR as the registered client. They must set RSVP hellos to use BFD. Additionally, CSR9 must create the backup tunnel to CSR10 that excludes the CSR9-CSR10 link. The command **mpls traffic-eng backup-path tun0** instructs CSR9 to protect any LSPs traversing the link over the backup tunnel0 if the link goes down.

The backup tunnel uses CSR9-XRv12-CSR10:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FaekwUDwDTE8yLofgeOP9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df60bee2c-4745-47a1-afac-d40fc4072dd1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8d115117bc733848d1d97edc342eea5d&sv=3)

We can see that BFD is up and the registered client is TE/FRR:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzzjEVjv7cLccNfp3Ib30%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D02e2a242-63a2-42a2-9d59-c55118b25238&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=704e5bdc75bb1de293f312f651b8da34&sv=3)

We can also see that tun0 is ready to protect the CSR8 TE tunnel if interface Gi2.590 goes down:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FX5ockBvycqSND4UgUkIw%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D22d2bb56-849b-4317-9bc0-fee61aff578b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=281b1f8c27dc55fe4fa00b7a3bd59738&sv=3)

Interestingly, we can also see that protection is available from the headend. This is included in the RRO:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fsel9iVl3VaU5yHJIuozH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D22295642-d6de-43c5-8f94-64606361a38f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6bcc381bdc37c036097c1d42332d8fdb&sv=3)

Another verification command we can use on CSR9 is shown below. Currently there is one protected LSP, zero LSPs active (undergoing backup protection), and zero interfaces currently undergoing backup protection.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FD6f88M7x9lXJypVBXBJL%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6fe1f3c5-fb7c-451c-97d9-18c5bfa115f4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2110b88c74697732907d7fe88bd5cbf2&sv=3)

If the interface goes down, CSR9 will push two labels and send to XRv12. It will push XRv12’s TE label for the backup path, and push CSR10’s TE label for the primary path. XRv12 will pop the top label, leaving only CSR10’s primary TE label on the packet as CSR10 receives it.

CSR9 is the point of local repair, or PLR. CSR10 is the merge point, or MP. This is where the backup tunnel merges back onto the primary tunnel.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0iUtMQLYps4mM4IGnyyU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8e9cda33-f702-468d-8e20-c4074041d0ec&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d1c9f36ad7354d6f8bddf602108c4d33&sv=3)

*   CSR10’s TE label (or FRR label) is 16.
    

The topmost label is 24002 as seen in the LFIB:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZY4idUK1zqbOjdCZFH9z%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Def2faa06-8aba-4948-adda-9e7ac7c0f293&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=46944ea46f02eedfa9ec9eada79cb2c2&sv=3)

To test this out, shut gi2.590 on CSR10. CSR9 should show that the backup tunnel is now “active”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FfHroLTSwYoannY2vIqLZ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df15bd054-cae4-4a7c-a379-848e16a16391&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7cd7d286228cf648b85c39dcf6a9f62d&sv=3)

On CSR8, we see that “reroute is pending.” CSR8 knows about the failure, but knows that the path is protected, so it can leave the LSP up and preform make-before-break.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FlAf2kOJyHXqRBeG3KGWG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D91a2be33-77b8-4345-baaf-752838fc4ef7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bde9d17cdc7c400cbecc85e1ef79974d&sv=3)

A few seconds later this dissapears, and we see “path option 1 reoptimization in progress”:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnwdxVAN0RQRuoKSzLccJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7b9e5f6d-ffda-4b81-ab0b-901eb7138ec8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e85eedd672f76622760a3bb79de1bbab&sv=3)

A few seconds afterwards, R8 finds a new path. We see in the tunnel History section that the last error was from R9 (PLR) that there is a PathErr but the tunnel is locally repaired:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FX9HNu8nopAeYv47xED2W%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5a17e30a-c68b-4945-869b-10bb5a76e6ec&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c7d3dcc0530979a5f0977a53a3cfe47e&sv=3)

On R9, the protection is now gone. This is because CSR8 has calculated and signaled a new path, which no longer uses Gi2.590 on CSR9.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FiAonuOiGVDDfDvpGsgWQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd3bd6838-d95f-4cec-af0e-c2a3b9955f95&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=be9a5002b30b20ca2b782feaada00027&sv=3)

If CSR8 could not signal an alternate path, the backup tun0 would protect the primary tunnel indefinitely. The path signaling for the primary tunnel would continue to ride over the backup tunnel.

[PreviousAuto-Bandwidth](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/auto-bandwidth)
[NextFRR Link Protection (XE, RSVP Hellos)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-rsvp-hellos)

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-bfd#id-0778779b-c5c9-4e5d-884d-c16a2cd3400b)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-bfd#id-77c206bf-e5e0-4b17-aea5-950822ab9a01)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-link-protection-xe-bfd#a557f098-4d82-4b80-8d2d-d4681153e561)
    

Copy

    #CSR8
    int tunnel0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng fast-reroute
    
    #CSR9
    ip rsvp signalling hello bfd
    !
    int Gi2.590
     bfd interval 500 min_rx 500 multiplier 3
     mpls traffic-eng backup-path tun0
     ip rsvp signalling hello bfd
    !
    ip explicit-path name AVOID_LINK_TO_CSR10
     exclude-address 132.9.10.10
    !
    int tunnel0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel dest 10.10.10.10
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name AVOID_LINK_TO_CSR10
    
    #CSR10
    ip rsvp signalling hello bfd
    !
    int Gi2.590
     bfd interval 500 min_rx 500 multiplier 3
     ip rsvp signalling hello bfd

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    ip rsvp signalling hello

# Profile 27 w/ Constraints | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-constraints.md)
.

Coming from the previous lab, color the XR1-XR3 link RED. Configure the static SR Tree-SID policy to exclude RED links.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-constraints#id-29eeb90f-3c87-4b67-b614-de089b3c4946)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-constraints#a5c479b5-da6e-45f2-830d-8711b0403a10)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Tree-SID allows us to use standard SR-TE tools to engineer the path an mVPN distribution tree takes. This is a big benefit over mLDP, as mLDP doesn’t give us this control.

To accomplish this lab we simply set the RED affinity on the XR1-XR3 link on both of those nodes.

The PCE must define the bit-mapping under the PCE config, and then include this as a constraint on the static Tree-SID policy.

We can see that the calculated policy now avoids XR3:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F7LVK9IRC7GDl5PiwS4Nv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da4e77bf8-b8a5-4124-8545-a31eb77a52a4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7d25bbbf3e17282440fa93029f174574&sv=3)

XR3 no longer has any Tree-SID state:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FWVchFUrMH1bTSzFoSmpf%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D61f152f6-e1b6-42bd-b8a3-f231a40ed850&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f2b6e8ccf9605cb57bef2c842029e97c&sv=3)

The multicast distribution tree is now taking this path:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FiDi2db7zDy3dlr3mAuWm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D86246280-1503-423d-834e-896cb8a98f87&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=427573e1d5b95e9cf4d5c93fa5109b79&sv=3)

[PreviousProfile 27](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27)
[NextProfile 27 w/ FRR](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-frr)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-constraints#id-29eeb90f-3c87-4b67-b614-de089b3c4946)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27-w-constraints#a5c479b5-da6e-45f2-830d-8711b0403a10)
    

Copy

    #XR1, XR3
    segment-routing
     traffic-eng
      interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.3013
       affinity
        name RED
       !
      !
      affinity-map
       name RED bit-position 1
    
    #XR9
    pce
     segment-routing
      traffic-eng
       affinity bit-map
        RED 1
       !
       p2mp
        policy Tree-SID-Pol1
         candidate-paths
          constraints
           affinity
            exclude
             RED

# RDM w/ FRR Troubleshooting | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting.md)
.

Load **rdm.frr.tshoot.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:rdm.frr.tshoot.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:rdm.frr.tshoot.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6UW69p7pg6qyojnEfE2V%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc82307fb-a7d2-4d73-8575-d7ee40e68096&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2544e49a64698873f3263c2791e73f5e&sv=3)

All nodes have DS-TE configured in IETF mode using RDM as the bc-model.

A TE tunnel is setup on the path CSR8-CSR6-XR12-XR11. CSR6 has a local backup tunnel configured and applied to the R6-XR12 interface, but the path does not seem to be providing backup to CSR8’s tunnel. Fix the issue.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#id-84197432-628b-42aa-8977-7987ccaf0087)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#id-36055bb3-0a4c-426a-8f2d-d266ec1b452d)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

A backup tunnel can use the **backup-bw** parameter to ensure that it takes a path that has available bandwidth. Primary tunnels will only use the repair tunnel if the repair tunnel can satisfy the bandwidth demand.

In this lab, we can see that R6 has given tun100 10M of backup-bw for CT1.

The tunnel is correctly applied to the interface as a backup tunnel, yet we see that it is not providing protection:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FBqtxrSheUco3uE0X8iI1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddbf73a94-4a39-4753-9646-1007fc75bac3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5fd2e862ccb9767f5275e0d8805c7c3a&sv=3)

The reason for this is that the primary tunnel uses 95M of CT0 bandwidth. The backup tunnel cannot satisfy this because it only provides 10M of CT1 bandwidth. The backup tunnel must be able to accomodate the primary tunnel’s pool of bandwidth and the amount of bandwidth.

We have several ways to fix this:

*   We can remove the backup-bw command altogether. This means that the tunnel does not have a specific bandup-bw pool so any LSP will be able to use it for a repair path.
    
*   We can set the backup-bw pool to use CT0 specifically
    
*   We can set the backup-bw pool to use any pool
    

### Using CT0[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#aadc7781-5fc2-413f-b9b2-8628ab137032)

We can configure R6 to have its backup tunnel use at least 95M of CT0 bandwidth as follows:

When the class-type matches, the available bandwidth on the backup tunnel needs to be at least the amount that the primary LSP is using. As long as we provide at least 95M of available backup-bw, the LSP can be protected:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbKz3ItGbdjFUzDMqkiyi%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5ff62d6e-50ef-4666-a363-60e37a98d210&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=feffe4db14781af90fe379baf6d2aef4&sv=3)

### Using “any” pool[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#id-06903043-8bab-487f-b14e-77b2522fffd1)

Alternatively, the backup tunnel can use “any” pool to allow both CT0 and CT1 LSPs to be protected by this backup tunnel. By omitting the **class-type** keyword, “any” pool is used.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FuBnj0aN48DhjSmY8Bnd3%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5c285cb9-0583-4ae8-8cd7-853c7f196f02&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ed63d4d93020e491389a2ad461d380b7&sv=3)

If we change the LSP at CSR8 to use CT1 bandwidth, this same backup tunnel can still protect it:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FaazQpw6LpTfBhtQGps1l%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5bc8dd4e-d72c-491b-9a1d-c7f9a57b0e7d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=956acb11588c49ad836b0058421cbf87&sv=3)

### Backup tunnel selection process[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#id-9b9cadd3-06d0-465c-9be0-78c621af9a51)

Multiple backup tunnels can be applied to an interface. When this happens, the router uses the following selection criteria to prefer one backup tunnel over another:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FBE1A8q312TdJ2uZTP1kl%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D65616f64-5b29-4089-b0f9-3bf196caa53b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e8708815bed3d92e9190c2595fb2ab49&sv=3)

*   NNHOP tunnels are preferred over NHOP, because they provide both link and node protection
    
*   Backup tunnels that have a limited amount of backup-bw are preferred over backup tunnels that have unlimited backup-bw
    
    *   This can be considered a “max-fill” decision
        
    
*   Backup-bw that comes from the same pool as the class-type of the protected tunnel is preferred
    

Remember that configuring backup-bw on a repair tunnel does not actually reserve bandwidth over that path. This is only a local decision at the PLR to make sure the backup path has enough bandwidth to satisfy the protected tunnel. It does not explicitly reserve bandwidth using RSVP over the backup path.

[PreviousIETF DS-TE with RDM](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/ietf-ds-te-with-rdm)
[NextPer-VRF TE Tunnels](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/per-vrf-te-tunnels)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#id-84197432-628b-42aa-8977-7987ccaf0087)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#id-36055bb3-0a4c-426a-8f2d-d266ec1b452d)
    
*   [Using CT0](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#aadc7781-5fc2-413f-b9b2-8628ab137032)
    
*   [Using “any” pool](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#id-06903043-8bab-487f-b14e-77b2522fffd1)
    
*   [Backup tunnel selection process](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/rdm-w-frr-troubleshooting#id-9b9cadd3-06d0-465c-9be0-78c621af9a51)
    

Copy

    # OPTION 1
    #R6
    int tun100
     no tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 1 10000
    
    # OPTION 2
    #R6
    int tun100
     no tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 1 10000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 0 95000
    
    # OPTION 3
    #R6
    int tun100
     no tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 1 10000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 0 unlimited
    
    # OPTION 4
    #R6
    int tun100
     no tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 1 10000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw 95000

Copy

    interface Tunnel100
     ip unnumbered Loopback0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel destination 12.12.12.12
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 1 10000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name AVOID_R6-XR12_LINK

Copy

    interface GigabitEthernet2.562
     encapsulation dot1Q 3562
     ip address 132.6.12.6 255.255.255.0
     ip ospf message-digest-key 1 md5 OSPF_AUTH
     ip ospf network point-to-point
     mpls traffic-eng tunnels
     mpls traffic-eng backup-path Tunnel100
     ip rsvp bandwidth rdm bc0 100000 bc1 10000

Copy

    #R6
    int tun100
     no tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 1 10000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 0 95000|unlimited

Copy

    #R6
    int tun100
     no tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw class-type 1 10000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng backup-bw 95000

Copy

    #CSR8
    int tun0
     no tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 95000 class-type 0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 8000 class-type 1

# Basic SRv6 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/basic-srv6.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.over.ipv6.core.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.vpnv4v6.over.ipv6.core.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.vpnv4v6.over.ipv6.core.cfg

L3VPN for IPv4 and IPv6 is currently setup between all CEs. The data plane is currently not working - neither MPLS nor SRv6 are setup.

Using SRv6, enable these L3VPN services. Use 2001:db8:400::/40 as the SRv6 locator block.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/basic-srv6#id-73efc43d-d674-49da-96ff-5c285fbf6546)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/basic-srv6#id-46cf7ead-1723-4ead-b4c4-f9ab76aef7a2)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

SRv6 uses IPv6 in the data plane instead of MPLS. The SID takes the form of an IPv6 address instead of an MPLS label. Otherwise, all SR concepts are essentially the same whether IPv6 or MPLS is used as the data plane.

The SRv6 SID is composed of three items:

*   The locator
    
    *   Consists of a common ::/40 locator block among all nodes in the SR domain, and a ::/24 Node ID portion. This produces a ::/64 locator prefix on each node.
        
    
*   The function
    
    *   This is the behavior of the SID. This might simply be that the SID identifies a specific node, and the node processes the SRH. (This is an END SID). Or perhaps the SID is a “VPN label” equivalent and the function is that the PE should forward the packet in the customer VRF.
        
    
*   The argument to the function
    
    *   So far this is only used for EVPN multicast flooding. The agrument is the ESI split-horizon “label” which tells the remote PE not to flood to a particular multihomed CE in order to implement split horizon filtering.
        
    *   Otherwise this is not usually present in the SRv6 SID.
        
    

In SR-MPLS, we use the **prefix-sid index #** command under the loopback. This defines a prefix SID and the index into the global MPLS block for the MPLS label value. However, in SRv6, we instead define the locator ::/64 block on each router. Technically, in this lab we can do this on only the PEs, but to support abitrary path steering and TI-LFA, we should configure a locator on every router in the SR domain.

We then advertise this locator into ISIS (OSPFv3 does not support SRv6 yet) using the following configuration:

Multiple locators (up to 8) can be advertised by a node. However, every locator prefix must belong to the same ::/40 block. This is because this single ::/40 block will hold SRv6 locator prefixes for the entire SRv6 domain. Each locator can be associated with a flex algo. However, in this introductory lab, we simply use the default algo #0.

We can confirm the SRv6 locator prefix using the following command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZc2P0ti093fQLvpksBpU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9e01d56d-8f7c-409d-8112-4b10716f125b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=66face4026e50d5563319196c4ef43f4&sv=3)

The router advertises its ::/64 locator prefix into the IGP. This allows all routers in the domain to simply steer SIDs for each router using normal longest-match IPv6 forwarding. For example, on XR6 we see a ::/64 route for every other router’s locator prefix:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPcVAis7o511TBmv50DK8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2046bfd7-419b-4038-90e3-9fe0fc5127d8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=60c7c9331a17410683985036ec265310&sv=3)

This happens due to the LSP each router originates into ISIS. We can see several details here:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FCcmv3YiLT1KLUri3975D%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1c469eb5-c91d-4489-8eff-71d376b981bc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=52965596977f36bf0a368b4535983e91&sv=3)

Above, we see that 2001:db8:400:6::/64 is advertised as a regular unicast prefix. This allows transit nodes to simply forward based on longest-match routing, without needing to support SRv6.

Additionally we see “node maximum SID depth” values for various SRv6 encap functions. We also see an SRv6 locator TLV. This contains the ::/64 prefix and the End SID (which is like an SRv6 prefix SID). This End SID appears to support both PSP (penultimate segment pop, where the second-to-last endpoint removes the SRH) and USD (the final endpoint, XR6, removes the IPv6 header completely). Note that the block length is 40 and node-ID length is 24. This doesn’t appear to be configurable. Finally, at the bottom, we see an END.X SID (SRv6 Adj-SID). One is listed for every adjacency.

We can see each SID allocated by the router using the following command. The VPN SIDs (End.DT4 and End.DT6) will be discussed later in this article.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FyKhcH4r2d1HZIfLHgqlX%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd0f46a97-89e8-4534-ba10-151671923b62&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b7b4b0d9033975f3f02ae6c6c27f59ea&sv=3)

Instead of stacking MPLS labels to steer onto a path that differs from the IGP bestpath, you stack IPv6 destination addresses by using an SRH (segment routing header).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPzS4R47ytFWlPzHlFv5n%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddf60b25d-440f-40ee-a672-8968a2be9939&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=93de7b1ccfb34efc4183127773b540e1&sv=3)

The SRH contains the upper layer protocol (next header), routing type (SRH is type 4), segments left (a pointer to the active segment), last entry (an optimization for the router to quickly find where the optional TLVs start), flags and tags (both unused currently).

The segments are listed in reverse order. The last segment is index 0, and the first segment is the last index. The segments left pointer then points to the active segment. (i.e. if there are three segments, and two segments are left, the active segment is the second segment at index\[1\]).

As the SRH passes through the segments, the segment list is kept intact. As each segment is processed, the segments left field is decremented by one, and the IPv6 destination address is updated to reflect the currently active segment.

### L3VPN Services[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/srv6/basic-srv6#id-512e537f-e9e6-4e5c-a751-34bd723f0e86)

Now that we have the locator configured and advertised into the IGP, we must configure BGP L3VPN to use an SRv6 SID instead of an MPLS label. First we configure segment-routing srv6 under BGP. This appears to enable SRv6 for BGP in general. We can also set the locator at this level. Optionally, we can set the locator under the individual VRFs instead.

Under each VRF’s address-family, we configure the SRv6 allocation mode. (In MPLS, this would be the label-allocation mode). Our only options with SRv6 are per-CE and per-VRF. There is no per-prefix allocation mode as we have with MPLS. (We only have 2^13=8192 possible values for local functions, so per-prefix mode would not be safe).

Each PE now includes the prefix SID path attribute with the VPN route. This is a PA, not an extcommunity. For example, let’s look at the route for 1.1.1.1/32 on XR6:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F73otfzbIYu51hL3HucuO%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3bc5c60b-4fce-4f72-80ba-4ea3c227347b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cf697c30ba096b668f77cb80c7fccae4&sv=3)

The prefix SID attribute is type 5 which is L3VPN. The TLV has a SubTLV which is the SID information. This SubTLV contains the SID of 2001:db8:400:5::. However, this is only the locator ::/64 prefix. The SubSubTLV contains the breakdown of each component of the SID, and an offset for the function. This tells the router to take the received MPLS label and place it in the function portion of the SID. This cannot be seen in the CLI output. However, we see that XR6 concatenates 2001:db8:400:5 with 0x41 to produce the correct SID for this L3VPN route:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FcKvvyW4aiL0ppgFxDzLC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2301d4e1-0d40-4574-b5cc-50405cbaad2a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=482ac07dc8e83772dac73f4d5c3b36dd&sv=3)

The encoding of the MPLS label in the VPNv4 route appears to be off, because the MPLS label is 0x410, yet the function is just 0x41.

Note that the entire purpose of transcoding the function into the MPLS label is for more efficient BGP update packing. Since all NLRI sharing the same PAs can be packed into an update, this allows multiple L3VPN routes to share the same prefix SID path attribute with the SID as simply the locator prefix. Then each NLRI’s label field determines the function field of the SID.

The H.Encaps.Red means that the ingress PE acts as a headend and encapsulates the customer packet with an IPv6 header that uses a reduced SRH. A reduced SRH does not include the very first segment in the SRH as an optimization. Since there is only one segment in the SID list, no SRH is needed at all. We can see this on a customer packet sent from 2.2.2.2 to 1.1.1.1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFsd1IepjHg6rX4HHnXAG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dea981a59-4c9e-4a71-a4a6-12e48b10d117&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5e49921b554b62fd1269aecf28260dea&sv=3)

When XR5 receives this packet, it does a normal FIB look for this destination address. The FIB lookup points to a End.DT4 behavior, which means decapsulate and forward in the IPv4 VRF table.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FQU2blFypZRxtZeVJtE8Q%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D520814e7-bde7-4d3e-ac9d-408d2fa72cb9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5a922bd751365f93d3449e7df6ab6083&sv=3)

This process works the same for VPNv6 routes. We can see that XR6 receives MPLS label 0x420 and the same prefix SID locator block:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTgriceM1fvTYBoz0gzB0%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6e6f09ec-170c-437b-8bef-fba090d9e8e5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=939df1c0ed543164cf82703a86e5de17&sv=3)

The VRF FIB contains a SID-list of 2001:db8:400:5:42::

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F8qRXLPjhCXdpX1Fk4AdF%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da2f47a19-6f52-43a5-9421-4c88864c78cd&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bb8b3ce00bc4af11ae6ffe0c24f70df8&sv=3)

XR5’s FIB has a End.DT6 function for this entry:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FxiuguBdMdCbVsjniY9Du%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D78fe7dd6-3825-4278-ada6-94b16c9a2eed&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=facef9ac53e7b60e444d470bfa3739eb&sv=3)

# Traditional DS-TE | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/traditional-ds-te.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0Gd9sWDKxXy8ySsL1pI9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df96b55ee-1456-4181-8af1-e9252544df6f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0116fb454969d41059cf9c10dd953831&sv=3)

Configure basic DS-TE so that the interfaces along the two bidirectional paths, CSR8-CSR6-XR12-XR11 and CSR8-CSR9-CSR10-XR11, have 10 mbps priority bandwidth available as a subpool.

Configure two TE tunnels on R8 to XR11 that each request 8 mbps of priority bandwidth.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/traditional-ds-te#id-97c124e2-8e2f-446e-a075-1b16e48f0c98)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/traditional-ds-te#a3d50988-5b1a-47e8-b978-ab3764bf7ec8)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Cisco’s proprietary “traditional DS-TE” was created before the IETF version. With “traditional” DS-TE, you simply have one additional pool for bandwidth allocation, which is a sub-pool of the global pool. This means that any sub pool reservation also equally takes away from the global available bandwidth. Also, global bandwidth can use up any unused available sub pool bandwidth. For this reason, you would need to ensure your TE tunnels using sub pool bandwidth have a low setup/hold priority.

The sub pool is simply an additional pool that is advertised in the IGP along with the global pool. We can see these values using “show mpls traffic-eng topology.”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTEYCbEIlrQz9em0kr1g7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8053b5c6-7574-489d-9cad-3b3f0ffdc2fb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d82ea93da170b031907f4470eaeb9731&sv=3)

We assign the sub-pool using the following command on IOS-XE and IOS-XR:

A TE tunnel can only use sub-pool bandwidth or global bandwidth. It wouldn’t make sense for a TE tunnel to use both anyways, since using sub-pool bandwidth also uses up global bandwidth.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/traditional-ds-te#id-5efb3eea-a0b6-46e1-87f0-cbdc19c7be96)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We have configured two TE tunnels on R8, and each requests 8mbps of sub-pool bandwidth. This might be a LLQ pool in a real network. Because all interfaces only have 10mbps of available sub-pool bandwidth, the two TE tunnels must take separate paths.

On R8, notice that the two TE tunnels are using completely separate paths:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZywreUU9cI9BF3wwLNyI%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D90cc2519-980f-4127-9737-b359ea5d5fe9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=672b2df600300a3413404befe9bda85c&sv=3)

Additionally, we can see that the routers for which these tunnels pass through only have 2mbps of sub pool left at priority level 7. Also notice that 8mbps has been subtracted from the global pool as well:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0mlaNk8fe6J0tVyUxtAR%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dbc04ac89-e76f-416b-b035-3839b61225f2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=181cd358fe6e0f462e1cba6f4c2ec01a&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FupEstdKKwsS4XxniDg0s%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0b9f4794-591b-4c2a-8215-979d537aec99&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=40e9c631d97e8d273202e5dd61e8da31&sv=3)

A TE tunnel can request global bandwidth that uses up the sub pool. For example, on R8 we’ll configure a third tunnel that requests 991000 kbps. This can only be achieved over the IGP shortest paths if we can use up any unused sub pool bandwidth.

The dynamic path crosses over the XR12-XR11 link which already had 8mbps of sub pool bandwidth reserved. The third TE tunnel used up 1mbps of this remaining bandwidth:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhWPSEDrbRDS5RB2m3jFa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D77878557-3fc1-4f5c-b381-251f04a16275&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5915086278c5e095f72a7ab7b51d7469&sv=3)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/traditional-ds-te#a3d50988-5b1a-47e8-b978-ab3764bf7ec8)

Copy

    #CSR8
    int GigabitEthernet2.568
     ip rsvp bandwidth 1000000 sub-pool 10000
    int GigabitEthernet2.589
     ip rsvp bandwidth 1000000 sub-pool 10000
    
    #CSR9
    int GigabitEthernet2.590
     ip rsvp bandwidth 1000000 sub-pool 10000
    int GigabitEthernet2.589
     ip rsvp bandwidth 1000000 sub-pool 10000
    
    #CSR10
    int GigabitEthernet2.590
     ip rsvp bandwidth 1000000 sub-pool 10000
    int GigabitEthernet2.501
     ip rsvp bandwidth 1000000 sub-pool 10000
    
    #CSR6
    int GigabitEthernet2.568
     ip rsvp bandwidth 1000000 sub-pool 10000
    int GigabitEthernet2.562
     ip rsvp bandwidth 1000000 sub-pool 10000
    
    #XR12
    rsvp
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.562
      bandwidth 1 gbps sub-pool 10 mbps
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.512
      bandwidth 1 gbps sub-pool 10 mbps
    
    #XR11
    rsvp
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.501
      bandwidth 1 gbps sub-pool 10 mbps
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.512
      bandwidth 1 gbps sub-pool 10 mbps
    
    #CSR8
    int tun0
     description TUN1_TO_XR11
     tunn dest 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth sub-pool 8000
    !
    int tun1
     description TUN2_TO_XR11
     tunn dest 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth sub-pool 8000

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int Gi1
     ip rsvp bandwidth global-in-kbps sub-pool sub-in-kbps
    
    #XR12
    rsvp
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.562
      bandwidth global-bw rate sub-pool sub-bw rate

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int tun0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth sub-pool 8000
    
    #IOS-XR
    interface tunnel-te0
     signalled-bandwidth sub-pool 8000

Copy

    #R8
    interface Tunnel2
     description TUN3_TO_XR11
     ip unnumbered Loopback0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel destination 11.11.11.11
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 991000
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cbts-pbts.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.cbts.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.cbts.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.cbts.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Two tunnels are configured between CSR8 and XRv11, but there is no traffic forwarding setup for them yet. (No autoroute announce). Configure tun0 (”LONG\_WAY”) to forward customer traffic matching the default EXP values, and tun1 (dynamic) to forward traffic matching EXP=5. Test this from the CEs to verify that traffic is taking the correct path.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cbts-pbts#bfada3ba-74a1-4c34-b725-43abb4be754a)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On IOS-XE we must setup a master tunnel which has the **autoroute announce** statement and sepcifies the member tunnels. Additionally we must set the EXP mappings on the two member tunnels directly.

On IOS-XR we simply define the EXP mappings and use **autoroute announce** directly on the individual tunnels. IOS-XR calls this feature PBTS (Policy-Based Traffic Selection).

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cbts-pbts#id-3864b917-1b76-4424-aa08-7df183e9452c)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can use the command **show mpls traffic-eng exp** to verify the EXP mappings are configured correctly on CSR8:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FHC3MnloWAQD7dPLjmnwx%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd5f40d7e-26b2-4318-abcf-15b56b59f999&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f3e1ab0938f33a184ca6df36b7804270&sv=3)

CSR8 will show the route for 11.11.11.11/32 via tun100 (the master tunnel):

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FdCpFQTGPj9jxNJVAwI2t%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da5f04276-975b-49e1-bfaa-304930899a32&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=91a1251d0e677ff876b19eb27bfa1019&sv=3)

Note that IOS-XE doesn’t validate that EXP values are uniquely mapped to tunnels. You can overlap mappings. If that happens, IOS-XE just randomly picks which tunnel to use. This does give you redunancy though - if one tunnel goes down, you know the other tunnel will forward that EXP traffic.

To verify in the data plane, we would ideally traceroute with dscp values, but IOS-XR doesn’t let us do this. Instead I set the IPP mapping on ingress on CSR8.

First, traffic with no marking should go via tun0 which is the “long way”:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFj231TPJbexoMascyAoV%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D09c4ef04-2bfc-48c6-9abb-62cb1fcac380&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2a7f05337668f0f7e146bc07d1aff978&sv=3)

Next I mark these packets as IPP 5 on CSR8:

Traffic is now taking the more direct path which was calculated dynamically on tun1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fn7tXeqfa5nVcYBSk2dVS%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D98445c76-bc2d-4006-afc0-5207bc8816c1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=826ff9217d35ef70384471c4b0366f09&sv=3)

An easier way to do this is by using ping with the **type** option, and watching the output count on the individual tunnel interfaces. From XR14 we ping XR13 with no DSCP value.

We see the counters only increase on tun0, which is used for **exp default**.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FskmOKN1pYkvAWkjKHlAH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd0f25722-21c9-4adc-a2fc-b8c46d5f5856&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e7eb9941aece022565528b62f8826ad0&sv=3)

Now we’ll ping with ToS byte = 160 in decimal, which is CS5.

We see the counters only increase for Tun1. This proves that the CBTS is working.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FY05tQGC8BRlO0iVobdyD%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd8a2ae65-4165-4633-948d-45bab4d074bf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3d608cf1174645eaafa7aae2166389d5&sv=3)

Also note that the EXP value used for CBTS is after inbound modification, but before outbound modification. (This is logical when you think about it - CBTS happens after the packet is received and before it is transmitted outbound).

IOS-XR Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cbts-pbts#c71cda62-4071-4f41-a057-d3cb278bc7d6)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We cannot verify in the data plane on XRv11 using ingress marking. (Ingress marking does not appear to be supported on XRv, as it is a data plane function). However, we can try to verify using ToS on the pings.

First we can use show commands to verify the correct mapping:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FQmTWKmWyCe1SMoGBSCwv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df234789e-4022-4274-a6b2-6681116f6ef2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=add10f64fa7865d45adc7282de871ee1&sv=3)

Note that unlike IOS-XE, IOS-XR does not let you overlap policy classes. If you try to assign the same EXP value to two tunnels, you will get a commit error.

Also, when no tunnel interface has the default policy-class, whichever tunnel interface has the lowest policy-class number will also implicitly use “policy-class default.”

We can also verify PBTS in the FIB:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FGYZMVlAawwUlL2fbr9V8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6bceeaf5-9235-4551-819b-893c6e59a8cc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b614c10ee45417b21d7203426469335e&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrCBRjrhTDoGjJcrhZLR1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D74bd7c33-eab8-4c44-a1d9-3ffb3363e2c1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3fbd32a72bb6c589227ddaea036d4cfd&sv=3)

From XR13 we ping XR14 with no DSCP value.

We see that only TE tunnel 0 has hits, which uses **exp default**.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F8X4iAitS0x0Gh23cQxQJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcf136834-fa7d-4640-92af-0cd5c94d8f73&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=01cc18c7bec0711cc080f88a07055dd0&sv=3)

Let’s now set the ToS value to 160 (DSCP CS5):

Unfortunately, the TE1 tunnel counters are not incrementing. It appears this was supported in an older version of XRv which Nick Russo was using, but not this current version. Perhaps this works on XRv9K?

[NextTraditional DS-TE](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/traditional-ds-te)

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cbts-pbts#bfada3ba-74a1-4c34-b725-43abb4be754a)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cbts-pbts#id-3864b917-1b76-4424-aa08-7df183e9452c)
    
*   [IOS-XR Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cbts-pbts#c71cda62-4071-4f41-a057-d3cb278bc7d6)
    

Copy

    #CSR8
    int tun0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng exp default
    !
    int tun1
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng exp 5
    !
    int tun100
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel dest 11.11.11.11
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng exp-bundle master
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng exp-bundle member tun0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng exp-bundle member tun1
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng autoroute announce

Copy

    #XRv11
    int tunnel-te0
     policy-class default
     autoroute announce
    !
    int tunnel-te1
     policy-class 5
     autoroute announce

Copy

    #CSR8
    policy-map EXP5
     class class-default
      set ip prec 5
    !
    int gi2.584
     service-policy input EXP5

Copy

    #CSR8
    clear counters tun0
    clear counters tun1
    
    #XR14
    ping 13.13.13.13 so lo0 repeat 30

Copy

    #CSR8
    clear counters tun0
    clear counters tun1
    
    #XR14
    ping 13.13.13.13 so lo0 repeat 50 type 160

Copy

    #XR11
    clear counters interface tunnel-te0
    clear counters interface tunnel-te1
    
    #XR13
    ping 14.14.14.14 so lo0 repeat 30

Copy

    #XR11
    clear counters interface tunnel-te0
    clear counters interface tunnel-te1
    
    #XR13
    ping 14.14.14.14 so lo0 repeat 50 type 160

# Start | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/start.md)
.

These labs use Nick Russo's multicast topology from his SPv4 workbook. The labs are influenced from Russo's workbook, as well as books such as _IP Multicast, Volume I & II_ by Loveless, Blair, and Durai, and _Interdomain Multicast Routing_ by Edwards. The book, _Developing IP Multicast Networks_ by Williamson, is an excellent book as well for building a foundational understanding of multicast.

To begin, run the following command on your containerlab machine:

Copy

    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    containerlab deploy -t russo-spv4/russo-spv4.clab.yml --reconfigure

Once all nodes are started, run the following command to transfer the config files to all nodes. These files will be used to change between startup configs for subsequent labs.

Copy

    python3 transfer_configs_to_nodes.py

The script will prompt you for a directory name. Enter "russo-spv4".

Use the MTPutty session file located in **russo-spv4/russo-spv4\_putty\_sessions.xml** to quickly setup your SSH sessions to the nodes. Go to **Server - Import Tree** and browse for the file.

When you are done with the lab, use the following command to wipe it:

Copy

    containerlab destroy -t russo-svp4/russo-spv4.clab.yml

[PreviousMulticast](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast)
[NextTopology](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/topology)

# Profile 3 with S-PMSI | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-3-with-s-pmsi.md)
.

Load **basic.profile3.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:basic.profile3.cfg
    Y
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:basic.profile3.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure the core so that customer multicast traffic is only delivered to PEs that have interested receivers. In other words, only PEs that have (\*, G) or (S, G) state in the C-PIM for that group.

To verify, join group 239.20.20.20 on C2, and ping this from C1 with size 1400 and timeout 1. This will create a flow that exceeds 1kbps.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-3-with-s-pmsi#answer)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Even though we are now using BGP ipv4/mvpn with profile 3, the data MDT configuration is the same as with profile 0 in which data MDTs are advertised in the data plane (the default MDT).

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-3-with-s-pmsi#id-90f815e5-7517-44ad-9ceb-e76280ce2579)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Test by creating a multicast flow on either C1 or C2. Remember that XRv (PE3) won’t switchover to the data MDT or S-PMSI properly, but it will join it.

After a few seconds, PE1 will advertise the S-PMSI using a group defined in the data MDT range (232.1.100.0/24).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FcvpZrFh8gKTxqIiRzaPU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D20fa7b60-dbc1-4ff0-8683-ea07883f90d2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0e05fde2549da4f88ded5bd96f7f1d7e&sv=3)

Above is a route type 3 which is a S-PMSI AD route. The NLRI contains the customer source and customer group, as well as the PE’s loopback. Here are the details of the route:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FCzGcy9UeugX7BeO7YpsD%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddb096cf5-2c4e-4d1f-a7f2-6600f36554d0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=709470ca1b5b930d855698c601eeda82&sv=3)

*   Notice the tunnel ID uses a group ID of 232.1.100.0
    

We can also see this by considering the S-PMSI as a data MDT. We can use the same show commands as with profile 0, where the data MDT was advertised in the default MDT. Now it is advertised in BGP as a S-PMSI.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FnOwpcn8Qx1cZ3FaHS9Jd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddae16a7a-b489-48a2-9c9c-a477a8e9701b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=79611b525ee1c45ff8ece43a3d8b81b0&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXfTLn2WujGx19xWuwBWM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D10cabdcd-9028-465c-a1aa-03e1d6133504&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=497723df6dbcf4af809746fb872e4a92&sv=3)

The expiration is stopped on PE2, I believe because the route is learned via BGP. With profile 0 this expiration actually has a timer. But because we are advertising using BGP in profile 3, once the source stops sending, the ingress PE can just withdraw the BGP route to tear down the tree immediately.

[NextProfile 11](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-11)

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-3-with-s-pmsi#answer)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-3-with-s-pmsi#id-90f815e5-7517-44ad-9ceb-e76280ce2579)
    

Copy

    #PE1, PE2
    vrf def CUSTOMER
     add ipv4
      mdt data 232.1.100.0 0.0.0.255
      mdt data threshold 1
    
    #PE3
    multicast-routing
     vrf CUSTOMER
      add ipv4
       mdt data 232.1.100.0/24 threshold 1

Copy

    #C2
    int gi0/1
     ip igmp join-group 239.20.20.20
    
    #C1
    ping 239.20.20.20 size 1400 timeout 1 repeat 10000

# Profile 27 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.tree-sid.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.tree-sid.init.cfg
    Y

The CUSTOMER L3VPN is already fully setup. PIM is already enabled on the PE-CE links. CSR3 and CSR4 have joined SSM group (1.1.1.1, 232.1.1.1).

Configure XR9 as PCE for XR5-XR8. Use static Tree-SID to achieve mVPN forwarding for the CUSTOMER VRF.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27#de0e1a55-b6e9-4710-8b07-7c59042ff4b4)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-27#id-1c038675-8244-4b2b-b1ae-3fb35d5099f6)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Tree-SID is a new option for building the multicast distribution tree in the SP core. Previously, you would run SR in the core but need to also use mLDP, RSVP-TE, or P-PIM to achieve mVPN tree building. Now with Tree-SID, you can eliminate these protocols and use SR for the mVPN tree as well.

Tree-SID requires the use of an SR-PCE, because the PCE needs to program the LFIB replication entries on all nodes in the tree. In RSVP-TE you do hop-by-hop signaling. In mLDP, you also do a form of hop-by-hop signaling by advertising the mLDP FEC and an associated upstream/downstream label. In SR, we do not have any mechanism like this. Also, a simple stack of labels is not suitable as you cannot signal replication that way. So a PCE needs to be used to install the state on all nodes.

Keep in mind that when using SR-PCE for Tree-SID, _all_ nodes in the network that will be part of the mVPN tree must have a session with the PCE. Not just the PEs. This is because the PCE needs to program the state on P routers involved in the mVPN tree as well.

First we configure SR-PCE as normal. The PCE needs to receive the IGP feed somehow (distribute link-state or BGP-LS), and all routers must configure a PCEP session with the PCE. Additionally, this init file is missing the router ID necessary for the SR-TED, so that is added to all routers as well.

In profile 27, we use a static Tree-SID. This is configured manually, so this typically would not be used much in the real world. Also keep in mind that this only allows for one PCE to be used. (You cannot have PCE redundancy).

To start, we enable mVPN on the leaf PEs. Remember that we are not running BGP ipv4/mvpn. Instead, we enable mVPN using static sr-p2mp. The name of the static SR policy must match exactly on all PEs and the PCE. In this lab, we use the name “Tree-SID-Pol1.”

The root has a slightly different configuration. This is the ingress PE, which will forward the traffic down the tree. It does not set the static sr-policy under the multicast VRF config. Instead, it sets the sr-p2mp-policy under **router pim**. We configure the static group (1.1.1.1, 232.1.1.1) to use this SR-P2MP static policy. This means that customer traffic sourced from 1.1.1.1, destined to group 232.1.1.1, will be forwarded down the Tree-SID-Pol1 SR-P2MP tree.

Finally, the PCE defines the static SR Tree-SID. This contains a list of the endpoints (R7 and R8) and defines a policy that uses a particular Tree-SID label value. The policy can use different metric types and link affinities just like normal SR policies.

Note that at this point, you will likely see ROUTING-FIB-3-PD\_FAIL messages. This seems to be an issue with both mLDP and SR Tree-SID on XRv9K. I decided to silence logging to the console.

On the PCE we can verify the p2mp policy as follows:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFYrxgMEOE855bZfYpYmS%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6854dadf-4b50-471e-b724-0e6ef3af5104&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7e71af39a67c1e6a7b6293a708552258&sv=3)

Above, the output seems to be ordered as transit nodes first (R3 and R1), followed by ingress (R5), followed by egress (R7 and R8). Notice that R3 accepts incoming label 17001 and replicates the traffic to both R7 and R8.

A transit node also has this policy. This is why it is important that all routers have a PCEP session with the PCE.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FV5z0gHqYeOxBOjK3MunU%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D01ff5e81-f026-446a-ac4c-5f24122bd883&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=292b712e8822f2c1dcd5a3508090f708&sv=3)

Using the following command, we can see the SR-P2MP state on the PEs:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4pX8kLOPL7QxQ7LTJnSk%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D33fb6922-c81f-4c5f-afb0-04e797506cc5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b05e0a83fbede1bdc47342739659f55f&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FBvUpExOCug56SsBPoMCq%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da5c60252-e78e-4f8c-a40f-673c73bca228&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f54c7ff6dd30eb21c61120ece26cd2ba&sv=3)

Tree-SID appears to use underlying mLDP internal functionality, which might explain why both mLDP and Tree-SID give an error on XRv9K. (It also does not work on XRd). Notice that the LFIB entry refers to “mLDP” even though this is SR Tree-SID.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F84IZYxdIrJF5DhOsyGe6%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5dbe0148-bab6-4611-99e4-ef884c42cfbb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=fa8fb1e2b78f13915eb619ff4e259558&sv=3)

Another way to see this is to use the **show mrib mpls forwarding** command:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FmTpkjxBwuim92Oeo8DnA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8daf4240-d282-4bda-a85e-865a748c2aba&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=be9099154ffe7e5cc47d6874e2e49562&sv=3)

Unfortunately the data plane does not actually work. XR5 shows that it will forward received traffic out the mdt interface, but the counters are not incrementing despite generating the traffic on CSR1.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FwqUbk6akPYXJ5NTJ3RAy%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D80d51a76-4feb-4073-8d38-9215b9ec9c2f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=15e38d047bfc28ee584be8c7907ff873&sv=3)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The documentation says that the global Tree-SID label is specified from the SRLB range. So in our lab, it would probably be more proper to use a label in the 15XXX range.

Interestingly, there is a command to limit the range of labels that can be used for Tree-SID policies on the PCE. This is used for dynamically created p2mp policies via BGP mVPN, not for static policies. If you try to set the dynamic label range for a range that already contains a label used by an existing static policy, you will get the below error.

# Profile 29 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-29.md)
.

Load **top1.vpnv4v6.srv6.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load top1.tree-sid.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y
    
    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:top1.tree-sid.init.cfg
    Y

PIM is already enabled on the PE-CE links. CSR3 and CSR4 have joined SSM group (1.1.1.1, 232.1.1.1).

Configure XR9 as PCE for XR5-XR8. Use a partitioned MDT via SR Tree-SID that is signaled via mVPN.

[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-29#undefined)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-29#undefined-1)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-29#f263dd5a-2e2a-47ee-9f7e-5798cc3adc30)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-29#id-49cbff0c-0cdb-4c62-a898-2e3951ead399)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Profile 29 uses SR-p2mp policies with partitioned MDTs. This is the same as with profile 14, except SR p2mp trees are used as opposed to mLDP trees.

In partitioned MDT, each PE sources a (\*, \*) S-PMSI route. Only interested receivers join a given PE’s partitioned MDT. This makes state in the core more optimal. With default MDT, you have a full mesh of default MDTs at all times, even if there is no multicast traffic present. With partitioned MDTs, the p2mp policies are only created as needed.

Notice that all PEs participating in the VPN source a type 3 wildcard S-PMSI route:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVUP1lMw46iFxZgeengCl%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D576e448f-f972-456c-93b2-ba5c1945474c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4406916855b711397fcd032b4a962b6b&sv=3)

XR7 and XR8 have interested receivers for (1.1.1.1, 232.1.1.1). The source 1.1.1.1 is behind XR5. Therefore they wish to join XR5’s partitioned MDT. Each type 3 route has the leaf-info-required flag set. So XR7 and XR8 create type 4 routes to signal interest in joining XR5’s (\*, \*) S-PSMI tree.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvCE21zPrznGR3URJWh1H%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D75baa8af-8a0b-4e78-af6c-d4aa33f82654&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c7fbc68e966409d5d8d34dbee04650b8&sv=3)

Now that XR5 has interested receivers, it signals the p2mp policy at the PCE. Note that this is the only p2mp policy created at this point. This is what makes partitioned MDTs so scalable.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAeD34BXUJEd1m9EIWnCo%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dece64256-322d-47f5-bb59-3044222a1185&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2e3584952265ca30918c5ec2c2714186&sv=3)

Using constraints and FRR with partitioned MDTs is not any different from how they are used with default MDTs. You simply set the color and enable FRR on the partitioned MDT. There is no option for using an RPL as you saw with data MDTs, because this only controls the single (\*, \*) type 3 S-PMSI route.

Additionally, data MDTs can be used with this profile too. They work exactly the same way as we saw in the previous lab.

Further Reading/Watching[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-29#id-7f4b1578-725c-497b-ba0d-88a0c3a4deb0)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/routers/asr9000/software/asr9k-r7-9/segment-routing/configuration/guide/b-segment-routing-cg-asr9000-79x/configure-sr-tree-sid.html](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/td/docs/routers/asr9000/software/asr9k-r7-9/segment-routing/configuration/guide/b-segment-routing-cg-asr9000-79x/configure-sr-tree-sid.html)

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wgOke3amhDY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wgOke3amhDY)

A note on IPv6/MVPN[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-29#id-41b79060-40ee-40e8-8baf-782adaba89a4)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

IPv6/mVPN does not appear to be supported with SR Tree-SID. Perhaps this will come in a future version.

Flex-Algo[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn-sr/profile-29#id-67b44b99-1dd0-4460-b921-f9e0184a07c6)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Using flex-algo in the ODN policy also does not appear to work. But this seems to be a general limitation with PCE in general. As far as I know, flex-algo cannot be used as a constraint when the policy is delegated to a PCE. (**Update 10-17-24:** Flex-algo can be used as a constraint on a general PCE-calculated policy since version 7.3.1 I believe).
