Copy

    #PE1
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 mvpn
      neighbor 10.10.10.10 activate
    !
    vrf def CUSTOMER
     vpn id 100:1
     add ipv4
      mdt auto-discovery mldp
      mdt default mpls mldp 20.20.20.20
      mdt data mpls mldp 100 immediate-switch
      mdt overlay use-bgp
      mdt overlay bgp shared-tree-prune-delay 45
      mdt overlay bgp source-tree-prune-delay 60
    
    #PE2
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 mvpn
      neighbor 10.10.10.10 activate
    !
    vrf def CUSTOMER
     vpn id 100:1
     add ipv4
      mdt auto-discovery mldp
      mdt default mpls mldp 20.20.20.20
      mdt data mpls mldp 100 immediate-switch
      mdt overlay use-bgp
      mdt overlay bgp shared-tree-prune-delay 45
      mdt overlay bgp source-tree-prune-delay 60
    
    #P1
    mpls ldp mldp add ipv4
    !
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 mvpn
     !
     neighbor-group IBGP
      add ipv4 mvpn
       route-reflector-client
    
    #P2
    mpls ldp mldp add ipv4
    
    #PE3
    mpls ldp mldp add ipv4
    !
    router bgp 100
     mvpn
     add ipv4 mvpn
     neighbor 10.10.10.10
      add ipv4 mvpn
     vrf CUSTOMER
      add ipv4 mvpn
    !
    vrf CUSTOMER
     vpn id 100:1
    !
    multicast-routing add ipv4 int lo0 en
    multicast-routing vrf CUSTOMER add ipv4
     mdt so lo0
     mdt default mldp ipv4 20.20.20.20
     mdt data mldp 100 immediate-switch
     bgp auto-discovery mldp
    !
    route-policy USE_MLDP
     set core-tree mldp-default
    end-policy
    !
    router pim vrf CUSTOMER add ipv4
     rpf topology route-policy USE_MLDP
     mdt c-multicast-routing bgp
      shared-tree-prune-delay 45
      source-tree-prune-delay 60

    #IOS-XR

     add ipv4
      mdt overlay bgp source-tree-prune-delay 60
    
    #IOS-XR
    router pim vrf CUSTOMER add ipv4
     mdt c-multicast-routing bgp
      source-tree-prune-delay 60

# MSDP Flood Reduction | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-flood-reduction.md)
.

Load **inter-as.multicast.msdp.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:inter-as.multicast.msdp.configured.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:inter-as.multicast.msdp.configured.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FU9ZYiVlgS3njRBWgXPfj%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc65fda64-7f6e-442c-856b-0e0635a785f4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c9d394cadb725fd925c4d8d46524b323&sv=3)

MSDP peering is already configured. There is a partial mesh of MSDP peerings. CSR9 and XR2 are not MSDP peers.

Currently, CSR9 will reflect MSDP SAs received from CSR10 to XR1 and vice versa. This also happens on XR2. Find a way to eliminate this redundant flooding on these two routers.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-flood-reduction#b5185569-e955-4272-a421-16b792269abd)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-flood-reduction#db776639-0649-4c2b-a3eb-f813c27b06ab)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

MSDP mesh groups sort of implement reverse BGP RR functionality. All MSDP peers in the same mesh group are treated as in regular iBGP, in which an SA from one peer is not flooded to any other peers in the mesh group. The idea is that all peers are fully meshed, so any flooding would be redundant.

MSDP mesh groups are typically used within an AS for Anycast RP, however we can use it in this inter-domain lab to reduce flooding.

MSDP mesh groups are also useful for turning off the RPF check. The RPF check for each peer in a mesh group is completely disabled. This is allowed because an SA from this peer will not be reflected to any other peers in the mesh-group, therefore the loop prevention is forced in the behavior of update propagation, just like iBGP split horizon.

All SAs from mesh group peers are still reflected to any peers that are _not_ in the same mesh group.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-flood-reduction#a4c6d2ce-c9a0-4df8-a065-24c65f71348b)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Source traffic from CSR2 and notice that CSR9 does not reflect the SA message to XR1.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FYl9IvvYJxSf5A4sY3wjW%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D46929e33-3c8d-4fa0-833e-718e17989ac8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a441347accd29b4d51ccbe54e7b02612&sv=3)

Note that strangely CSR9 will show no “accepted-SAs” from CSR10 even though the SA is in the cache. My guess is that this is because RPF checks are completely disabled for this peer, and the “accepted-SAs” must reflect SAs that passed an explicit RPF check.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FIRptqXOHEo3wDXGoTzNJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db90e11d5-96f2-4b1d-8c46-2eb41ac94328&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c607ebf7596f2ef21ac857735d873940&sv=3)

We can see the same thing on XR2 but using a slightly different method. Examining MSDP stats we can see that no SAs have been sent to either peer.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FexBLoRD7AqjajtglDlvM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D34329539-c945-4ddb-814d-a7a44aebddd1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0d94aab6d8d9279edd69c13da5152cec&sv=3)

[PreviousMSDP Filtering](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-filtering)
[NextMSDP Default Peer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-default-peer)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-flood-reduction#b5185569-e955-4272-a421-16b792269abd)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-flood-reduction#db776639-0649-4c2b-a3eb-f813c27b06ab)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-flood-reduction#a4c6d2ce-c9a0-4df8-a065-24c65f71348b)
    

Copy

    #CSR9
    ip msdp mesh-group MG1 7.0.0.11
    ip msdp mesh-group MG1 9.0.0.10
    
    #XR2
    router msdp
     peer 7.0.0.11
      mesh-group MG1
     !
     peer 9.0.0.10
      mesh-group MG1

Copy

    #CSR2
    ping 231.2.2.2 repeat 3

# PIM-SM with Auto-RP | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-sm-with-auto-rp.md)
.

Load **multicast.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:multicast.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:multicast.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

*   Configure R2 and R4 to join (\*, 239.1.1.1)
    
*   Configure R9 and XR4 as RPs for 239.1.1.0/24 using AutoRP.
    
*   Both CSR9 and XR4 should be mapping agents as well.
    

Use R1 and R3 as the sources to verify that multicast traffic is working.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-sm-with-auto-rp#id-2bb9d40e-e047-4d91-b5e1-abdb9644fa49)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-sm-with-auto-rp#id-10991fe2-d9f9-40c7-9dd2-7cca2886f3dc)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Auto-RP was the first mechanism created to automatically propagate RP information within a domain. This was created by Cisco and is Cisco-propreitary. Auto-RP is not supported for IPv6, so in this lab we will only test IPv4.

In Auto-RP, we configure candidate RPs to announce their group mappings to 224.0.1.39. A candidate RP is configured as follows:

Mapping Agents listen to 224.0.1.39 to learn about candidate RPs. Mapping Agents then select the best RP for a given mapping (the highest IP address), and disseminate this information to 224.0.1.40, which all PIM-SM routers listen for.

For this to work, 224.0.1.39 and 224.0.1.40 must be treated as dense mode. By default, IOS-XR treats this as dense mode, and you can disable this using **auto-rp listen disable** under router pim. IOS-XE requires you to use the global command:

A common deployment model is to use the same routers as mapping agents and candidate RPs, however this does not have to be the case. You can separate these functions onto different routers. Also note that when you have multiple mapping agents, all will actively propagate RP mappings. This is not a problem though, as all mapping agents will use the same selection method and end up all relaying redundant information.

The default interval for candidate RP messages is 60 seconds. Likewise the default interval for candidate RP mappings from the mapping agent is 60 seconds. This can be changed by setting the **interval** on the command enabling the feature. The **scope** keyword sets the TTL on the packets. The **group-list** keyword can refrence an ACL to set which groups the RP announces its interest in serving. This can be used to facilitate better failover which we will see later. Also remember to enable PIM-SM on the loopback that is used for AutoRP messages.

An RP announcement to 224.0.1.39 looks as follows. The default 224/4 announcement is “positive” because a “negative” announcement can be used to indicate that a given range should be treated as dense mode. Dense mode is not even supported on IOS-XR, so we won’t explore this.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FNAIsS0WH4kAhrhjCQjwo%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6af5e459-6412-4901-974e-0471db32e147&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=30fbddc22e98fe119fb994c50678e221&sv=3)

The mapping agents will learn of all candidate RPs through these RP annoucements. We can see that R9 knows of both candidate RPs and has only selected R14 as the Auto-RP RP based on the higher IP address:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FalcffrpaYBlu2GznoJr3%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc97c6576-5dc4-49df-bb45-4744b1da186f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=315485c494237aaaf23076ed59c8addc&sv=3)

IOS-XR appears to only display the winning candidate RP:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FBbpmbXP0Eh3Sv51jB8Tk%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D60275ec5-8aca-499a-be8e-2618eac61e75&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=408d087c70079f346f4ca35e655eccf9&sv=3)

The RP mapping looks as follows. It is sent to 224.0.1.40 which all Cisco routers by default listen for.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6srcFT81Fv1uJ6ZN6WLJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D599c72c7-52e9-4740-a0e3-e3a5e4add724&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=22fe26d7f866603627ac9d9aafcf641f&sv=3)

We should see on any other router in the domain that it only knows of XR4 as the RP:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVTevrRDgElyslkkcRcbm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D5f436ae7-2900-4186-b551-20d8ba749cef&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d098a2aa8a0476a146ec065b291515ee&sv=3)

We can now test multicast traffic by joining a group on the listeners:

We see on the LHRs that XR4 is the RP for the group:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F1P4L7exiVhtYwgVO934e%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfde03edd-26a9-4ee8-b32a-5abeac7667a0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3c3ab1f6397c99c88a1296231295166c&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F9Yyuo8p1UZU1gXKQt6rx%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D42cc9055-20ab-4bdf-a811-35a89e0ea4cb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2ae5eaa93099b5660bf1a14919b91cc2&sv=3)

The distribution tree is now setup between the RP and receivers.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fg423Ydnogm2VzymdqFyh%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dde5fc530-63f3-42f7-8fa3-c50e9dbf88d6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=dba9f84f6d12f315b47601ff3d8d7570&sv=3)

The PIM register process works exactly the same as we have seen, so this is not demonstrated.

### Failover Considerations[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-sm-with-auto-rp#id-8c78d015-14e1-47fa-a8f6-dd354602e923)

Currently, we can say that we have an active/standby setup. R9 is also advertising itself as candidate RP, but it cannot be propagated because XR4 has a higher IP address, and both RPs are advertising the same group mapping.

Unfortunately, failover in this situation is very slow. Let’s see what happens if we shut down Lo0 on XR4:

At this point, no new RP distribution trees can be built, and no new sources can be registered. The candidate RP announcement on the mapping agents will time out in three minutes. After three minutes, the mapping agents will select the next best RP, which is 1.0.0.9 in this case. So total failure time is three minutes, which is quite unacceptable in today’s networks.

The expiration time for a candidate RP advertisement is present as the “holdtime” in the RP announcement. This is three times the interval. So to speed up convergence, we can alter the interval for the candidate RP announcement.

The holdtime that XR4 advertises is now 6 seconds:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhV4vxlvRL3qoVe0fh6yp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dea6d1533-41a7-4f5d-8f0c-a8220797ca00&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=63df6dfd36b454bdb2e52903d24572e1&sv=3)

The RP mapping on R9 reflects that XR4’s candidate RP status will always expire within 6 seconds. XR4 must continually send RP announcements every 2 seconds. These are dense mode flooded, so this is not the most graceful solution.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FkcPObl1lovA6NBTjau6j%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3ba5eaad-bc2f-4e38-9303-0f7a65604c20&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b11c0f39826e417a69529179f3a3d497&sv=3)

However, this does work to fix the slow convergence. If we shut down XR4’s loopback, all other routers will learn of R9 as the RP from the RP mapping after 6 seconds. The mapping agent will immediately send the new RP mapping when XR4’s entry expires, even if its own interval is slower (i.e. 60 seconds).

Note that there is no priority configuration on candidate RPs in order to select one RP over the other for an identical mapping range. The mapping agents simply use the highest IP address, which is a bit crude. There is also no way to do load sharing for multiple RPs mapped to the same range, as only one is selected and propagated to all other PIM routers. BSR solves both of these issues, which we will see in the next lab.

[PreviousPIM-SM with Anycast RP](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-sm-with-anycast-rp)
[NextPIM-SM with BSR](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-sm-with-bsr)

# UMH (Upstream Multicast Hop) Challenge | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/umh-upstream-multicast-hop-challenge.md)
.

Load **umh.challenge.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:umh.challenge.init.cfg
    Y
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:umh.challenge.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FkzbFbTIrIcF4OTtcncDQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8e08c8f1-3241-4dd2-bbce-a4a33c2d8018&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3513101caea3b0a2b9ce967a7e27d052&sv=3)

Profile 13 is pre-configured, and all customer routers are using PIM-SSM for the default range. PE2 and PE3 are originating a dummy 100.100.100.100/32 route in the CUSTOMER VRF. C1 has joined (100.100.100.100, 232.1.1.1).

The operator has noticed that PE1 is selecting PE2 as the upstream router due to the lower IGP cost. However, the operator has other routers in the network that are older and only support using the highest IP address as the tiebreaker. Find a way to fix PE1 so that it selects PE3 as the upstream router without changing IGP costs or influencing the BGP path selection for the unicast 100.100.100.100/32 route. Configure all PEs with this setting.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/umh-upstream-multicast-hop-challenge#id-5f54e3e8-fb31-4085-a029-7c669c73d676)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/umh-upstream-multicast-hop-challenge#id-7aa796ca-15d6-4a0e-a75b-43d4096c8eea)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

When a PE has multiple nexthops to a unicast VPNv4 address, it must make a decision as to which PE to “direct” the (S, G) type 7 route towards. The egress PE decides which import RT to place in the type 7 route, which controls which ingress PE will import the route and install the (S, G) state in the VRF MRIB.

It is important that all routers in the network use the same logic when selecting the upstream multicast hop (UMH). If some ingress routers choose different ingress PEs, there could be duplicate traffic in the network. By default, IOS-XE and IOS-XR choose the IGP closest PE as the UMH. This can produce duplicate streams in itself depending on the placement of the egress routers in the topology. It appears that IOS-XE and IOS-XR simply use the bestpath VPNv4 route to decide which PE to use.

Examine the current state of PE1. It’s bestpath to 100.100.100.100 is via PE2 because of the lower IGP cost to the nexthop.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FWbTOB3i7UQm9lvnotjcV%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D66996e94-15e6-4e19-9f1e-b2688ce89ee0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=82ee34298fafabfca28c92c73209763c&sv=3)

PE1 uses PE2’s MVPN VRF route target for the type 7 route that it generates based on the received (S, G) PIM Join from CE1.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FfsusP1F7xpZS4Z6CML6g%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfb9d734a-57c3-44e8-bf1e-9bc2902d016c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d5554b2dd518241dd3cf52908334217e&sv=3)

To make this more predictable, and solve cases where you don’t want multicast ingress PEs sending duplicate traffic, you can set the UMH decision to always use the highest IP address, regardless of the best unicast VPNv4 route. This is configured under the BGP VRF ipv4/unicast AFI on both IOS-XE and IOS-XR.

Notice that the VPNv4 route is still best via PE2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FQl5gzzJ9D2TNcIUB4vql%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc709e255-d06e-4fd6-a912-b6c7c2256517&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9546e33266132908cc812ca7a0b27cc4&sv=3)

However, now the type 7 route is generated using PE3 as the ingress PE, not PE2. This is simply because PE3’s loopback is higher.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Ftn4nkBxTl8LTh0P9AqHK%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D64b45d64-e2bc-4ba8-9477-91a61e1017cd&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d8a90c4082aaf3d4f4f534fd8ad9e19b&sv=3)

When all routers are configured for this setting, then only the PE with the highest loopback address will send multicast traffic onto the MDT.

[PreviousProfile 13](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-13)
[NextProfile 13 w/ Configuration Knobs](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-13-w-configuration-knobs)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/umh-upstream-multicast-hop-challenge#id-5f54e3e8-fb31-4085-a029-7c669c73d676)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/umh-upstream-multicast-hop-challenge#id-7aa796ca-15d6-4a0e-a75b-43d4096c8eea)
    

Copy

    #PE1, PE2
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 vrf CUSTOMER
      mvpn single-forwarder-selection highest-ip-address
    
    #PE3
    router bgp 100
     vrf CUSTOMER
      add ipv4 unicast
       mvpn single-forwarder-selection highest-ip-address

Copy

    #PE1, PE2
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 vrf CUSTOMER
      mvpn single-forwarder-selection highest-ip-address
    
    #PE3
    router bgp 100
     vrf CUSTOMER
      add ipv4 unicast
       mvpn single-forwarder-selection highest-ip-address

# Profile 19 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-19.md)
.

Load **basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg
    Y
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg
    commit replace
    y

The basic IP addresses, L3VPN, and C-PIM between the PEs and CEs is pre-configured.

*   Configure multicast VPN using unicast ingress replication in the core.
    
*   You cannot use PIM or mLDP in the core.
    
*   Use BGP for auto-discovery of participating PEs.
    
*   Configure PIM-SSM in the C-PIM.
    
*   PEs must form C-PIM adjacencies between each other.
    

NOTE: Profile 19 is not in the v5.1 blueprint.

See answer below (scroll down).

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-19#a54dc284-3ca6-4cff-9c35-8d01fef26a8a)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Instead of P-PIM or mLDP, we will use unicast ingress replication as the underlay. PEs must auto-discover each other using BGP.

Notice that we did not need to enable mLDP in the core. Ingress-replication uses the same unicast LSPs as unicast L3VPN. The difference is that the service label now represents multicast for the VRF instead of unicast.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-19#f899c1b0-d328-4aae-bb7f-ee7ec064af53)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ensure that each PE sources a type 1 BGP route. The details should show that the tunnel type is IR and that a label has been allocated.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FcXZsjqrAdloRDerViBPi%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D74d61af0-243d-49a7-b453-292481a139a9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a30323d8e7d6778be5713ec557ea7514&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FB9c1kaYRlTnFR6zNzVZJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dbfa6b522-0763-4dfb-9a06-d5d5e161cf8f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d3fdd0c7a49789fa84d1283a34acbc25&sv=3)

BSR did not work with this profile for me. Instead I enabled PIM-SSM in the C-PIM and joined a (S, G) on C2 for C1 as the source.

Traffic from C1 to 232.2.2.222 is encapsulated with two labels just as with unicast L3VPN. This pcap was taken on the Gi0/0/0/0 interface of P1.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FaizTiLoy2WBL0cakakAm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D49404d85-cdb3-41fa-8c65-efab5735b75a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=008b22fdb731bfbd476b2742e7dc3a69&sv=3)

*   24002 is P2’s label for 2.2.2.2/32
    
*   24 is PE2’s service label for multicast on the VRF. This was advertised by PE2 in the type 1 route.
    

Profile 19 does not appear to work on XRv. We can verify that XRv is receiving PIM Hellos from PE1 and PE2, but PE1 and PE2 do not receive Hellos from PE3.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fm9pL6d9gRJHMmDX8k76Z%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D32241037-56bb-4320-8c25-f81165cf98d3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ad11d98de06d341cdbaf2922aeb2441d&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FqLbGwni6RrEqfcnhiQcA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd31608f5-71e0-4789-966f-9906eda9bdb8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d6a76b09e1a6e0cb9c2a50c6df9258b1&sv=3)

Additionally, XRv will not send PIM Joins out the IRmdt interface.

Otherwise, the C-PIM works the same as we have seen before. The difference with profile 19 is that the default MDT is a collection of P2MP ingress replication trees.

S-PMSI[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-19#id-5a3d7827-2102-49d2-8a50-bcd5ffb6a2b6)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On PE1, configure support for data MDTs, or S-PMSI. C1 is the sender so we only need to enable this on PE1.

Start the stream on C1 and observe how PE1 advertises the S-PMSI.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzJckZjUk6Du5eLo56yYL%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Def3d8104-2196-4233-bc40-0bc69cb91052&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=eb756889066ab565640c1c275263a555&sv=3)

Once the data crosses the defined threshold, PE1 advertises a type 3 route (S-PMSI autodiscovery). We have seen this in previous profiles. This advertises the customer S, G and the usually the tree to switchover to. However, we have no P-PIM or mLDP trees in the core. So this just contains an annoucement that “I have a customer S,G I would like to optimize by only doing IR to interested receivers.”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOrRZ029iJl1tv75sHT1S%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1f0f1515-57d8-43db-9d8b-f5f721333a92&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=639933204b5b4ddb0df069eb6f58dafa&sv=3)

PE2 sends its own type 4 route which is a leaf auto-discovery route. PE2 is saying “I am interested in still receiving traffic for this S, G.”

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FERUMGPTEk03gHwlkj1Xa%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6f33980f-4364-4b98-9932-99e24b889a5d&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=59d5e824167c9fe8ad378dbfc87c91d3&sv=3)

The NLRI of the type 4 route contains the type 3 route that PE1 originated in brackets, plus PE2’s own loopback. PE2 includes its service label - the same label as seen in its type 1 route.

So the difference with IR S-PMSI is that the switchover occurs via auto-discovery of interested PEs using type 3 and type 4 routes. This happens with profile 19 even though we are still using C-PIM in the overlay instead of BGP as the overlay.

Copy

    #PE1, PE2
    vrf def CUSTOMER
     add ipv4
      mdt default ingress-replication
      mdt auto-discovery ingress-replication
    !
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 mvpn
      neighbor 10.10.10.10 activate

     add ipv4 mvpn

      add ipv4 mvpn

     set core-tree ingress-replication-def
    end-policy

    !
    multicast-routing add ipv4 int lo0 en
    multicast-routing vrf CUSTOMER add ipv4

     mdt default ingress-replication
    !
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 mvpn
     neighbor 10.10.10.10
      add ipv4 mvpn

# Profile 1 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1.md)
.

Load **basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg
    Y
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg
    commit replace
    y

The basic IP addresses, L3VPN, and C-PIM between the PEs and CEs is pre-configured.

*   Configure multicast VPN using MP2MP mLDP in the core. You cannot use PIM in the core.
    
*   C3 should be able to ping 239.1.2.3, with C2 responding.
    
*   CE1 is configured as the RP using BSR.
    
*   PEs should form C-PIM adjacencies directly between themselves.
    

See answer below (scroll down).

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1#c8ec0aef-4266-41fb-b964-b0a9b3a6f3e7)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Enable mLDP on the IOS-XR devices. On IOS-XE, mLDP is already enabled.

Configure the VPN ID on the PEs

Configure the default MDT to use mLDP and configure the root of the MP2MP tree as some arbitrary router. P2 is chosen in this solution.

On IOS-XR we must also enable multicast on the lo0 interface (in the global table) and fix the RPF check to use the mLDP core tree instead of trying to use PIM. We also must explicitly set the MDT source to be the loopback.

Join a group on one of the C routers and ping it from another C router. Ensure that you wait long enough for the customer RP to propagate to CE2 and CE3.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1#id-2899d207-77b9-484f-9443-f95a99f8c43a)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The mldp database on the root (P2) shows the local and remote labels for each directly connected neighbor.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fnx1OhCLob0BO5LPJcKN7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2d9de484-fdd5-49fe-a9f5-a5e348c5b532&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6562055a47660e41fe45e732086a1c0c&sv=3)

The default MDT using MLDP creates a MP2MP tree. This is analogous to PIM-BiDir, and for this to work, an arbitrary router must be set as the root of the tree, preforming a role similar to the PIM-BiDir RP. In this lab we used P2 as the root.

Each leaf advertises a downstream label out the RPF interface for the configured root. This is very similar to PIM, except the RPF neighbor is an LDP neighbor that supports MP2MP MLDP, not a PIM neighbor.

In order to create loop prevention, the root of the MP2MP tree creates a unique local label per incoming interface. This local label is installed in the LFIB with an operation to swap to all downstream labels except the interface for which this local label is associated. For example, local label 24006 is allocated for Gi0/0/0/1. This is installed in the LFIB with outgoing labels 24009, and 24007. This means that traffic received with label 24006 is replicated out Gi0/0/0/2 and Gi0/0/0/0. To control flooding, label 24006 is only advertised out Gi0/0/0/1, so it is sort of a per-interface label.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FHcphkM0UspmxbPgQ9K2x%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Daa4a7675-f45f-4515-8027-9b174c87dd2f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7b77cc92e9fd75b252b46767a4164991&sv=3)

P2 will forward and replicate any traffic recieved on any single interface out all other interfaces with the remote label. Notice above that P2 has no upstream neighbors since it itself is the root.

On P1, we see an upstream neighbor and a single downstream client (PE1):

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FouxPqtmui0Y4XBVGMzG5%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De85bf0bc-8d22-4411-adf6-126cd7cf5fc9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8bac7e223bfc757bce6fe9b1d3b454ab&sv=3)

The IOS-XE PEs automatically create Lspvif0 (LSP virtual interface) as a sort of tunnel interface. The source is lo0 by default just as with the GRE interface in profile 0. On IOS-XR this interface is called Lmdt<VRF\_NAME>. The routers will form C-PIM adjacencies over this interface. C-PIM packets are transported using the default MDT which is transported using MP2MP MLDP.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FdEAB9OpKr5VZWqP1dyEt%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6fd538cf-8612-4bbc-88d7-e49e12440fba&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0cf9f98f7c558cc6027382f86999cf3e&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F7bh7c6VMMkUT8rA0xEU3%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4ae7d750-93df-4969-b2ff-73c3c21ae4af&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=39b7e67f73f360fb0322b8fd0c812184&sv=3)

This virtual interface is used in the C-PIM mfib as well. On PE1, C1 is sending traffic to 239.1.2.3, and CE1 is the RP so it is receiving (\*, G) Joins for this group.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAHUomIBHi2Akv7Lzw8Ac%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8879ba54-5e41-49fa-9152-7356897f23c5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b295ad36118d5be11b5d708ff0f1dee9&sv=3)

On PE2, traffic for the (S, G) entry is incoming the Lspvif interface.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FNc7LE20xSsFZcLspCUA9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D570dc2c4-ebfc-4000-ace4-269d80e96450&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4598dfda3220a8ac15c295d2155850ef&sv=3)

Same for PE3. Traffic is incoming via the virtual interface.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4mQQZvWDJKmEMpR4U3VN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6d156f42-979e-4abc-aed9-73fca1c21127&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cf6c0f058aaeb9e417642ba8f34ef548&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzBH68WwY7BBWO9UjoMGb%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6d4b2fed-2cbe-4681-b7a1-4e81ff460472&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=aea415203b10e23bcd088ab369c72a67&sv=3)

*   A = Accept
    
*   EG = Egress
    
*   LMI = mLDP MDT interface, as opposed to the MI flag which is just MDT interface. LMI indicates “labeled” MDT interface.
    

A note on the IOS-XR rpf topology command[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1#id-04c59d5a-6e36-411c-93ed-f10c2c440485)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, IOS-XR only uses the unicast routing table for the RPF check. This works fine when you are using profile 0 (P-PIM) in the underlay, because the RPF check naturally uses unicast RIB, finds the RPF neighbor is a PE reachable via a multicast-GRE tunnel, and this tunnel is used as the RPF interface.

However, when we use anything other than P-PIM for the underlay/transport, we have to tell IOS-XR to look at this transport for the RPF check. The following config tells IOS-XR to use the MLDP default MDT for the RPF check.

We can see on PE3 that the RPF check for the customer’s RP is currently via the LMDT interface:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FDeAvLrsExcsZXgafFtyP%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6010540a-13cd-460a-bc8d-0e06b72e65d5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a6938a1742e67302aae1d45db129ea57&sv=3)

If we remove the RPF topology command, we see that the RPF check for the customer’s RP now resolves to null. The RPF check cannot be completed, because it is looking for a MDT tunnel (multicast GRE) in the P-PIM underlay to use for the RPF, which cannot be found.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVThcGbpIZK899fos1cwM%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2abe7166-66ea-4279-8038-47cb5aa2f14b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e45aba63937595d95f2971a7acc8a1fb&sv=3)

Note that we only see this output because we previously learned of the RP via BSR. Previously we correctly set the RPF check to use MLDP. If we forget to do this in the first place, the customer’s BSR message will fail the RPF check, and IOS-XR will never learn the RP. We would see the following output, because the **show pim rpf** command only shows active mappings from the MRIB. (In fact, this is what we see if we wait a few minutes and let the BSR information time out after breaking the RPF check mechanism).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F86yM0DHk5HrE9jptivx6%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc2db4dbd-faa4-49ac-9f0d-62ebf07b6bb7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cc2c1ef05b7d790d98729573c640c780&sv=3)

The C-PIM adjacencies will still be able to form, because the PIM Hellos are still sent out the LMDT interface and received in the LMDT interface, regardless of the RPF check mechanism. But PIM Joins cannot be sent due to no RPF interface, and BSR messages will not pass the RPF check.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPOCk3YcduEV9qOTlXA4s%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db2843fae-e2ea-429f-8d8f-ebbb18473ee9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=222f15d8961db88152817d0c1c6b6879&sv=3)

It is interesting that IOS-XE does not require this for any profile. Personally, I don’t see why this is necessary on IOS-XR, because it seems that the router should be able detect what we are using in the underlay the same way IOS-XE apparently can detect this. If we configure the default MDT for the VRF using mLDP, then the router should just use this for the RPF check. Unfortunately, this is not the case, and we must remember to use this **rpf topology** command.

Summary[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1#b4f9f87b-20a2-49b2-b3e4-675bdeaf1332)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is sometimes referred to as LSM or label-switched multicast. PIM is no longer necessary in the core, which is a big advantage. LDP is simply extended to provide mLDP capability in which a MP2MP tree is built in a PIM-BiDir fashion. An arbitrary root is selected, and participating leafs (PEs) initiate a branch onto the tree towards the root.

In mLDP, a single label can have an instruction to replicate and swap label out multiple interfaces.

The MP2MP tree is built by the PEs advertising a downstream MP2MP FEC towards the root. This is the label the PE expects to see when receiving traffic. It’s “downstream” because the root uses this label when sending downstream towards the PE.

The root then initiates a upstream MP2MP FEC out each interface leading towards a PE. This the label the PE uses when sending traffic upstream towards the root. This label is unique from how normal LDP operates, in which a FEC on a device has a single label per-platform. (For example, IGP prefix 1.1.1.1/32 has label X and this one label is advertised to all neighbors on all interfaces). On the root, a single MP2MP FEC now has multiple labels, one per receiving interface, so that loop prevention can be preformed. This ensures that traffic arriving via one interface is replicated out all other interfaces (except the receiving interface).

Additionally, these mLDP FECs have an opaque value which multiplexes trees built that are rooted at the same source. In profile 1, this opaque value is the VPN ID plus 0 for the default MDT, and some non-zero value for data MDTs (which we will see next). This value is “opaque” because it is only relevant to the ingress and egress PEs, not any transit LSRs in the path.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fw9lpOMoxZiVVYeD40AI8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D181a18a6-cb74-4cc0-b1c6-a8b45101c169&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0dd33d8621c6bfeff4b1dfe5364e66f3&sv=3)

*   Upstream MP2MP FEC advertised from the root of the tree

    #P1, P2, PE3
    mpls ldp
     mldp

Copy

    #PE1, PE2
    vrf def CUSTOMER
     vpn id 100:1

    vrf CUSTOMER
     vpn id 100:1

Copy

    #PE1, PE2
    vrf def CUSTOMER
     add ipv4

Copy

    route-policy USE_MLDP
      set core-tree mldp-default
    end-policy

      interface Loopback0

# IETF DS-TE with RDM | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/ietf-ds-te-with-rdm.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.base.config.with.ospf.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Configure DS-TE in IETF mode so that the interfaces along the bidirectional path, CSR8-CSR6-XR12-XR11 have 90M CT0 bandwidth available and 10M CT1 bandwidth available. Allow CT0 to use any unused CT1 bandwidth. Disable MPLS-TE on the R8-R9 and R8-R1 links, and on the XR11-R5, XR11-R10 links.

Configure two bidirectional TE tunnels between R8 and XR11 as follows:

*   One which requests 95M CT0 bandwidth at priority 0
    
*   One which requests 8M CT1 bandwidth at priority 7
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/ietf-ds-te-with-rdm#id-3f3f2ad2-d3bb-4312-a5c7-ef533089c1fe)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/ietf-ds-te-with-rdm#id-50153d54-1f23-47b5-9da0-b1237b7545ac)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Using RDM instead of MAM allows BC0 to use any unused BC1 bandwidth. However, BC1 can preempt BC0 LSPs based on priority. So a BC0 LSP will be preempted if a BC1 LSP wants to use this bandwidth based on priority. If the BC0 LSP has priority 0, and the BC1 LSP has priority 7, then preemption will not happen. Also, if both priorities are 0, preemption doesn’t happen. The BC1 priority must be _better_ (not the same)_._

Note that RDM is the default bc-model. For this reason, you do not need to configure the bc-model on either IOS-XE or IOS-XR. IOS-XE allows you to specify the bc-model, but warns you that this is now a hidden command.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FtpeoaPY7uBr0MDcrM9sQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D51b9c0bc-9d9b-4084-9104-a6a50f0b918c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=86eab07f1ca0afe5116c4649c6ca729c&sv=3)

The TE classes work exactly the same as in the previous lab where we used MAM. We can verify the pre-defined TE classes using **show mpls traffic-eng ds-te te-class**.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F9yrDxo2LHmB4O0XoOvGJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dde8cf3dc-3488-459d-913f-faebb875d6bf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6f78fec093c0c0bbcfee516ecd1a9fde&sv=3)

We can verify the bc-model by looking at the TED:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FahtvTF1kP8mPsfbyIORs%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6dcbe1da-3279-464e-abdf-d34910455ac5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=00b486ca213cf754305c9d3cf87603d0&sv=3)

Notice above that the max\_reservable value is now equal to BC0. It is expected that BC0 encompesses BC0+BC1. In RDM, you don’t configure a separate max reservable value on the interface, as we were able to with MAM.

So if you want 90M for BC0 and 10M for BC1, you could interpret this as BC0 = 100M and BC1 = 10M. Admittedly, this is fairly confusing. It’s difficult to know when you’re referring to _only_ BC0 or BC0 as (BC0+BC1). It is easier if you call BC0 = CT0 + CT1 and BC1 = CT1.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/ietf-ds-te-with-rdm#id-63aafdb2-2168-4e55-af3e-5a7bd1d343a7)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Let’s signal the first LSP from R8. This uses 95M of BC0 bandwidth. There is only 90M of BC0 bandwidth, so 5M from BC1 will also have to be reserved. This is only possible with RDM.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPO9lLFqbIx5DE9KdtWyG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4025a985-8273-45fe-8bfa-3618ab7e0f10&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=105579044365815f9f545aab2c4e0d11&sv=3)

We then configure a second LSP which requests 8M BC1 bandwidth at priority 7. There is only 5M available, so what will happen?

The answer is that the tunnel cannot be setup. Tun0 uses priority 0, so it cannot be preempted.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FLrVuW8P5F9sLl1e8DAQZ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D75fe3690-78a2-4b7c-9aff-71763dd0ccba&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=060c0c677b27d37dfb724b955edad362&sv=3)

If we change this to priority 0, still the LSP will not come up. Both LSPs have priorities of 0/0, so whichever was established first wins.

Only if we change tun0 to priority 7, can we get tun1 to reclaim its BC1 bandwidth. Let’s first shutdown tun1 and change tun0 to priority 7.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FYzPMu76mgvSKsW4mFC4J%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd0547cb0-48ea-435b-8c30-2995daf5e64e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=943598c9f3206d2c66baa5b1cf29dd1f&sv=3)

Now we’ll change tun1 to priority 0 and no shut it.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FWqVnRc8bVPEx41r5wrh8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De3b6704d-112d-42bf-a3f5-74f71c664792&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=828a3dfa3c7861103ba176a5b31bf0c5&sv=3)

Tun1 has successfully re-claimed its BC1 bandwidth, only because its priority was better than BC0. Essentially, you can remember that priority is always used to determine which tunnel is setup. The BC doesn’t play a role in preemption. Also notice that when BC1 bandwidth is reserved, it takes away available bandwidth from BC0. This is because BC0 = BC0+BC1.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFbW8t4ysVv28x4AGFmZg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db9e70435-76c3-4988-a7f2-539f1dbe6952&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9ada1d4707e7e60e1a3228b9df9965f4&sv=3)

Let’s setup the two TE-tunnels on XR11. First we setup Tun0 which uses 95M BC0 bandwidth.

Like we saw with R8, this LSP must borrow 5M from BC1 at priority level 0.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FgN6YDaTiqVL2RcIdZkBG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8d970886-28a3-4f79-88d9-facb69a39fc8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4a10c8c7d47d9ea6cdd4b525b046e5fd&sv=3)

We now setup the worse-priority tun2.

This tunnel cannot be setup.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FiMfkgxaWTw1ksgn1lCby%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D336d518d-806c-4ce4-afa6-5f6cb5a88f00&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8a0eae65d96d5dd0be86cc6be57bd72a&sv=3)

Only if we change the priorities around, can we can tun1 to preempt tun0.

Now tun1 has preempted tun0:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsJAQ42NpQsDCM3mXmWtn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4001af67-3a5a-4ec7-bb5c-621203a72b5f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=30b53886e21d8c0dc20061913f570b51&sv=3)

Copy

    #CSR8
    mpls traffic-eng ds-te mode ietf
    mpls traffic-eng ds-te bc-model rdm
    !
    int GigabitEthernet2.568
     ip rsvp bandwidth rdm bc0 100000 bc1 10000
    !
    int Gi2.589
     no mpls traffic-eng tunnels
    int Gi2.518
     no mpls traffic-eng tunnels
    
    #CSR6
    mpls traffic-eng ds-te mode ietf
    mpls traffic-eng ds-te bc-model rdm
    !
    int GigabitEthernet2.568
     ip rsvp bandwidth rdm bc0 100000 bc1 10000
    int GigabitEthernet2.562
     ip rsvp bandwidth rdm bc0 100000 bc1 10000
    
    #XR12
    mpls traffic-eng
     ds-te mode ietf
    !
    rsvp
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.562
      bandwidth rdm bc0 100 mbps bc1 10 mbps
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.512
      bandwidth rdm bc0 100 mbps bc1 10 mbps
    
    #XR11
    mpls traffic-eng
     ds-te mode ietf
     no interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.501
     !
     no interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.551
    !
    rsvp
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.512
      bandwidth rdm bc0 100 mbps bc1 10 mbps
    
    #CSR8
    int tun0
     description TUN1_TO_XR11
     tunn dest 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 95000 class-type 0
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng priority 0 0 
    !
    int tun1
     description TUN2_TO_XR11
     tunn dest 11.11.11.11
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 dynamic
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng bandwidth 8000 class-type 1
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng priority 7 7

    int tunnel-te0
     dest 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 dynamic
     priority 0 0

    !
    int tunnel-te1
     dest 8.8.8.8
     ip unn lo0
     path-option 1 dynamic
     priority 7 7
     signalled-bandwidth 8000 class-type 1

# RP Discovery Methods | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/rp-discovery-methods.md)
.

Load **inter-as.multicast.rp.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:inter-as.multicast.rp.init.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:inter-as.multicast.rp.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrFioSHXABSYMPH3IyKb4%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfe6b5705-ce73-42b5-8992-59bcd3d13b46&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a36b577a476ae4c4bf0772ce3a3c922d&sv=3)

Routing for IPv4 unicast and BGP IPv4/Multicast is already setup. Configure RPs in each AS as follows:

*   XR1 should be RP using AutoRP
    
*   CSR10 should be RP using BSR
    
*   XR2 should be RP using BSR
    
*   CSR9 should be RP using static
    

Configure filtering on the inter-as links so that BSR and AutoRP information does not leak to other domains.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/rp-discovery-methods#d51d5f46-5513-41a1-a2d0-225bdbc47fac)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/rp-discovery-methods#d01dcc56-78eb-4b06-8d82-3dd6a2d211e7)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

You should be familiar with Auto-RP and BSR on IOS-XE devices. If not, INE’s RSv5 workbook has good exercises.

On IOS-XR, you specificy the BSR using the IP address, not the interface:

On IOS-XR, the Auto-RP configuration is roughly similar. The Auto-RP groups appear to already be in the “listening” mode by default. The XRv forwards this in dense mode without any extra configuration.

On the edge routers in the domains running BSR, we must use the **bsr-border** feature to filter BSR messages in/out of the interface.

To filter Auto-RP messages, we must filter the multicast traffic for the group itself. Auto-RP is not a control message as in BSR (which uses PIM). We can filter the _contents_ of the Auto-RP message using **ip multicast boundary filter-autorp** _**ACL**_ on IOS-XE, but this command does not allow us to filter the messages altogether. Instead, we must use a general multicast boundary filter and deny the Auto-RP groups.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/rp-discovery-methods#id-2560fd14-012f-4523-b6a9-fe62e6c476b2)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Use the command **show ip pim rp mapping** on all routers to verify the correct RP is learned in each domain.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FK9EytyGeCyagdZTxMXrJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7d374d88-78b2-4c0b-9446-b6d3b63d1bd5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1de057e74c21b7a7b1ff3236360ccc13&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FofAyJZ49xlV7VGWjZE0m%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D04679188-d82f-4c55-bcaf-6778570d5ac6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=40e77641e201ee68140105f0718f1aa4&sv=3)

*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/rp-discovery-methods#id-2560fd14-012f-4523-b6a9-fe62e6c476b2)
    

Copy

    # AS 9
    #
    # CSR10
    ip pim bsr-candidate lo0
    ip pim rp-candidate lo0
    !
    int GigabitEthernet2.501
     ip pim bsr-border
    
    # CSR6
    int GigabitEthernet2.562
     ip pim bsr-border
    int GigabitEthernet2.569
     ip pim bsr-border
    
    # AS 8
    #
    # XR2
    router pim
     add ipv4
      bsr candidate-bsr 8.0.0.12 
      bsr candidate-rp 8.0.0.12
    !
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.524
      bsr-border
     int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.562
      bsr-border
    
    # AS 7
    #
    # XR1
    router pim
     address-family ipv4
      auto-rp mapping-agent Loopback0 scope 255
      auto-rp candidate-rp Loopback0 scope 255 
    !
    multicast-routing
     add ipv4
      int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.501
       boundary DENY_AUTORP
    !
    ipv4 access-list DENY_AUTORP
     10 deny ipv4 any host 224.0.1.39
     20 deny ipv4 any host 224.0.1.40
     30 permit ipv4 any any
    
    # XR4
    multicast-routing
     add ipv4
      int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.524
       boundary DENY_AUTORP
      int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.594
       boundary DENY_AUTORP
    !
    ipv4 access-list DENY_AUTORP
     10 deny ipv4 any host 224.0.1.39
     20 deny ipv4 any host 224.0.1.40
     30 permit ipv4 any any
    
    # R7
    ip pim autorp listener
    
    # AS 11
    #
    # CSR9
    ip pim rp-address 11.0.0.9
    
    # XR3
    router pim
     address-family ipv4
      rp-address 11.0.0.9

Copy

    # XR2
    router pim
     add ipv4
      bsr candidate-bsr 8.0.0.12 
      bsr candidate-rp 8.0.0.12

Copy

    # XR1
    router pim
     address-family ipv4
      auto-rp mapping-agent Loopback0 scope 255
      auto-rp candidate-rp Loopback0 scope 255

Copy

    # XR2
    router pim
     add ipv4
      int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.524
       bsr-border
      int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.562
       bsr-border
    
    # CSR6
    int GigabitEthernet2.562
     ip pim bsr-border
    int GigabitEthernet2.569
     ip pim bsr-border

Copy

    # XR4
    multicast-routing
     add ipv4
      int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.524
       boundary DENY_AUTORP
      int GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.594
       boundary DENY_AUTORP
    !
    ipv4 access-list DENY_AUTORP
     10 deny ipv4 any host 224.0.1.39
     20 deny ipv4 any host 224.0.1.40
     30 permit ipv4 any any

# PIM RP Troubleshooting | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rp-troubleshooting.md)
.

Load **pim.rp.tshoot.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:pim.rp.tshoot.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:pim.rp.tshoot.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Currently, R9 is the RP via BSR. The operator has been asked to configure R10 as the new RP, using static RP assignment.

The operator has configured R10 as a static RP and it has brought up its decap tunnel, so that looks correct. The operator has also configured R10 as the static RP on R5 and XR3. However, every group that R2 or R4 joins still uses R9 as the RP.

Explain the issue and find a way to fix it.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rp-troubleshooting#id-2c62c4cc-b258-461a-8417-c86cf3aed859)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rp-troubleshooting#aa4a733a-6e8f-4c84-877e-e42fbaa73370)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The problem is that BSR and AutoRP mappings take precedence over static RP mappings. This is somewhat opposite how static definitions usually work. For example, a static unicast route always has a better AD than any dynamically learned unicast route.

The command **show pim rp mapping** doesn’t show which RP is really in use.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fn27vtlrTwY6JcUJBy1Rw%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7304516e-1823-413c-875f-00138df14261&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f13206c29ad39afcf64b3572b5d9a32f&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FboK0vkPDHXF0T4HLJe0f%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D882397d7-36d7-4b0c-8f34-61c1a5817882&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=994a70c44c21d8ae627c94833caecc07&sv=3)

Note that on IOS-XE, using the **show ip pim rp-hash** command is not a way to verify whether a static RP is used. This command only shows the result among BSR-learned RPs. This command will always output a BSR-learned RP address no matter whether the **override** keyword is associated with the static RP.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhkA3CB5zf3bgINXJ3Tic%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da44d9196-7fff-4068-aba6-b16e6a5dbac5&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=20b06a393db3d3e396a0fa9fdceceac4&sv=3)

The problem can also be verified in the MRIB table. All ASM groups are using R9 as the RP:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Ftfz4yhOiEqL6BDrvpwGb%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc46c179b-685c-46b2-9512-e0af85cbbcc2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4be868a8c7bad1e3566b5542949e6d53&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fr9WxhnMLRZOXETc4PFje%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D89f6a65e-96d2-4108-9b48-da1491e6611e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=db11dcf101520b8fa943d604abaa4098&sv=3)

We must use the **override** keyword to force the static RP mapping to take precedence over dynamically learned RPs (BSR or AutoRP).

The PIM RP mapping output now shows that the static mapping has **override** on IOS-XE.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fk5sqzNWCLiUogHHE0ymr%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6f9ef89c-9787-461c-b9dd-5201fdf46f02&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=64147b2c5c590baeec7a14da1a8382d7&sv=3)

On IOS-XR, there is no **override** indication. The static mapping is now placed above the BSR mapping. I’m unsure if that is coincidence or because the static mapping is now taking precedence.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F3TFKU8LZHJLf44pukNMR%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddd6ef64d-072b-4812-b12f-fd77304cf8c9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cdd6c9e7d26c1ef8a3f2f831a7746fa0&sv=3)

We now see that MRIB entries use R10 as the RP:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPoypwApKPSVZkKSMrYVd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0e0613a1-9568-437f-b56f-dff4985a9af9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=333879cc5c33ad37e8cef2190b49b49a&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F0uVOjQNfkcJlsf6pHCLd%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcc5cc559-2b95-4ad2-be70-f9656b1bddc7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4e7015481682c3d0afe962a09b505b59&sv=3)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rp-troubleshooting#aa4a733a-6e8f-4c84-877e-e42fbaa73370)

    #R5
    ip pim rp-add 1.0.0.10 override

# SR/LDP Design Challenge #1 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/sr/sr-ldp-design-challenge-1.md)
.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FBmC0dt5np512LkKnkYZ7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D53aaed63-a79f-4d36-a748-af85cdbaba50&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=192f70a2bd90a46481c3019a5209fd22&sv=3)

An operator wants to build their network so that the core uses SR-only, and the edges use LDP-only. The edges are running on older hardware that does not support SR. Is an SRMS needed in this case?

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/sr/sr-ldp-design-challenge-1#id-8892946e-5b17-4ec1-86f2-053c7b7151ad)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Yes, an SRMS mapping server is needed within the SR-only domain. An LSP that has a destination of an LDP-only node must have an SR prefix SID within the SR-only domain. So the SRMS will advertise mappings for all LDP-only nodes.

[PreviousSR/LDP SRMS OSPF Inter-Area](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/sr/sr-ldp-srms-ospf-inter-area)
[NextSR/LDP Design Challenge #2](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/sr/sr-ldp-design-challenge-2)

Last updated 1 year ago

# Start | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/sr/start.md)
.

These labs were directly influenced from Ovi's SR course, and Filsfils' SR books. I highly suggest you go through the course and read the textbooks before, or while, doing these labs. You will notice that I made these labs based on ideas from the course and chapters.

Ovi's course: [https://www.udemy.com/course/ios-xr-sr-te/?couponCode=0C249BCDA6CC673E1720](https://www.udemy.com/course/ios-xr-sr-te/?couponCode=0C249BCDA6CC673E1720)

Filsfils' books: [https://www.amazon.com/Segment-Routing-Part-Clarence-Filsfils/dp/1542369126](https://www.amazon.com/Segment-Routing-Part-Clarence-Filsfils/dp/1542369126)

[https://www.amazon.com/Segment-Routing-Part-II-Engineering/dp/1095963139](https://www.amazon.com/Segment-Routing-Part-II-Engineering/dp/1095963139)

The lab topology is based on Ovi's topology used in his course. The nodes are all XRv version 6.6.3 nodes. There are minor differences in version 7.x, but not enough to warrant me re-doing these labs. If you learn SR with these labs using XRv 6.6.3 you will not miss out on anything. When doing final preparations for the real exam, you will of course use XRv9K nodes with 7.x.x (probably 7.9.2) and discover any minor differences. (The only difference that comes to mind is a different syntax for SR-TE static policies, plus some added support for newer features like the ability to include affinities for flex-algo. On 6.6.3 you can only exclude affinities, not include them.)

To begin, run the following command on your containerlab machine:

Copy

    cd ccie-spv5.1-labs/
    containerlab deploy -t ovi-sr/ovi-sr.clab.yml --reconfigure

Once all nodes are started, run the following command to transfer the config files to all nodes. These files will be used to change between startup configs for subsequent labs.

Copy

    python3 transfer_configs_to_nodes.py

The script will prompt you for a directory name. Enter "ovi-sr".

Use the MTPutty session file located in **ovi-sr/ovi-sr\_putty\_sessions.xml** to quickly setup your SSH sessions to the nodes. Go to **Server - Import Tree** and browse for the file.

When you are done with the lab, use the following command to wipe it:

[PreviousSR](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/sr)
[NextTopology](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/sr/topology)

Last updated 1 year ago

Copy

    containerlab destroy -t ovi-sr/ovi-sr.clab.yml
