# One-Hop Auto-Tunnels | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/one-hop-auto-tunnels.md)
.

Load **flash:mpls.te.onehop.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.onehop.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.onehop.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

Currently the network is fully operational with LDP enabled everywhere. However, the operator is concerned about outages due to link failures in the paths between CSR8 and XRv11. This includes routers R8, R9, R10, R6, XR12, and XR11.

Using MPLS-TE auto-tunnels, enable onehop tunnels and fast-reroute on these nodes. This will allow the operator to dynamically use MPLS-TE’s FRR capabilities without having to deploy a complex full mesh of TE tunnels. It also saves the operator from having to upgrade their equipment to run SR.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/one-hop-auto-tunnels#id-08d16195-d6d0-4f09-b56b-cb06d42498e1)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/one-hop-auto-tunnels#d3ae3a75-98d3-43da-805f-7db926791841)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Onehop primary auto-tunnels are a useful feature for implementing MPLS-TE FRR functionality without actually using a mesh of TE tunnels for traffic steering. MPLS-TE is simply used for its FRR capability.

The idea is that each router automatically forms a onehop tunnel with each directly connected neighbor. Every tunnel will simply have an outgoing label of imp-null. However, the power of this is that you can now protect this tunnel using auto-tunnel backup. The routers will only create NHOP tunnels (there is no NNHOP with a onehop tunnel), so only link-protection is achieved.

You might be thinking - what is the difference between this and just doing basic IP FRR using LFA? I believe the big difference is that you can achieve 100% link protection, because an explicit path can be signaled even if the underlying IGP backup path is not loop-free.

Let’s examine this on CSR8. It has four tunnels for which it is a headend: two that are primary onehop tunnels, and two that are backup NHOP tunnels.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F4M6lxqSNXYWbwNvjcFay%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da3313223-e8a7-4a13-afc8-05383b0d652c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=56a564e398c042d27f8b02a953730bd6&sv=3)

Let’s examine the tunnels to CSR6. The first, primary onehop tunnel, simply has an explicit-path which includes the outgoing link to CSR6.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FZ25FCqPuQGuRk0E5Uzmm%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D83e85b2a-941e-4f7a-9230-f8a198ec2112&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=98535fb0770e2eaefb33f661e9a421ed&sv=3)

We can see the derived-config of this onehop auto-tunnel. Notice that FRR is enabeld, no bandwidth is reserved, and autoroute is enabled. As far as I know, this can not be changed. If you wanted to change this, I believe you would have to use the auto-tunnel mesh feature and manually specify your nexthops as your directly connected neighbors in an ACL.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FwXLwPkSVStryedMUx9Nl%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dcac435a6-5845-4b8f-b5c2-7238db83c0cf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=53d34e799fddfb7657a2ec5da97b38ea&sv=3)

The backup tunnel that protects this onehop tunnel is shown below:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FIAGipqlWN8YDzHm1dkL8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd83667ec-fad6-4ab0-bebe-b83cd16f00a3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a8a68f166e84a6895516ecc6aed0a89e&sv=3)

Because this is a onehop tunnel, the router knows not to try to attempt to form a node-protecting backup tunnel.

Let’s now get into the configuration. On IOS-XE this is very straightforward. We enable the feature with a single command. We also must enable tLDP sessions so that LDP labels can be learned over these tunnels and pushed onto the stack when forwarding over these tunnels.

Additional features that can be configured are very similar to backup auto-tunnels, such as the unnumbered interface, timers, and tunnel range.

Remember to also enable MPLS-TE for the IGP and all interfaces. A TED needs to be built in order for the onehop tunnels to come up. But RSVP bandwidth does not need to be allocated for these onehop tunnels, so you do not need to explicitly enable RSVP on each interface. (RSVP is enabled by default by the **mpls traffic-eng tunnels** command under the interface. **ip rsvp bandwidth** is only needed to define the available bandwidth. Without this, a value of zero bandwidth is advertised into the IGP.)

Configuration on IOS-XR is much more complex. First, the onehop feature is hidden within the auto-mesh configuration. You also must specify the tunnel range, unlike IOS-XE. Additionally, we must specify options using an attribute-set. IOS-XE automatically enables autoroute and fast-reroute on the onehop tunnels, but this is not the case on IOS-XR. Finally, you must also remember to set the unnumbered interface globally!

Additionally, there is no way to dynamically enable LDP on the onehop auto-tunnels on IOS-XR. You can manually specify each dynamically created interface under LDP, although this isn’t an ideal solution. But it works.

Finally, enabling backup auto-tunnels is the same as usual. You must specify the range manually and then activate the backup auto-tunnel per-interface.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/one-hop-auto-tunnels#id-48859485-ce18-4747-b473-bd222c662940)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Let’s examine CSR9. We have four backup tunnels that are ready to protect four primary onehop auto-tunnels. There is one auto-tunnel for each directly connected neighbor: CSR8, CSR6, CSR10, and XR12.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOJF4JsfYHrXNoPyeKd0P%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1bb1b827-a348-4414-b511-8f55f3bc90b0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e5bea04056aa0f0f46d4ea3b55f48a42&sv=3)

Note that the order in which you apply the config might affect this. I activated the auto-tunnel features before activating MPLS-TE globally. This resulted in some backup-tunnels not working correctly. However, if you remove and re-add the feature, you should be able to get the output above.

Let’s enable RSVP Hellos between CSR9 and CSR10 and test failover.

We must also force traffic to take this path. To do this, we can lower the IGP cost of the CSR9-CSR10 link to 1.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhNKRb2RZGHjdYjYpTZ8O%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7952186f-3042-4ce5-a09a-1e25a3db18a9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d372ec16c94664a5d77c416df78e73f6&sv=3)

Now we can initiate an extended ping and watch for lost packets.

We see only one packet is lost. The backup tunnel on CSR10 will remain active indefinitely, however, the IGP will update routing on CSR10 to avoid this link now. So this backup tunnel is only used while the IGP is in the process of reconverging. The primary onehop tunnel uses an explicit-path that includes the link, so the onehop tunnel will fail to come back up until the link is restored. By default, the onehop primary auto-tunnel is never deleted. You can use the **timer** keyword to set how often the router checks for tunnels which can be deleted.

[PreviousFull Mesh Dynamic Auto-Tunnels](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/full-mesh-dynamic-auto-tunnels)
[NextCBTS/PBTS](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/cbts-pbts)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/one-hop-auto-tunnels#id-08d16195-d6d0-4f09-b56b-cb06d42498e1)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/one-hop-auto-tunnels#d3ae3a75-98d3-43da-805f-7db926791841)

# FRR Multiple Backup Tunnels (Link Protection) | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-link-protection.md)
.

Load **mpls.te.frr.multi.link.init.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:mpls.te.frr.multi.link.init.cfg
    
    #IOS-XR (XR1, XR2 only)
    configure
    load bootflash:mpls.te.frr.multi.link.init.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FyLlad9shzQz3I58S1lEV%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df411087e-9503-4707-bd0e-034c8b297329&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=11c6f3019e5f0252d810d8620ec4913f&sv=3)

There are two TE tunnels setup on the path CSR8-CSR9-CSR3-CSR2.

Configure CSR9 for link protection, using a different backup tunnel per primary LSP. One backup tunnel should use CSR9-CSR1-CSR3, and another should use CSR9-CSR10-CSR3.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-link-protection#id-01e75bfa-185c-45c2-a493-493b6cca99b8)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-link-protection#id-77dd6079-f5ba-4486-a2d7-f964de7f4ac7)

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

We saw in the previous lab that multiple backup tunnels can be applied to an interface. When multiple NNHOP tunnels exist, the router is smart enough to figure out which ones match which primary LSPs.

When multiple link-protecting backup tunnels exist, all tunnels have the same destination. So the router will load share each primary LSP among the available backup tunnels. This allows you to share the load among multiple backup paths incase one single backup path can not handle the load of all primary LSPs.

We can verify this on CSR9:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FlNcov7yc21rT2xqkPfLn%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D09e45b79-c65b-48c0-bdee-9a447f8acdd0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=6a66b955f821501ac893f5d5acf5a62d&sv=3)

[NextFRR Multiple Backup Tunnels (Backwidth/Link Protection)](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-backwidth-link-protection)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mpls-te/frr-multiple-backup-tunnels-link-protection#id-77dd6079-f5ba-4486-a2d7-f964de7f4ac7)
    

Copy

    #CSR9
    ip explicit-path name CSR9-CSR1-CSR3
     next-address 1.1.1.1
     next-address 3.3.3.3
    !
    ip explicit-path name CSR9-CSR10-CSR3
     next-address 10.10.10.10
     next-address 3.3.3.3
    !
    int tun0
     tunnel dest 3.3.3.3
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng 
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name CSR9-CSR1-CSR3
    !
    int tun1
     tunnel dest 3.3.3.3
     ip unn lo0
     tunnel mode mpls traffic-eng 
     tunnel mpls traffic-eng path-option 1 explicit name CSR9-CSR10-CSR3
    !
    int gi2.539
     mpls traffic-eng backup tun0
     mpls traffic-eng backup tun1

# PIM RPF Troubleshooting #2 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rpf-troubleshooting-2.md)
.

Load **pim.rpf.tshoot2.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:pim.rpf.tshoot2.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:pim.rpf.tshoot2.cfg
    commit replace
    y

CSR2 has joined two SSM groups:

*   (7.1.7.1, 232.1.1.1)
    
*   (2007:7:1:7::1, FF35::1)
    

CSR1 has joined two SSM groups:

*   (9.2.5.2, 232.1.1.1)
    
*   (2009:9:2:5::2, FF35::1)
    

When CSR1 pings 232.1.1.1 or FF35::1, it does not receive a response from CSR2. Explain the issue and find a way to fix it.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rpf-troubleshooting-2#id-1f8545ad-1580-4fa6-8c65-6a488792a956)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rpf-troubleshooting-2#c89ed287-a13c-4fb6-8fea-fb1ffd966a88)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Currently multicast traffic that uses R1 as the sender is not working. We’ll verify that we have (S, G) state for R1 as the source at the LHR, R5:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fa16TBjE1rnf1uTmDZaxv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8aca7976-f374-438d-9798-24fcbf4172fe&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=12284c17d2fd37fe192cbe93d7976530&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FOnSwVcMicC4nFdT0qtPJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd1020ad1-5fc8-4643-98a1-da8bf1bf8e33&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ce3c10cc5f43dfed38aeab05b7677183&sv=3)

Indeed we have state and have the correct RPF interface. We’ll next check R10, which is not shown, but also has the correct state and RPF interfaces.

Next we look at XR1 and notice that the RPF interface is wrong.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAudpkQKEfT7cdD8TuXT1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De48b9515-fcbe-4495-aa30-7fccee328c2f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b34c544273bef3a489136fa8f07e3c80&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FfQyBSmReVz6GS0TUoNmC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0cac8689-85b7-4294-95d2-72836d50e6b9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=aeb337ecd5a04e5101b80979627475f4&sv=3)

Note that a faster way to find the fault would be to run an mtrace from as close to the receiver as possible. This verifies where the break in the PIM signalling occurs. The syntax is <sender IP> <receiver IP> <group IP>. Notice that the RPF interface is creating a loop. R10 points to XR1, but XR1 points back to R10.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FAvy5C1BeKeqr3panVBTu%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D335a582d-bb6e-4a10-8049-52024ee7ca7c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5a2d10c71930ccc9650d7f83d358f52b&sv=3)

Looking at the RPF check on XR1, we don’t see many clues explaining why this is, except for the admin distance of the route. The admin distance is BGP (20) which gives us a clue that this may come from a multicast BGP route.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FC776Y2RKLIwZrJDfFwOk%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D41267a90-8c8f-4a88-a6a6-2268c59131a0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=93316866881edcb091cba743f592150f&sv=3)

As a side note, on IOS-XR, the **show pim rpf** command only shows the RPF results for entries that are actively in the MRIB table. To see an RPF result for any arbitrary source, you can use the command **show pim rpf hash** and **show pim ipv6 rpf hash**.

On IOS-XR, when the router enables BGP ipv4/multicast or ipv6/multicast, a multicast RPF table is created. This can be seen with **show route ipv4|ipv6 multicast**.

We see on XR1 that several BGP routes appear in this table, as well as a few OSPF routes which are inherited from the unicast RIB. This is very similar to IOS-XE’s **show ip route multicast**.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FRYCIWzlK45p2ddSlGwYO%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D11fcc9e7-488f-4f0c-8401-4383d98230f4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8d8a832bde2341b2999bc40348d3cea9&sv=3)

If we look at 7.1.7.1 sepcifically, we see that it matches a BGP route via R10:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fka4MsUhH6MvVDdLHUoDv%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D044cdd3c-8f3b-4261-b8a2-8d4070130563&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4dbc8ae6369a0378b3b3d45a467dc2a4&sv=3)

The reason this is happening is that XR1 and R10 are running BGP ipv4/multicast and R10 is redistributing OSPF into ipv4/multicast. Not only that, but R10 is setting **next-hop-self** on these routes as well.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FHdHsa0X0DEcy9MMtI6ks%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1dcb5c06-610a-4ba0-aaa0-102d75c627bf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=06b6a273e343f6c47be1af047ed63934&sv=3)

On R10, these routes are injected into the BGP ipv4/multicast table with the nexthop from OSPF. Even though R10 and XR1 are eBGP peers, R10 will not change the nexthop for routes that are reachable out the subnet used for peering. In this case, by default R10 will not change the nexthop for the routes that point to XR1. (This is called third-party nexthop).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FHmI7viAELv5wOitOZ1p2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7710ba29-c845-4ac6-b01d-6a014fb156a7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e15f9004cb32d35ac3f158ad84910701&sv=3)

However, R10 has the additional command “next-hop-self” which changes these nexthops to itself too. We can remove that so that R10 goes back to not changing these nexthops, which are essentially third-party nexthops.

XR1 now only has the routes for which it is not the nexthop.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FyWo0tZtIQQJR7a6DZCF8%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0f5bef09-7fac-4665-8bbf-e09e85ebb8c1&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2776734ab8c4a1cefb9766572f8cfdda&sv=3)

This is because XR1 rejects routes for which it is the nexthop:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F9EphM0LgM6MdL4KtXBOc%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1a522f02-4a28-47b2-81f4-5f16a99dae8c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0459b9561474e54ace6be29f262033b0&sv=3)

XR1 now falls back to the OSPF route for 7.1.7.1 and traffic works again.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fyoj1cy8cPpSdxAOprbGT%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc59406a0-dfdc-425c-a2d8-ee02e2aa104c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=dcd310c08463427569d91666cfa7d736&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FBSbcDhH7rY0fLRtKhItr%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8532a59a-ef1d-40a3-82a3-81681b3418e3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=881019080263063a86f806eee8522de0&sv=3)

IPv6/multicast does not appear to use this third-party nexthop mechanism. R10 is not setting next-hop-self on ipv6/multicast routes, yet XR1 sees all BGP routes with R10 as the nexthop. To fix this, the easiest way is to just turn off BGP ipv6/multicast or stop redistributing OSPF routes into BGP.

XR1 falls back to the OSPFv3 route and traffic works again.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2KDX6hLUHS6QWy7zXO5I%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dd4e4218f-56b4-45b8-957d-f7eb12e5fc25&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=b201bfb413b7ebcfc6525d5f4d53ddad&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FkdPJN1MmHDL5u3SPtYka%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D39731f8c-06c4-4dc2-b43d-b8fbeefeb632&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f7e0ea840f56eaf6db40e1c797cb6bd4&sv=3)

      no neighbor 10.10.11.11 next-hop-self

# PIM Security | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-security.md)
.

Load **multicast.anycast.rp.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:multicast.anycast.rp.configured.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:multicast.anycast.rp.configured.cfg
    commit replace
    y

R9 and XR14 are configured as Anycast RPs. Configure the following protections:

*   The RPs should not have more than 100 MRIB entries
    
*   The RPs should only allow Registers for multicast traffic sourced from R1.
    
*   The RPs should rate limit registers to 8kbps on IOS-XE and a maximum of 250 Register states on IOS-XR
    
*   The LHRs R5 and XR3 should only allow IGMP Joins to group 239.1.1.0/24. These routers should also limit the total number of IGMP group entries to 100.
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-security#id-3e6b567c-4544-4287-81f2-89830715f8f3)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-security#f3039371-26f3-47ba-ae69-ea0146cf985e)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The multicast group range is quite large (224/4). This presents an attack vector on the router. A bad actor can exhaust the resources on a router by creating thounsands of multicast state entries. To prevent this, we can limit the number of MRIB entries and IGMP entries.

Note that we can also set the maximum IGMP groups on a per-interface basis as well:

Additionally, we can limit which (S, G) pairs we accept Registers from on the RPs. This feature refrences an extended ACL, in which the first parameter is the source sender (not the router originating the Register, but the source itself) and the second parameter is the destination multicast group.

We can verify this is working by sourcing traffic from another router. For example, if R4 tries to send traffic, we will see that R9 is not willing to act as an RP for this (S, G) pair.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FUDks0vnDeVo9eeW5kuX2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dad49bf12-f0ec-4c1e-bbff-97764aa1ad37&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=1b39ccca08d96a7b36290b84c0960663&sv=3)

We can also see this on XR4 if we source traffic from a router such as R3. We use **debug pim protocol register**:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTz0hlJMctOQr90CJgnle%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0affb669-e649-4cf0-bc1b-42d678960895&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bbd4a0bba0def6967891eead289ff8ec&sv=3)

Additionally we can rate limit the Register traffic on the RP. On IOS-XE this is simply a pps rate limiter. On IOS-XR this is the number of Register states. I believe this is how many (S, G) pairs can currently be in the Register state. I am not clear whether this command actually belongs on the FHR.

Finally, we can limit the IGMP Joins based on the group address at the LHRs. This references a standard ACL that simply matches the group address. Anything denied by the ACL is not permitted as IGMP state on the LHR. Note that for IOS-XR, the ACL appears to be backwards. The source portion is really the group address.

We can verify that the filter works by trying to join denied groups on the hosts.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKgewqJL0jthLAWZFOgFg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D35d5420d-1835-4703-9d48-302a5025f2ba&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0777ef5e6e8dec98a0008ab7b1273909&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVgPfapx2CNmM6FgkdtYo%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da61a59ea-206d-40e2-83d5-c0c3f0bd5b59&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7ffef6907feda4442316a1d49654c29c&sv=3)

### A note on IPv6[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-security#id-95e813c3-0407-4cb3-95d9-dcf21ecf8c11)

IOS-XE does not appear to support limiting the number of IPv6 MRIB entires or rate limiting registers.

However, it does support **ipv6 accept-register list <ACL>**. It uses the same ACL format as IPv4, where the first parameter is the sending source address, and the second parameter is the group address.

IOS-XE also supports limit the number of MLD state entries and filtering MLD Joins. The filter for MLD Joins uses the source as the first parameter and group address as the second parameter.

IOS-XR appears to support everything for IPv6. Note that the IPv6 ACL syntax is flipped compared to IOS-XE. The group must go in the first parameter. (This is just like IPv4 IGMP).

[PreviousPIM-BiDir with Phantom RP](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-bidir-with-phantom-rp)
[NextPIM Boundaries with AutoRP](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-boundaries-with-autorp)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-security#id-3e6b567c-4544-4287-81f2-89830715f8f3)
    
*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-security#f3039371-26f3-47ba-ae69-ea0146cf985e)
    
*   [A note on IPv6](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-security#id-95e813c3-0407-4cb3-95d9-dcf21ecf8c11)
    

Copy

    #R9
    ip access-l ext ACCEPT_REGISTER
     permit ip host 7.1.7.1 any
    !
    ip multicast route-limit 100
    ip pim register-rate-limit 8000
    ip pim accept-register list ACCEPT_REGISTER
    
    #XR4
    ipv4 access-list ACCEPT_REGISTER
     permit ip host 7.1.7.1 any
    !
    router pim
     address-family ipv4
      maximum routes 100
      maximum register-states 250
      accept-register ACCEPT_REGISTER
    
    #R5
    ip igmp limit 100
    !
    ip access-l standard IGMP_FILTER
     permit 239.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
    !
    int Gi2.525
     ip igmp access-group IGMP_FILTER
    
    #XR3
    ipv4 access-list IGMP_FILTER
     10 permit ipv4 239.1.1.0/24 any
    !
    router igmp
     maximum groups 100
     !
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.543
      access-group IGMP_FILTER

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    ip multicast route-limit 100
    !
    ip igmp limit 100
    
    #IOS-XR
    router pim
     address-family ipv4
      maximum routes 100
    !
    router igmp
     maximum groups 100

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    int Gi2
     ip igmp limit 100
    
    #IOS-XR
    router igmp
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0
      maximum groups-per-interface 100

Copy

    #R9
    ip access-l ext ACCEPT_REGISTER
     permit ip host 7.1.7.1 any
    !
    ip pim accept-register list ACCEPT_REGISTER
    
    #XR4
    ipv4 access-list ACCEPT_REGISTER
     permit ip host 7.1.7.1 any
    !
    router pim
     address-family ipv4
      accept-register ACCEPT_REGISTER

Copy

    #R9
    ip pim register-rate-limit 8000
    
    #XR4
    router pim
     address-family ipv4
      maximum register-states 250

Copy

    #R5
    ip access-l standard IGMP_FILTER
     permit 239.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
    !
    int Gi2.525
     ip igmp access-group IGMP_FILTER
    
    #XR3
    ipv4 access-list IGMP_FILTER
     10 permit ipv4 239.1.1.0/24 any
    !
    router igmp
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.543
      access-group IGMP_FILTER

Copy

    #R2
    int gi2.525
     ip igmp join-group 239.2.2.2

Copy

    #R4
    int gi2.543
     ip igmp join-group 239.4.4.4

Copy

    ipv6 access-list ACCEPT_REGISTER
     sequence 10 permit ipv6 host 2008:8:3:8::3 any
    !
    ipv6 pim accept-register list ACCEPT_REGISTER

Copy

    ipv6 mld state-limit 100
    !
    ipv6 access-list MLD_FILTER
     permit any ff08::2/128
    !
    int Gi1
     ipv6 mld access-group MLD_FILTER

Copy

     permit ipv6 host 2008:8:3:8::3 any
    !
    router pim
     address-family ipv6
      maximum routes 100
      maximum register-states 250
      accept-register ACCEPT_REGISTER
    
    #XR3

     10 permit ipv6 ff08::2/128 any
    !

     maximum groups 100
     !
     interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0/0.543

# MSDP Filtering | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-filtering.md)
.

Load **inter-as.multicast.msdp.configured.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:inter-as.multicast.msdp.configured.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:inter-as.multicast.msdp.configured.cfg
    commit replace
    y

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FU9ZYiVlgS3njRBWgXPfj%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc65fda64-7f6e-442c-856b-0e0635a785f4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c9d394cadb725fd925c4d8d46524b323&sv=3)

MSDP peering is already configured. Configure filtering as follows:

*   R10 should limit the number of SAs from XR1 to 500
    
*   R10 should filter inbound SAs from XR1 that are not sourced from XR1 itself
    
*   R10 should filter inbound SAs from XR2 that are for group 237/8
    
*   R10 should not originate SAs for 239/8 to any MSDP peer
    
*   R10 should filter outbound SAs for 236/8 to XR2
    

*   XR2 should limit the number of SAs from CSR10 to 500
    
*   XR2 should filter inbound SAs from XR1 that are not sourced from XR1 itself
    
*   XR2 should filter inbound SAs from CSR10 that are for group 234/8
    
*   XR2 should not originate SAs for 239/8 to any MSDP peer
    
*   XR2 should filter outbound SAs for 236/8 to XR1
    

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-filtering#ff088f4f-9d3c-4452-84ed-2958d97ef886)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Pitfall[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-filtering#id-6a41dc02-81b5-4ee8-bfcb-0ba4e148319b)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

On IOS-XR there does not appear to be a way to filter (S, G) states that are “redistributed” into MSDP. Instead, we can apply a global sa-filter outbound. However, when you apply an outbound filter for a specific peer such as XR1, this will override the higher-level outbound SA filter. You must remember to deny 239/8 outbound for each peer that has an explicit outbound SA filter.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-filtering#id-66d1163e-e2aa-4ff1-bef8-7ad3e884e65f)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### CSR10[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-filtering#id-66d1163e-e2aa-4ff1-bef8-7ad3e884e65f-1)

Verify the SA limit for XR1 is set on CSR10:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2zgi3xA51hc5OatWIxbX%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D87aaeb28-759b-4f2f-bbfc-9e40db211a5e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=9b366a6f2af1e887bf745545bb986e88&sv=3)

Verify that SAs using any other originator-ID on XR1 are rejected on CSR10. For example, we can change XR1’s originator ID to 10.10.11.11:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6nG9Gfcv0z242BoJ75iS%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Ddc9855a7-1bf3-4874-bd67-fd3752a45dcf&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e64204b82c4f681f0649b8a20448a750&sv=3)

SAs from CSR9 that are reflected by XR1 should also be filtered out.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FVyUQGFDJNrOrwjS4p87O%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da6b3ed30-2866-4c29-b7db-e5baab0263cd&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=82742aca8d4edfade2e0c1a142020d86&sv=3)

Verify that SAs from XR2 for group 237/8 are filtered, but any other group is not filted. Ping these groups from CSR3 to generate the SAs on XR2.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFtAcdrVvqWXkLXxASXWJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dac49c94c-37b6-4bf1-824b-a7b76b305bec&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=41e9df67cc3fe0d7f9c346262e967e67&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fd0CLY8rdhKdXInRE0CbF%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D72559020-de5a-4e2d-ae28-30b092c12e4e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c14424aac5dee5b466a79d81c08a5d77&sv=3)

Verify that traffic from CSR2 to 239.0.0.0/8 does not produce an SA on CSR10, but traffic from any other group does.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FMB0tS6dWAAFvUC5GlYfA%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dba823b18-5904-4cf4-8f92-9f14656dd1d7&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=60412efb2c0503c1da88937ac799ec36&sv=3)

Verify that traffic from CSR2 to 236/8 creates an SA that is advertised to CSR9 but not XR2.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F8xzKsEqjSqEAPYigiKnD%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc0215802-1f8f-46e9-b6aa-d0fe36a94e46&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=32983457891ee8ba2a537d99606de479&sv=3)

### XR2[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/msdp-filtering#fb4a83c1-4bb4-4297-8e05-abf61a5d4114)

In IOS-XR there does not appear to be a way to display the max SA limit.

Verify that SAs reflected from CSR9 to XR1 to XR2 are rejected on XR2 due to the originating RP address not being XR1’s loopback. Currently XR2’s best path to CSR9 is via XR1 due to the best path to 11.0.0.9 being via AS 7. If CSR4 originates multicast traffic, we should see no SA state on XR2. The SA reflected via CSR10 is rejected for RPF check, and the SA reflected via XR1 is rejected for originator ID.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhTBu8NyoBT2dYQzGy5vV%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D0a0538f9-8ed1-4038-aa78-d6aa6eccddf3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3e37d53c9f6adf979ecca2bbe2ecd48b&sv=3)

Verify that traffic from CSR2 (which generates an SA by CSR10) is filtered for group 234/8 on XR2.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2hQ6BN9fERvMIMmhFOFQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1e390999-9cb9-4628-9a60-7e957019600a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2440f9ba8126fede5f1693992ca5702a&sv=3)

Verify that traffic from CSR3 to 239/8 is not advertised to any peers, but any other group is.

On IOS-XR, there doesn’t appear to be a “show advertised-SAs” command, so we can verify this on CSR10.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbtFdK3XWvPhb0XYu6a0o%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4b4ba096-55a4-4ed7-95fc-d7546ebb6da4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4d130e9a575df9af064266a180e88761&sv=3)

Verify that traffic from CSR3 to 236/8 is advertised to CSR10 but not XR1.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fre0BU1hXvepkjZDn66iZ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D67b1f664-d9e5-4bab-b9db-3708fbbd0ccc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=878ad54b2aba33419ddc107c3ed88e3a&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXWHwC1wwhcEepguTYlz7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dfc53872a-b904-4e6e-a029-d26bde0afe86&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8867b46f726479591234321e73af8493&sv=3)

Copy

    #CSR10
    ip msdp sa-limit 7.0.0.11 500
    ip msdp sa-filter in 7.0.0.11 rp-list XR1_RP_ADDRESS
    ip msdp sa-filter in 8.0.0.12 list XR2_FILTER_IN
    ip msdp redistribute list LOCAL_TO_MSDP
    ip msdp sa-filter out 8.0.0.12 list XR2_FILTER_OUT
    
    ip access-l stand XR1_RP_ADDRESS
     permit host 7.0.0.11
    
    ip access-l ext XR2_FILTER_IN
     deny ip any 237.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
     permit ip any any
    
    ip access-l ext LOCAL_TO_MSDP
     deny ip any 239.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
     permit ip any any
    
    ip access-l ext XR2_FILTER_OUT
     deny ip any 236.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
     permit ip any any
    
    #XR2
    ipv4 access-list XR1_RP_ADDRESS
     10 permit ipv4 host 7.0.0.11 any
    !
    ipv4 access-list CSR10_FILTER_IN
     deny ip any 234.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
     permit ip any any
    !
    ipv4 access-list DENY_PRIVATE_GROUPS
     10 deny ipv4 any 239.0.0.0/8
     20 permit ipv4 any any
    !
    ipv4 access-list XR1_FILTER_OUT
     deny ip any 236.0.0.0/8
     deny ip any 239.0.0.0/8
     permit ip any any
    
    router msdp
     sa-filter out list DENY_PRIVATE_GROUPS
     !
     peer 7.0.0.11
      sa-filter in rp-list XR1_RP_ADDRESS
      sa-filter out list XR1_FILTER_OUT
     !
     peer 9.0.0.10
      maximum external-sa 500
      sa-filter in list CSR10_FILTER_IN

Copy

    ipv4 access-list DENY_PRIVATE_GROUPS
     10 deny ipv4 any 239.0.0.0/8
     20 permit ipv4 any any
    !
    ipv4 access-list XR1_FILTER_OUT
     deny ip any 236.0.0.0/8
     deny ip any 239.0.0.0/8                  <------- Remember this
     permit ip any any
    
    router msdp
     sa-filter out list DENY_PRIVATE_GROUPS
     !
     peer 7.0.0.11
      sa-filter out list XR1_FILTER_OUT

# PIM RPF Troubleshooting #1 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rpf-troubleshooting-1.md)
.

Load **pim.rpf.tshoot.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:pim.rpf.tshoot.cfg
     
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:pim.rpf.tshoot.cfg
    commit replace
    y

CSR2 has joined two SSM groups:

*   (7.1.7.1, 232.1.1.1)
    
*   (2007:7:1:7::1, FF35::1)
    

CSR1 has joined two SSM groups:

*   (9.2.5.2, 232.1.1.1)
    
*   (2009:9:2:5::2, FF35::1)
    

None of this traffic is working. Troubleshoot the issue and find a way to fix it.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rpf-troubleshooting-1#id-4ab86b82-7ebd-48fe-863b-37791a64423f)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/multicast/pim-rpf-troubleshooting-1#id-65dde099-a6e8-42eb-84fe-beaa9c32d826)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As a first step, we can verify that the LHRs have the proper state entries. Each LHR should have the locally-joined (S, G) entries, and the (S, G) entries that were initiated from the remote receiver.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FEsPauC6wy5fH8bNWsl82%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De23b0ffd-fac6-4db3-ae1b-6bf123304ec6&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=62c6cdff81a56e9591d28cbfd009fb37&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrZK25EpYO6jA8KYGJCgP%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D7505e99b-30f8-4aaf-b4f8-d9f8110fd887&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=db3b35df991db702ace9451fee79eb56&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FtTVp8VNxYRDzh4w1WHsP%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D76e345e6-05a7-46e8-87fa-97a0010d223c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=50fecd74dbd5501dc7ac2031259323d8&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FORrIeRHV5gvnlbRskWJ1%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D94cbf9e7-1c36-4991-9565-6af25797df9a&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=bd28a591083d4cdd40eb8d73f27a659b&sv=3)

All we see are the locally-joined (S, G) trees, not the trees built from the receiver at the other end. This means that the PIM signalling must not be working somewhere in the path between R1 and R2.

Let’s go to the next routers upstream, R10 and XR1. We’ll look at R10 first.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F42JpzFywb6tPQoMbdyjB%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3112d69c-db50-4799-b975-3bb5799b47e9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f4f8c43e71656de6f79b63d6677382c9&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FaBVPegaXztGEeFFkSM9q%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D11d70ac9-ac5b-42bb-aa84-cb154e1c1ae0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=365d9b9ce106fc0d4640496f649ca480&sv=3)

Notice above that both entries point to the same RPF interface, which doesn’t make sense. Also, one entry has an OIL that is null.

Let’s look at the routing for the entries with the null OIL.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FFc9VTtrsBlBOrW2cNn2f%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D9d1c592f-c606-484d-a56c-9c30e94f3b83&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d870f4479848359bfb7b98f2d8e32424&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FIqNyjAZlt4zDxQAqrFzp%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db4f7debe-3d55-456a-8806-2d52f6822d89&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=0ea73d97c5e5ca1803bebd25765f5e1c&sv=3)

We see that R10’s unicast route towards the R2 source addresses and the RPF interface do not match. The output also tells us that the RPF check is using a static mroute.

We can further verify this by looking at the multicast RPF routing table. Notice that the IPv4 table is only populated with a 0/0 route and connected/local routes.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FrdZoEnfDl6io3yXi7YQH%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D642b4325-9d28-40bc-b55c-99ba8e441828&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=e4c30eafa7d853644b6fd8ebd2dc83bd&sv=3)

This is due to an interesting caveat with IPv4 mroutes. IPv4 RPF checks do not use a longest-prefix-match like you might expect. Instead, a static route overrides all longer-matches that are a worse admin distance.

Checking the IPv6 RPF table reveals that mroutes do not override longer matches. We can see a ::/0 static mroute, but all longer-matches are still present.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FsGbMOuP5fWJIFQW988eN%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D74b69f38-dcd1-4986-b2e6-fe8940eeb927&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=7fb3d99a936d26aa1e26a3962e332015&sv=3)

The ipv6 mroute giving us trouble is a /128:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fwu1Z4MTn9jkUKyjMwOML%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D660d04c7-3c97-406c-9465-f33eb3a859a9&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c804be05401437fc4e87450189513e55&sv=3)

Removing these static RPF routes will solve our issue:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FG2LM2nQLIlXOtclveV2i%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D1fc7c3a5-25a6-4aaa-9df1-472ec9065f0e&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=5a2b0ca0681df0c5124783fe6abdd2aa&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FtbdFrxp6pPkaXNLy7NT2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da885728b-2899-43b2-bb2e-20bf54d7b7bc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=76cf1eb4707d0ea793a9663c331fff86&sv=3)

Traffic sourced from R2 now gets a reply from R1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F5KAUpLf9BDL1wVf4feFQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Db6367bad-6985-4f48-b8ff-ba5194a77d19&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=8284c1145021f7c350af3dbe42a133a6&sv=3)

We’ll now move on to XR1. XR1 shows that the R1 source addresses have an RPF interface of the interface facing R10, which is incorrect.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FCvxmOAjEktXrCNF6swqg%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3De5999602-4035-41b0-a4f4-4a9f7733ca1f&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2085eb5c60fb44e1a350a3834e676eb3&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FPQZFUd3JuxmfHOl8UlDJ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D3a683919-80e6-4949-8efa-32826817a679&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=255a26915830c667b5c705f5774ff761&sv=3)

We can verify the RPF check on XR1:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FTYGfDlxQj4G1LCcrEWdC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4e344319-0705-4a0c-ba7c-5df609c1f141&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=64a020e188c60ac68a689af5df8341d5&sv=3)

A clue that this is wrong is that these are matched against host routes, while the unicast route match is a subnet:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FXlX0GHnrWnZiYbEKPF0V%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D97a20012-09c7-434e-8821-22f3a018ade8&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f3fcdbb9668a5ebff85b9a77de26641b&sv=3)

IOS-XR only allows host routes for RPF “mroutes.” These are considered static RPF entries. If we remove these, the RPF check should resolve to the unicast route again, and the PIM Join should be directed to R7 instead of R10.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6l3UoC9wH8orhjGn47lw%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D63ba949c-2118-445a-aff9-ace3a3f6461b&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a7281a7af8cf171b9f0e56c3c723b7f3&sv=3)

Traffic sourced from R1 is now getting a reply from R2:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F6eMslFvUkk4pGRfedOQq%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D633a4d71-5b5b-4a21-93b7-28b9469b8417&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=dfba396903e1f7ef1c710df5b066a158&sv=3)

In summary, the RPF static override routes behave differently on IOS-XE and IOS-XR:

*   For IOS-XE, the IPv4 RPF table uses admin distance instead of a longest-prefix-match. A shorter match but better admin distance overrides a longer match.
    
*   For IOS-XE, the IPv6 RPF table uses longest-prefix-match, which is more intuitive and more inline with how normal routing works.
    
*   For IOS-XR, a static RPF entry must only be a host route (/32 or /128). So there is no concern about longest-prefix-match behavior.

    #R10
    no ip mroute 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.10.11.11
    no ipv6 route 2009:9:2:5::2/128 FD00:10:10:11::11 multicast
    
    #XR1

# Profile 12 | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12.md)
.

Load **basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg
    Y
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg
    commit replace
    y

The basic IP addresses, L3VPN, and C-PIM between the PEs and CEs is pre-configured.

*   Configure multicast VPN using mLDP in the core using only P2MP trees.
    
*   You cannot use PIM in the core.
    
*   CE1 is predefined as the RP in the C-PIM via BSR.
    
*   PEs cannot form C-PIM adjacencies between each other. Instead use BGP for the overlay.
    

See answer below (scroll down).

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#id-17b2c3b7-405a-4e5b-adc1-dadcde43157f)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This is similar to profile 11, except we use mLDP in the underlay instead of GRE (P-PIM). Because BGP is used to learn of PEs participating in the VPN, a MP2MP tree is not required. BSR still works because the BSR message is sent down the default MDT that is rooted at each PE. Instead of a single default MP2MP tree, there is a default MDT for each PE for which that PE is the root. This is analogous to P-PIM in the underlay using PIM-SSM.

Also notice that there is no VPN ID necessary for the VRF. The FEC opaque value becomes an auto-generated global ID value.

Verification[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#eec5bada-6c7c-43e4-8461-7e5b8f98bc33)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Each PE will advertise a type 1 route that includes the FEC for its own default P2MP MDT rooted at itself.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FKF4dhoREFlRbYh7VJweh%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D538bdb25-0e09-4bef-a054-a406bbabbc08&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=be015a6e559706fd7781602ef61ce7ec&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FvjEOlGkDG8jUyotyILT9%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D23572229-df37-43ed-8346-e6ac1afbd008&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=2782dd8b3aa6df7ece06cb9d943ef423&sv=3)

The C-PIM BSR messages will be sent down this P2MP. Specifically, because the BSR is CE1, PE1 will send the BSR message out the default P2MP MDT rooted at itself.

There is no C-PIM between PEs. Remember this is BGP in the overlay instead of C-PIM. However, because of the bug mentioned in a previous profile, XRv will continue to send Hellos.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FzhEIiChYYmKsyUZE8EXQ%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D6ff4362a-7eed-4dc4-9a66-659f9a2d0acb&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=ae5066d78c3c6c28f85adb344167bd87&sv=3)

Any (\*, G) Join that a customer joins will be converted into a type 6 route, as we have seen before. For example, join 239.3.3.3 on C3 and verify that PE1 sees this as a type 6 route originated by PE3.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F7KTjLxWOUoENHX9u32QI%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D77752a83-5674-48fc-a28a-b73450fea1a2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=777122cf19071cb5d071fd1d94b3b2ae&sv=3)

When traffic is sent from C2 to 239.3.3.3, this should prompt a type 5 route (source active) from CE2, and a type 7 route (S, G Join) from CE3.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252Fbz7Zr1ZIrV9ilHBFJ0RF%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da758d3cd-abfb-4b5a-8812-7252ebdab805&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4ad0ad69c3d34b2dc27f5b5bbb9a0dfa&sv=3)

Theory[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#id-0c62df80-82cf-41ba-859f-d22b3ca62167)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Saying profile Z is “like profile X excepting doing Y” can become a bit confusing, so let’s breakdown each component:

*   Underlay: mLDP using only P2MP trees
    
*   Underlay discovery: BGP ipv4/mvpn (how PEs participating in the same VPN discover each other)
    
*   Overlay: BGP ipv4/mvpn (how PEs signal C-PIM state to each other)
    
    *   C-PIM converted to BGP route converted back to C-PIM
        
    
*   Data plane encapsulation: MPLS
    
*   C-PIM BSR works inter-site?
    
    *   Yes, BSR is sent out the data MDT as usual. The data MDT is just a P2MP tree instead of MP2MP. PEs join every other PE’s data MDT by learning about it via the type 1 route.
        
    

What happens when both the RP and LHR join the (S, G)?[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#d488037b-50f4-462b-bed7-cba727b64255)

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I tested joining 239.3.3.3 on C3 and pinging this from C2. What happens is that PE1 generates a source active route (type 5), and both PE1 and PE3 generate their (S, G) Joins (type 7). However, these two type 7 routes are identical from the RR’s perspective, so it only chooses one.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F8uMnLE8E7CMC35X9thit%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D4585b99e-025b-40c0-83a3-ee85ffa436a3&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c26b65b774af1334a69ee015160fb1f6&sv=3)

Which one it chooses shouldn’t really matter though, because they say the same thing: “Translate this into a PIM Join for (10.1.2.1, 239.3.3.3)” The originator does not matter. Both PE1 and PE3 are already joined to the P2MP default tree rooted at PE2, so they both receive the traffic. If PE2 switches over to S-PMSI, it will originate the appropriate type 3 route. So again, this route type 7 is just a PIM Join equivalent - nothing to do with the mLDP tree.

Reducing state in the core by omitting “mdt auto-discovery mldp”[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#id-93507b54-f966-4d3a-95e1-f47834ef3779)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

By default, a full mesh of P2MP trees is used for the default MDT. However, leaf PEs (which only connect to receivers and never connect to sources) don’t really need a P2MP rooted at themselves.

Let’s say that C2 and C3 are only receivers. We can omit the command **mdt auto-discovery mldp** under both PE2 and PE3, and everything still works. Receivers behind these PEs can join groups and receive multicast traffic.

In the core, you will now only see one P2MP default tree rooted at PE1. Likewise PE1 is the only router originating a type 1 route.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FElnyJSoUIDRNg5YkNZD7%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D33534168-9fb6-41cf-a11d-75f457b9bb50&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=34c871f387448307155b903a081ad6cc&sv=3)

Above, C2 has joined (\*, 239.22.22.22) and C3 has joined (\*, 239.33.33.33). Source 10.1.1.10 is sending to both groups.

Note that a better way to handle this is to use the builtin **receiver-only** knob. This works just as we saw in profile 11. IOS-XE omits the type 1 route entirely, and IOS-XR removes the PMSI attribute from the type 1 route.

[PreviousProfile 9 with S-PMSI](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-9-with-s-pmsi)
[NextProfile 13](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-13)

Last updated 1 year ago

*   [Answer](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#id-17b2c3b7-405a-4e5b-adc1-dadcde43157f)
    
*   [Verification](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#eec5bada-6c7c-43e4-8461-7e5b8f98bc33)
    
*   [Theory](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#id-0c62df80-82cf-41ba-859f-d22b3ca62167)
    
*   [What happens when both the RP and LHR join the (S, G)?](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#d488037b-50f4-462b-bed7-cba727b64255)
    
*   [Reducing state in the core by omitting “mdt auto-discovery mldp”](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-12#id-93507b54-f966-4d3a-95e1-f47834ef3779)
    

Copy

    #PE1, PE2
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 mvpn
      neighbor 10.10.10.10 activate
    !
    vrf def CUSTOMER
     add ipv4
      mdt auto-discovery mldp
      mdt overlay use-bgp
      mdt default mpls mldp p2mp
    
    #P1
    mpls ldp mldp add ipv4
    !
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 mvpn
     neighbor-group IBGP
      add ipv4 mvpn
       route-reflector-client
    
    #P2
    mpls ldp mldp add ipv4
    
    #PE3
    mpls ldp mldp add ipv4
    !
    router bgp 100
     add ipv4 mvpn
     neighbor 10.10.10.10
      add ipv4 mvpn
     vrf CUSTOMER
      add ipv4 mvpn
    !
    multicast-routing add ipv4 int lo0 en
    !
    route-policy USE_MLDP_DEFAULT
     set core-tree mldp-default
    end-policy
    !
    router pim vrf CUSTOMER add ipv4
     rpf top route-policy USE_MLDP_DEFAULT
     mdt c-multicast-routing bgp
    !
    multicast-routing vrf CUSTOMER add ipv4
     mdt so lo0
     mdt default mldp p2mp
     bgp auto-discovery mldp

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    vrf definition CUSTOMER
     address-family ipv4
      mdt auto-discovery mldp
      mdt auto-discovery receiver-site
    
    #IOS-XR
    multicast-routing
     vrf CUSTOMER
      address-family ipv4
       bgp auto-discovery mldp
        receiver-site

# Profile 13 w/ PE RP | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-13-w-pe-rp.md)
.

Load **basic.startup.config.with.cpim.and.bgp.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.and.bgp.cfg
    Y
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.and.bgp.cfg
    commit replace
    y

BGP ipv4/mvpn and mLDP is already enabled in the core.

Using profile 13 (MP2MP tree with BGP overlay and BGP AD), configure the core to only use SPT trees. A PE should never signal a (\*, G) type 6 route. Configure PE1 as the RP using BSR.

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-13-w-pe-rp#id-81a3769c-a763-47d8-ac0b-d257e9991fcb)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-13-w-pe-rp#id-9742b5ca-f8cc-43d7-8d98-7bf726b89efc)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Using the **spt-only** keyword on IOS-XE and **suppress-shared-tree-join** on IOS-XR causes the PE to never translate a (\*, G) entry into a BGP type 6 route.

This can be used to help scale the mVPN. In order for this to work, one of the PEs must be the RP. This is because the RP will receive PIM Registers for active sources and must generate a type 5 SA route to allow ingress PEs to learn of new sources in order to build (S, G).

First, verify that the CEs learn of the new RP, PE1. A common mistake is to forget to redistribute the loopback into the BGP VRF on PE1. If you fail to do this, the BSR messages will be denied on all routers due to failing the RPF check. (Also note, for some reason the last time I did this, I had to **wr mem** and reload PE1 for the BSR propagation to work).

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FThe3l5Y55Xqu6UTyYeKC%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dbb659622-53cb-4e0d-bbdf-37e5712a7e70&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=f3ce589b22436609743f065218732c69&sv=3)

Join an ASM group from C3:

PE3 installs this as MRIB state, but a type 6 BGP route is not generated.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FbBFaHEmJ92RIu0OBu4Az%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D01206d78-2fb0-4545-80e4-1ae49c55587c&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c6f17a763d947ad22a78ae316a41d6d9&sv=3)

The RP, PE1, therefore has no (\*, G) state. This helps for scalability, as there is no (\*, G) signalling in the core. (\*, G) states are confined to the receiver-site only.

But how does PE3 learn of an active source then? Let’s configure C2 as the source.

As C2 starts sending, CE2 unicasts a PIM Register to PE1. Even though PE1 has no receivers for this group, it still sources a type 5 BGP S-A message. This is analagous to MSDP SAs.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FEnZglz969Z5Q4a1c1Bai%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc007e749-1623-4069-b470-c1c553049e93&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4a0f7120102c28990adb59be6a6377ca&sv=3)

PE3 learns of the source via this type 5 route, and issues a type 7 route to join a (S, G) rooted at the source. We’ve replaced the PIM Register and SPT switchover process with BGP routes.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F1ZDTZ8aKpfXuG6lZGTOk%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D66277949-2159-4e40-9ac9-27031b844e15&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=a35f80705d372b39c5f00f767ad10627&sv=3)

Unforunately we don’t see any replies. PE2 is not actually forwarding the traffic onto the default MDT, despite having the Lspvif in the OIL. This appears to be a bug. **(Note 5/18/24**: This appears to be working this time. The Lspvif is 2 instead of 0.)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FhsFXtHW0qcuJf0pfLAPG%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Dc66dec3b-ee37-47cd-bf44-5e76da6e4033&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=3b0d251eb5925712f9ff9471dd432963&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FtqoJzgpX1M31uz1aTfsy%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D081da7ee-8ac2-4f2d-92ad-447c4ec828c0&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=4a212f3d043086bbf2e28c324c9df906&sv=3)

However, if we make PE3 the ingress PE, this works correctly:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FcsrKYWDs3YnJg405iwDX%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D2ae7143d-5b5c-46a3-8c72-c223cf3783d2&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=c33e84d7466f1b83d49b971b2db63c0d&sv=3)

What happens if the RP is in a customer site? (Not on a PE)[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-13-w-pe-rp#id-8d9a57a8-437e-481e-abfd-20fa920eb872)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

If the RP is in a customer site, traffic will not work if receivers are located in a remote site. The RP will never have any (\*, G) state, and will send Register Stops to the FHR of the sender. The remote site never learns of the active source.

However, if a receiver is present in the same site as the RP, then it would work. The RP in that case _does_ have (\*, G) state, so it joins a (S, G) rooted at the sender. This causes a type 5 route to be generated, which the remote site uses to learn of the active source and join the (S, G) tree.

# Profile 1 w/ Redundant Roots | CCIE SPv5.1 Labs

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/llms.txt)
. This page is also available as [Markdown](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1-w-redundant-roots.md)
.

Load **basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg**

Copy

    #IOS-XE
    config replace flash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg
    Y
    
    #IOS-XR
    configure
    load bootflash:basic.startup.config.with.cpim.cfg
    commit replace
    y

The basic IP addresses, L3VPN, and C-PIM between the PEs and CEs is pre-configured.

*   Configure multicast VPN using MP2MP mLDP in the core.
    
*   You cannot use PIM in the core.
    
*   C3 should be able to ping 239.1.2.3, with C2 responding.
    
*   CE1 is configured as the RP using BSR.
    
*   PEs should form C-PIM adjacencies directly between themselves.
    
*   Use root rundancy by configuring PEs to use either P1 or P2 as the root (whichever is closer) and failover to the other root upon failure of the primary root.
    

See answer below (scroll down).

Answer[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1-w-redundant-roots#f8b11738-db49-4bb5-a4bf-26c8a1231c75)

---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Explanation[](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1-w-redundant-roots#id-1ee1cb53-58e6-4874-a5a2-5bf0f84c63bc)

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In the previous lab, we statically configured P2 as the root for the default MDT, which uses a MP2MP tree. Just like with PIM-BiDir, the root of a MP2MP tree plays an important role. If P2 fails, the default MDT will be broken, C-PIM adjacencies will time out, and the customer’s Multicast L3VPN will be broken.

To provide redundancy we have two options:

1.  Configure multiple core routers with the same Anycast IP, but use a longer match on the one we want to be primary.
    
    1.  Only one mLDP MP2MP tree is setup at a time. During failover, a new tree is rebuilt.
        
    
2.  Define multiple roots for the default MDT. The primary MDT will be the one with the root that has the lowest IGP metric.
    
    1.  Both mLDP MP2MP trees are built, but PEs only send traffic down one tree at a time.
        
    

Using the second method produces two default MDTs, but only one will be used at any given time. To configure this, you simply define a second default MDT on each PE:

Note that all PEs must define both default MDTs. This is because different PEs will use different MDTs as the primary MDT, depending on which root is closer. So all PEs must join both MDTs to ensure they can receive all traffic on either default MDT.

On IOS-XE, we can verify which root is used as the primary. Traffic is only sent down this tree as long as the primary root is up. PE1 is closest to 10.10.10.10, and PE2 is closest to 20.20.20.20.

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FoCjWOUKNuTqtpTna5Xnj%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Df7c430ec-d2d5-4bcb-8a6e-d4470e54edc4&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=d7eea1fefdae790afd7ac093d2c9b332&sv=3)

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252F2NxNS6F0HeRYo6v3ZH4W%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D8e39db93-a6c1-4f09-b457-e147be5c8d00&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=00e41f72ff3dfb63d02883dd1a0396e7&sv=3)

(As a side note, the VPN ID is entered in hex, not decimal. This explains why the opaque value has 100 in it instead of 0x64.)

PE3 is also closest to P2 in terms of IGP metrics:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FqmSQN9CLbhZlbuGqsvS2%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3Da9e14af8-02de-43b5-8139-709c2b93fd36&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=88fa27d8baaa4815e5189329e50ed4af&sv=3)

If the IGP metrics tie, then the MP2MP tree with the highest root IP address is used.

If P2 fails, all PEs will detect this via the RIB and use P1. This can’t be easily demonstrated right now because the loopback we are using for the root is also tied to LDP. Let’s reconfigure the root to use new loopbacks. We can shut this loopback down to observe failover.

Currently we are not using data MDTs, so we can start a multicast ping on one host, shutdown a loopback, and observe how long it takes for the multicast traffic to reconverge. We’ll use C1 as the sender, because PE1 uses P1 as the MP2MP root. C3 as the receiver uses P2 as the MP2MP root.

We’ll shutdown Lo1 on P1. This will force PE1 to detect the change and switchover to using P2 as the root for the active MP2MP MDT.

Only one ping is lost:

![](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/~gitbook/image?url=https%3A%2F%2F3072390383-files.gitbook.io%2F%7E%2Ffiles%2Fv0%2Fb%2Fgitbook-x-prod.appspot.com%2Fo%2Fspaces%252FkUz2C3GqnZcWhoVL6jfk%252Fuploads%252FDaf8XU2kowVqOQEzl43y%252Fimage.png%3Falt%3Dmedia%26token%3D79262db2-dc44-4c44-b61a-0b060ceff0dc&width=768&dpr=3&quality=100&sign=cf7f65054f4f8fc2788663e86aef0d71&sv=3)

The downside to this method is that there are twice as many default MDTs pre-built and signaled in the core. However, the redundancy may be worth the trade off.

[PreviousProfile 1](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1)

*   [Explanation](https://ccie-sp.gitbook.io/ccie-spv5.1-labs/labs/mvpn/profile-1-w-redundant-roots#id-1ee1cb53-58e6-4874-a5a2-5bf0f84c63bc)
